speakerposition: topic
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I rise on a matter of privilege. I have on very few occasions indeed felt any need to call the attention of the House to anything that may have been said in the newspapers with regard to myself; and although during the last few days some of the newspapers in Toronto have been devoting a good deal of their valuable space to matters of a more or less personal character so far I am concerned, I should not have taken up the time of the House to say one word with reference to those matters but for a statement which I find in the Toronto ' World ' of yesterday morning. The statement, which is at the end of several columns dealing with matters of the description to which I have alluded, is worded in this way :
A lawyer said that there was dissatisfaction imong legal men because the Minister of

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Justice has given so much work to G. I1'. Shepley, K.C., and the firm with which he himself was formerly connected.
With respect to Mr. Shepley I have nothing to say except that in regard' to any work which as Minister of Justice I have sent to him, I have been guided wholly and entirely by the identical business principles upon which I think any business man would have acted. Legal work of important character on behalf of the government has been sent to Mr. Shepley since I have been Minister of Justice, has been freely sent to him, because with a knowledge of Mr. Shepley extending now over more than 35 years, and with a considerable knowledge of the legal practitioners of Ontario, I have thought that that work would be better attended to by him than it would probably be by any other legal gentleman of the province within my acquaintance. With that portion of the statement which I have read I am not in any degree concerned. But with reference to the remainder of the statement, by which it is charged that since I have been Minister of Justice I have sent a large amount of work to the firm with which I myself was formerly connected, I want to say first that since I have been a member of this House and from the day I became a member of this House I have had no manner of financial interest in the earnings of that firin. I have a natural interest in the success of that firm certainly, not only on account of former associations during the whole period of my professional life, but also because my son is now and has been for a few years a member of that firm. But with reference to the principal matter contained in this newspaper statement, namely, that I have taken advantage of my position as Minister of Justice to send legal work to that firm, I wish to say that there is not one word of truth in it, and that, although prior to my becoming a member of this House, that firm, with which I was then connected, received a very considerable amount nearly every year for the doing of public business for the government, from the day when I became Minister of Justice not one dollar's worth of legal work has been sent to that firm by me or by any department of the government so far as I am aware.

Mr. Speaker, last night the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) asked certain questions which I was not able to answer at the' time, regarding certain grievances, which I may mention as follows :	Over
classification of grades; the necessity for sufficient registration of terminal elevators; the necessity of preventing the eliminating of competition by terminal elevators and Mr. AYLESWORTH.
other elevators; the further elimination of competition by the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk Pacific railways leasing their terminal facilities to alien interests. He said :
The government purposes to apply some remedy in an indifferent way to one of these grievances. I would like to ask the members of the government who were present at that interview why it is that the application of a remedy to the other three grievances is being deferred by the government?
In reply, I beg to say that I was in the office of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when Messrs. McKenzie and Hen-ders, representing the Western Grain Growers Association, were there for the purpose of presenting their views regarding possible improvements in grain trade conditions. If I remember correctly the securing of amending .legislation was not the chief purpose of their representations. As I understood it was not so much to advise as to legislation as to suggest to the government the propriety of removing the lake front elevators from operation by persons or companies who were traders _ in grain; preferably to secure their operation by the government. The government has had the suggestion under careful consideration, but it was felt that the matter was one of such importance as to require more full and careful consideration than could be given it in order to reach a satisfactory decision before the close of the present session. On the first paragraph:
The committee have carefully considered the present rules of the House and have agreed to certain amendments and additions to the same, which they beg leave to 6ubmit herewith.
1.	That present rules Nos. 73, 74 and 75 be cancelled and the following substituted therefor :

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
A petition to the House may be presented by a member at any time during the sitting of the House by filing the same with the Clerk of the House.
Petitions presented before I p.m. on any day shall be entered in the Votes and Proceedings of that day. Petitions presented after 4 p.m. are to be entered in the Votes and Proceedings of the next day.
Any member desiring to present a petition in his place in the House must do so during routine proceedings and before introduction of Bills.
On the presentation of a petition no debate on or in relation to the same shall be allowed.
Members presenting petitions shall be answerable that they do not contain impertinent or improper matter.
Every member presenting a petition shall endorse his name thereon.
Petitions may be either written or printed; provided always that when there are three or more petitioners the signatures of at least three petitioners shall be subscribed on the sheet containing the prayer of the petition.
On the next day following the presentation of a petition the Clerk of the House shall lay upon the table the report of the Clerk of 265J
1 etitions upon the petitions presented and such report shall be printed in the votes and proceedings of that day. Every petition so reported upon, not containing matter in breach of the privileges of this House and which, according to the rules or practice of this House, can be received, shall be deemed to be read and received.
No debate shall be permitted on the report but a petition referred to therein may be read by the Clerk of the House at the table, if required; or if it complain of some present personal grievance requiring an immediate remedy, the matter contained therein may be brought into immediate discussion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps I may explain what the change is. This new rule deals with the method of presenting petitions to this House. At the present time, the only way in which a petition can *be presented to the House is for the hon. member to present it here, on the floor of the House of Commons. It is the first thing that is done after the Speaker has taken the chair and the doors have been opened. It is suggested that we adopt in this respect the British practice, that is to say, that petitions can be presented to the House not only openly as is done at the present time, but also by filing them with the Clerk of the House.
It can be done either way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It can be done either way. If the member who presents a petition marks an asterisk upon it, it is sent to the. Clerk of the House and dealt with accordingly. But there may be some petitions to which members might attach some importance and to which they might desire to draw attention and therefore the old method is kept whereby they can be presented on the floor of the House. So the only change is that it is optional for a member either to.move or to file with the clerk. I think the rule can be adopted.

The only observation I would make upon this, I am not objecting to the change, is that it might be misunderstood. It first says ' a petition to the House may be presented by a member at any time during the sitting of the House,' and then it says ' any member desiring to present a petition in his place in the House must do so during routine proceedings and before introduction of Bills.' The one part gives a whole day to a member to present a petition and the other says it must be done during the routine proceedings. I would be inclined to think that a good many members might misunderstand that. A member might be in his place in the House at any part of the day, whereas it means I take it, that he must present his petition by standing in his place during the routine proceedings.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Exactly. The only alternative is that a member can hand his petition to the clerk. If he hands it in before 4 o'clock it will appear on the proceedings of the following day, if after 4 o'clock it will go over one day.

I see plainly enough what it means, but what I refer to is the fact that a great many members might misunderstand it. One part says you can present it at any time during the whole day and the other part says you must present it during routine proceedings.

Yes, but in the one instance the petition is presented to the clerk and in the other it is dealt with in the House by the member who presents it.

36. (1) Questions may be put to ministers of the Crown relating to public affairs; and to other members, relating to any Bill, motion, or other public matter connected with the business of the House, in which such members may be concerned; but in putting any such question or in replying to the same no argument or opinion is to be offered, nor any facts stated, except so far as they may be necessary to explain the same. (3)	If in the opinion of Mr. Speaker a question on the order paper put to a minister of the Crown is of such a nature as to require a lengthy reply, he may, upon the request of the government, direct the same to stand as a notice of motion, and to be transferred to its proper place as such upon the order paper, the Clerk of the House being authorized to amend the same as to matters of form.
(4)	If a question is of such a nature that in the opinion of the minister who is to furnish the reply such reply should be in the form of a return, and the minister states that he' has no objection to laying such return upon the table of the House, his statement shall, unless otherwise ordered by the House, be deemed an order of the House to that effect and the same shall be entered in the Votes and Proceedings as such.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The next question refers to the item of questions. The present rule No. 36 is as follows :

speakerposition: topic

speechtext:
1. Questions may be put to ministers of the Crown relating to public affairs; and to other members relating to any Bill, motion, or other public matter connected with the busi-Mr. SPROULE.
ness of the House, in which such members may be concerned; but in putting any such question or in replying to the same no argument or opinion is to be offered, nor any facts stated, except in so far as may be necessary to explain the same. And in answering any such question the matter to which the same refers shall not be debated.
(2) If in the opinion of Mr. Speaker a question on the order paper put to a minister of the Crown is of such a nature as to require a lengthy reply, he may, upon the request of the government, direct the same to stand as a notice of motion, and to be transferred to its proper place as such upon the order paper, the Clerk of the House being authorized to amend the same as to matters of form.
The new rule is as follows: The first paragraph is maintained. Questions may be put to ministers of the Crown relating to public affairs and to other matters, there is no change. But a new provision is put in:
Any member who requires an oral answer to his question may distinguish it by an asterisk.	...	.
If a member does not distinguish his question by an asterisk, the minister to whom the question is addressed hands the answer to the Clerk of the House who causes it to be printed in ' Hansard.'
There are many questions which are asked simply for information, and if the member does not require an oral answer to such question, the minister hands the answer to the Clerk of the House, who causes it to be printed in the 'Hansard. There are some questions to which members may desire an oral answer, and he may continue to have it. There is no change as to the next paragraph. But there is a new provision which I think is an important one:
If a question is of such a nature that, id the opinion of the minister who is to furnish the reply such reply should be in the form of a return, and the minister states that he has no objection to laying such return upon the table of the House, his statement shall, unless otherwise ordered by the House, be deemed an order of the House to that effect and the same shall be entered in the Votes and Proceedings as such.
The House will understand the meaning of this rule if I remind them that very often a question is asked for information, and the minister will answer. There is no objection to that, but if it is too long to be answered, it will stand as a notice of mo* tion. Then the question is put as a notice of motion and it can be called as such. If, when a question is put asking for information and the minister says: There is no objection, but the answer would be too long to give verbally, but I will supply the information; the order of the House issues at once, and that question will stand as an order of the House.

I think an objection to the first part would be that most members of this House usually listen with a good deal of interest to the answers to these questions. It is one of the educative ways by which members keep themselves familiar with the work of the House going on from day to day. If this suggestion is followed out it will deprive them of that advantage. I know for mv own part I have often listened eagerly to answers that are given to questions in the House. Many members will ask questions, and by that means draw the attention of other members to them when otherwise the subject matter would escape the House entirely. But if, under the proposed rule, the answers are handed in without being read, the members may never take the trouble to look them up. The new rule seems to be following the customs which obtains in the United States Congress, where questions may be handed in and the answers to which are never brought to the attention of the House. It seems to be drifting towards the practice that obtains there and 'which I think is not quite as good as our own.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: So far as answers to questions in this House are concerned, I am bound to say that I have never been able to understand the answers to ten per cent of them, I always have to look them up in ' Hansard ' the next day. Having questions answered by the method which is suggested in this amendment, is the rule which prevails in Great Britain, and it has been found to work very conveniently, and I am inclined to think it will work conveniently here. If a member should desire to see the answer before it appears in ' Hansard he could go to some officer of the House to whom the minister has entrusted the answer, and get it. But apart from that, he can star his question, and have it answered orally if he desires. Therefore any member of this House who desires to have a question answered orally may retain that right by simply making a mark upon it.

It is to be remembered that sometimes answers given by ministers are not correct, some portions are omitted, and then the member who puts the question calls attention to the omission. Under this new method there will be no opportunity of correcting the answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will understand that many questions which are put on the floor of the House have no interest except to the member himself who puts them. But if a member desires to have an oral answer, he has only to put an asterisk to his question and it will at once come before the House.
Amendment No. 3,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The following new rule is to be added after Rule 36:
Notices of Motion for the production of papers which the member asking for intends to make without discussion should be marked by him with an asterisk and should be placed by the Clerk on the order paper above ' Notices of Motions,' under the heading ' Notices of Motions for the production of papers.' All such notices when called should be forthwith disposed of; but if on any such motion the government may desire a debate, it will be transferred by the Clerk to the order of Notices of Motions.
The object of this rule is obvious. Almost every day we have notices of motion which go through unopposed, and these may be marked by the member with an asterisk, and the motion may pass without any discussion.
I think this suggestion is a wise one and will result in economizing time.

What would happen supposing an hon. gentleman puts a notice of motion in * the way indicated to show that he did not want to discuss it, while another hon. gentleman might want to discuss that very matter? I do not think any one hon. gentleman should have the right to prevent a matter being discussed iby simply indicating by an asterisk that he did not want it discussed; he has no right to control the opinion of the whole House on that matter. I appreciate what the Prime Minister is trying to do and I am with him; but it seems to me we are going further here than we intend to go. We do not want to have half a dozen different notices of motion on the same subject on the order paper. When a notice of motion is on the order paper it seems to me that the consent of the House ought to be obtained if that motion is not to be discussed; else we would be in the incongruous position that, because some matter was -of great importance and several hon. gentlemen thought it should be discussed, one of them would be able to say that it should not be discussed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I doubt that, in point of fact, that this is very likely to arise. If any hon. member on the other side puts a motion on the order paper asking for the production of papers and desires that the motion should be presented without discussion, I do not know that anybody on this side will object. The government may object, and, if they do, the motion is transferred to the notices to be debated.

But suppose that a no-
[DOT] tice comes from the other side, and a discussion is desired on this side, it would seem that there is no provision for that. If the government have a right to transfer a motion to the orders by requiring discussion, there should be some provision by which members on this side should have

the same right with regard to notices from the other side.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think there is something in that. The difficulty could be obviated by providing not ' if on such motion the government may desire debate/ but ' if on such motion debate is desired.'
That is my point.
How would that affect it so far as the order paper is concerned? Would it go to the foot of the orders?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would go to notices of motion.
But if it went low on the order paper it might not be reached again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would take its place at the end of notices of motions of that day. The clerk will see to that.
' If there were many notices on the paper and it were put at the foot, it might never be reached again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Possibly-it will take that chance.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['Possibly-it will take that chance.']

While we are dealing with notices of motion, .something should be done to prevent the use of what are known technically here and in England, as ' blocking motions.' Our order paper of this session contains examples of tactics of this kind. Notices of motion are given in grandiloquent terms of legislation supposed to be for the benefit of the people, and these are allowed to stand day after day taking precedence of other motions. And, under our rules, so long as a motion stands on the order paper, the subject matter cannot be referred to in debate, except on that notice of motion. Here, for instance, on our order paper is a notice of motion that has stood there for five months and has blocked the debate of a subject which it is very desirable to have debated. This is a very old legislative trick and was first played by Mr. Gladstone and his friends to prevent the discussion of disagreeable subjects. They put notices on the paper covering these subjects, and then, when a member desired to refer to these subjects, whether on a motion for supply or in any other way, he was called to order, reminded that there was a notice on the paper covering that subject and told that it could not be discussed until such notice of motion was reached. And the notice of motion would be allowed to stand and never discussed. I referred to this once before in an attempt to prevent what is obviously a blocking motion. The difficulty could be overcome by providing that, if a notice of motion is .called twice and it is not proceeded with, Mr. CRD^NET.
it should go to the foot of the list, and, if called the third time, dropped altogether.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have such a rule now, but it is not acted upon. We have had no blocking motions in this House this session, nor has there been such a motion within my memory. I think the hon. member (Mr. J. A. Currie) has only to recall what has been going on this session to see that I am correct in that statement. No one has stood in the way of any one else. The rule we have is that, when a notice of motion is called, it must be gone on with or dropped, unless it is allowed to stand at the request of the government.

I am well aware that that is the rule. But, unfortunately, the government is interested and sometimes orders call for notices of motion to stand. I have a distinct recollection of instances of two hon. members being blocked in mentioning the agricultural item. This occurred in my hearing this session, the Speaker calling the attention of these members to the notice on the order paper in respect of this matter, and ruling that they were not free to discuss the subject. I think that is very unfair. I do not think the government should have the right arbitrarily to order a notice of motion to stand. The government and everybody concerned should go on with the motion, except by unanimous consent of the House. Anyone who knows the parliamentary history of England knows that these ' blocking motions ' have been adopted again and again to avoid the discussion of matters that were regarded bv some parties as unpleasant. I think we should have no more of that system, but, when a motion is called the second time and not preceded with it should go to the foot of the list, and when called the third time, it should be dropped.
Present rule 32 to be amended by striking out the words ' or Thursday ' in the second line from the top.

I think I understand what the object of that is. I apprehend the point is that Thursday is a government day after the first four weeks of the session. But for the first four weeks of the session, certain matters, public Bills, for instance, have precedence, and if on one of these Thursdays, there is a long debate with the intention of talking out a public Bill, it had a perfect right to the floor of the House under the rules until the government took the responsibility of taking Thursday. At the time that change in the rule was made, some four or five years ago, I protested because I thought the government ought not to take Thursdays until they could give to the House some good reason for preventing any more discussion of public Bills. If we should adopt this amendment, it wrnuld be possible for a number of mem-

bers to kill any public Bill by talking on it until the proper hour of adjournment had arrived. Instead of striking out 'on Thursday' make it read 'and on Thursday after the first four weeks of the session.'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend has any cause for such apprehension as he now expresses^ but if 'he thinks the proposed change will at all interfere with the privileges of hon. members opposite, I am quite willing to leave it as it is.

I have had reason for apprehension, because in the last two or three sessions hon. gentlemen have had important public Bills, and the Prime Minister will remember that until four years ago public Bills had preeedence all session, prima facie, but the government undertook to arbitrarily take Thursday by the amendment in the rule. As the rules are to-day, public Bills have no precedence, and are not likely to be reached except in the first four weeks. The House generally meets on a Thursday 'and as that day is consumed in organization there are practically only three days available. Public Bills are sometimes very important. If the government wish to take Thursdays they should assume the responsibility for doing so bv a motion as in the case of Mondays and Wednesdays.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is entirely in error, but if he thinks the privileges of the opposition are interfered with by this change I shall not press the matter. The existing rule is quite intelligible so far as Wednesday is concerned, because the House adjourns at 6 o'clock on Wednesdays. It is not so on Thursday. Years ago, at the time of confederation. notices of motion had precedence on Wednesday and Thursday up to 6 o'clock, and after 6 o'clock the House went into public Bills and orders. Then the rule was introduced for Wednesday and Thursday. There has since been a change; Thursday is now devoted to public Bills and orders after notices of motion all day from 3 o'clock and therefore there is no reason to make any provision for the business of the House on Thursday evening, because it is the same as on any other day. I do not think my hon. friend is justified in his fear, but I am quite willing to leave the rule as it is.
Why not add ' after the first four weeks of the session'?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think it would meet the case at ali.

As I said, if my suggestion is not acceded to hon. gentlemen could practically talk out a Bill, because when public Bills were next called another Bill would go on instead of it and it would lose its right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As far as I understand the matter, the word ' Thursday ' was inserted in the new rules by the clerk or some one else two or three years ago under a misapprehension. Six o'clock on Thursday is just the same as 6 o'clock on any other day except Wednesday. Nothing happens, the business goes on at 8 o'clock just where it left off at 6 o'clock on Thursday, and therefore the insertion of Thursday in a rule regarding Wednesday for which there is special provision, is unnecessary and confusing, and for that reason it was thought best to drop it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
By our present rule, for the first four weeks of the session, on Thursdays, we take public Bills and orders after motions at 3 o'clock, and they are to continue until the end of the sitting. It does not matter what is before the Chair at 6 o'clock, if a Bill is before us at 6 o'clock on Thursday it goes on again at 8 o'clock. The rule in 1867-78 for the order of business on Thursday was:
Until the hour of 6 o'clock p.m questions put by members, notices of motion, public Bills and orders; and after 7.30 o'clock p.m. public Bills and orders.
So if, at 6 o'clock, a notice of motion was under discussion, it dropped when the House met again at 8 o'clock and we went into public Bills and orders.

Does the Prime Minister mean that the reason Thursday is now in the rule is simply because it has been forgotten in the revision since 1867? And is the leader of the opposition quite sure that no harm of the kind I suggest is likely to result? I do not want to run counter to the opinion of both the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition in this matter. They have been on the committee and I have not, and I would like to know from the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) that he is quite certain there would be no danger to public Bills under this amendment to the rules.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I feel quite confident that there will not.

Well, 1 am relevant occasionally. There is no necessity for the application of a clause of that kind. I have

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: been here for two sessions, and I know a little about the work of the House. I have never known of anything in the nature of what you call blocking the work of the House or trying to hold the rules of the House up to contempt. It is true that some Bills have been talked out, especially private Bills. We have a recollection of some private Bills here this session that had to be talked out, and with respect to others we had to talk until we got some amendments to them. I think that the application of a closure rule is not going to benefit the public. Any one who has followed the legislation this year must come to the conclusion that next year we will have more calls from corporations demanding blood and more strenuous efforts will be put forth for the purpose of getting something that is contrary to the interests of the public. Whatever merit the rule may have as applied to public business, certainly, when the House is in committee on private Bills it should not be applied. I have no recollection that the country has ever suffered one particle by these discussions or all night sessions. I have never heard of an all night session by which anybody was injured, but on the' contrary the all-night sitting, and the fight which took place this session ftas for the benefit of the public. The reason why the rules were restricted in the English House of Commons do not obtain here. There the Nationalists deliberately proceed to hold the rules of order up to contempt by.discussing every motion that was produced by the Speaker, even such a simple motion as: ohall this Bill be read a week hence or tomorrow? We have had no trouble with obstruction of that kind in this House. This House has always had absolute freedom in debate and the members of the opposition have never taken advantage of the laxity of the rules to unduly harrass the government or hold up the business.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would be inclined to think that this is the rule of the committee now, if the chairman of the committee sees fit to guide himself according to what should be the practice of the committee. I think it is merely placing in the written code of this House, in respect to its work in committee, that which at the present time is and ought to be in the unwritten code.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I be permitted to observe that my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) that this was a standing rule of the House of Commons in England long before the Nationalists were heard of, and I think moreover that it is a rule which is in line with common sense. This is a deliberative body and the discussions ought to be confined to the question which at the moment is before the House. My hon. friend says there may be occasions Mr. J. A. CURRIE.
when the opposition should fight strenuously a proposition put before it and he instanced the all-night sitting which took place during the present session. There have been all night sittings almost every session of this parliament since I have been in this House, and that runs back for more than thirty years. But the all-night sitting which took place during the present session was an exception to all the all-night sittings that I have ever heard of. It was not my good fortune or misfortune to be present, but I read the debate carefully and, I was surprised at the high character of the discussion which took place. It was not at all confined to one side of the House. All-night sittings for the purpose of obstruction are generally confined to one side of the House, the other side taking no part, but on the occasion of that all-night sitting both sides of the House discussed and discussed strenuously the proposition which was before the House. There was no irrelevant discussion as far as I could see in the debate. The discussion was of a very high character and under the circumstances I do not think the chairman would have been justified in imposing such a rule because there was no occasion to do it. I have also his word for it that he was impressed with the high character of the debate. But, if the debate goes on in a rambling manner, without any purpose, I think it is. only right that the dignity of the House should be preserved by having such a rule as they have in Great Britain. We are only following the provision of the British House of Commons and I must say that I am shocked that my hon. friend, who is a Britisher, should even interpose an objection.

My right hon. friend knows and we all know that from the time that rules were first provided for parliamentary usage there has been a general rule that a speaker must speak to the question. In the Committee of the Whole the practice has arisen of allowing greater laxity in discussion than when we are speaking directly to a motion, and a member has only one chance of speaking. Of course,
I do not care-I am only one member of the opposition, but I feel that the House, by putting this rule in, is casting a reflection upon its past action. I do not feel like giving up any privilege or right in the way of obstruction than I have at the present time as a member of the opposition in any legislation which I consider not to be in the interest of the country is being forced through this House against my will.
I do not think the Speaker has ever had occasion, since I have been a member of the House, to bring us up very strongly: it is only occasionally that things"get a little hot and then he does it under the old rule. I do not see why there should

be any rule of this kind unless it is intended to do something that has not been done before.

In every Bill there are certain formal clauses. Is this new rule going to confine us strictly to the formal clause that may be under discussion, or will it be allowed under such a clause to discuss the merits of the Bill? If not, 1 think this will considerably restrict the discussion.

If this new rule is applied, a member cannot discuss a Bill in committee in a general way, or the chairman will immediately shut him off. If a certain clause is before the committee, it will not be allowable to refer incidently to its bearing on other clauses.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not regard the rule as going that far. In the discussion of one clause, it would, of course, be allowable to refer to its meaning taken in connection with other clauses.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:

speechtext: CLARKE moved the second reading of Bill (No. 218) respecting the Guelph Junction Railway Company.

This Bill is very objectionable and. it was doubtful whether it is likely to pass this session. I know there are _ several members who strongly object to it. Whether it would make any difference objecting to it at this stage I do not know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

We have this disadvantage that when a Bill comes from a committee it has the stamp of the committee upon it and it is urged as a reason in this House why the Bill should go through-as a matter of form. Now to my mind the principle of this Bill is a very dangerous one. It is absolute confiscation, there is

no doubt about it. We have never so far as I remember in my acquaintance with parliament adopted the principle that is embodied in this Bill of compelling a man to sell or hand over to another his property without fair and reasonable compensation, or by arbitration. We do give people the right to expropriate property, but this is under the rule of arbitration, and for the public good. But we have never adopted, so far as I know, the principle of compelling any man to give up his property to another without the individual who is sacrificing the property having some reasonable say in what he should receive by way of compensation. So we are adopting in this parliament a principle that has never been adopted in the history of the Canadian parliament to my knowledge, and I think it is a very bad one, and one which will undoubtedly be quoted in the future as a precedent. I think we should go slowly before adopting any such principle.

"On section 1,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose of this legislation, as I very briefly explained in introducing the Bill, is to supplement legislation which has just been passed by the provincial legislature of Manitoba. In the Act of the provincial legislature, which was assented to on 16th March last, provision is made for the establishment of an industrial home within the province to which girls or women may be sentenced. Under the present Dominion statute with reference to prisons and reformatories, no provision is made for sentencing prisoners to such an institution, because none was in existence until the passing of the legislation to which I have just referred. Accordingly, this Bill proposes to repeal the four sections of the Prisons and Reformatories Act here named, which four sections apply to the province of Manitoba, and to substitute for these four sections the sections of the Bill. The only difference made

by these sections is that the Bill introduces the word ' industrial home.' In line 15 of the first section of the Bill, power is conferred upon the court to commit a prisoner to either some reformatory or industrial home for boys or girls in the province of Manitoba. Under the existing law, the power to sentence is simply to the provincial reformatory for boys. The same thing is true of sections 140, 141 and 143 of this Bill. Section 142 is entirely new and has been introduced at the suggestion of the deputy attorney general of the province, who tells me that he has been urged to secure it by Hon. Mr. Daly, police magistrate of Winnipeg, who is also judge of the juvenile court in Winnipeg, and who is of opinion that a short term of imprisonment for girls or women who have gone astray is often of very little use in the way of their reformation. Mr. Daly's experience suggests the advisability of an amendment to the Dominion law, such as this section 142 proposes, by which the court may, in its discretion, sentence such an offender to any term it thinks fit, not exceeding three years. The provisions of section i42 are new; the provisions of the other sections are mere amendments of the existing law in the way I describe.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Bill (No. 206) respecting escheats, read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I may explain briefly the purpose of this Bill. We have no provision upon our Dominion statute-book for the disposition which is to be made of property which may escheat to the Dominion Crown. The ordinary escheat of property within any of the older provinces of the Dominion goes to the provincial Crown, and with such escheats the Dominion has nothing to do. But in the case of the territories where there is no provincial representative of the Crown, the estate of any person who dies entirely without heirs, escheats to the Dominion. As a matter of fact, there is at the present time in the hands of the Receiver General as part of the consolidated fund of Canada, the proceeds of an estate of this character amounting to nearly $50,000. There is no statutory provision for the disposition which should be made of such estates, and while the bulk of any such estate would of course simply go to add to the resources of the country, it is thoueht that in many instances it is desirable that there should be power to do something out of the estate for people who have not a legal claim, but a moral and equitable claim, upon the property, or upon the individual who had, during his lifetime, owned the property. The case out of which the money I have spoken of has arisen, presents features of that character. A man owning a considerable amount of property in what, in his day, was the Northwest Territories, died, having made a will, but having no descendant or legal heir. The will does not dispose of the whole of his property, and there is this surplus of nearly $50,000 which falls to the government. Now, there are people who, while not legally related to him, are still of his own blood, kin of the half blood, chidren who I think were of the same mother. At all events, in a relation, naturally speaking, as distinguished from legally speaking, they are half _ brothers or half sisters This Bill provides that the Governor in Council may

make a grant out of property which becomes the property of His Majesty in circumstances such as I have described to
Any person, who in the opinion of the Governor in Council had a legal or moral claim upon the previous owner, or a just or natural right or claim to succeed to his property or to any part thereof.
The power is also sought by this legislation to the Governor in Council to carry into effect any disposition of the deceased owner's property which it is believed he may have intended. I do not know that that situation arises in the particular case I have been alluding to, but a case might arise in which a man had made a will which, as a matter of law, was defective, which might, for instance have been signed before only one witness or might otherwise be of such a character that the courts would have no power to carry it into effect. It would seem only right that in such circumstances, or if in any way a clear intention was demonstrated on the part of the owner of the property to make some disposition of it, there should be power in the Governor in Council to carry out, to the extent which may seem just, such clear intention. Finally, power is asked to devote some portion of an estate of the character I have mentioned, in the way of reward, to any person who may make discovery of such property to the Crown. These are, in outline, the provisions of the present Bill.
I take it that ' the Governor in Council' means the federal authority. It would not apply to the provincial authority?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.

Would this not bring on a conflict between the rights of the provinces and of the federal authority? The provinces believe and have acted upon the belief that it is their right to claim escheated property. Fot instance in the old Mercer escheats case, the estate was taken possession of by Sir Oliver Mowat, on behalf of the province, and both real and personal property disposed of by -the provincial government. Would this not be assuming to the federal government the same authority which is believed to be vested in the provincial government ? If it becomes law would it apply to personal property in the shape of money held by the banks and for which there was no owner ? We find many of these unclaimed balances in the reports made every five years. Suppose some person gave notice of an unclaimed balance in the bank to the credit of some one who had died intestate, and to which there were no heirs, would that individual be entitled to the remuneration which this Bill provides might be given to him and in both
cases would the property go to the provincial or federal government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Bill is drawn with the effort to make it impossible that there should be any conflict with the well-estaJblished provincial authority. It can have no application to a case of tan escheat in any of the older provinces of the Dominion. In the province of Ontario and also in the province of Quebec it has been authoritatively established by decisions of the courts that in case of escheats the property escheated goes to the province. The same law must, upon a like reasoning, apply to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and I suppose to British Columbia. I do not know that any case has ever arisen in these latter provinces in which the question has been discussed, but so far as I am aware there is no ground for supposing that escheated property in those provinces of the Dominion does not go to the province. I am not so clear as to the position of property which might escheat in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, because in those provinces the ungranted land of the Crown is the property of the Dominion, and the whole origin of the legal doctrine of escheat foT want of heirs, is a remnant of the feudal law of the land reverting to the hand which gave it. In those circumstances it may be that the courts would hold an escheat of propertv in the three provinces I have mentioned should fall to the Dominion and not to the province. That question, however, has not practically arisen. In the case to which I have alluded and which has produced this considerable sum of money in the hands of the Dominion government, the estate fell into the Crown before the provinces were created, while the property was still within the Northwest Territories of Canada, and to-day, if a man died without legal heirs, owner of property in the Yukon or in the Northwest Territories, Keewatin, Mackenzie or Ungava, such property would necessarily fall to the Dominion government, because there would be no provincial government to which it could go. So this Bill, as hon. gentlemen will see, opens with the statement :
Where His Majesty the King, in his right of Canada, is entitled to land or other property, &c.
And the whole Bill is posited upon the case wherein right of the Dominion government, the Crown becomes entitled to a windfall such as this. In all other cases, of course, this Bill has no application; wherever it is His Majesty in right of a province or of any other jurisdiction than that of the Dominion, this Bill does not touch the matter.
With reference to the other point, the unclaimed balances which may remain in

banks, if there was any such unclaimed balance the property of a man who died without legal heirs, it would, like any other portion of his property, fall into the hands of the Crown but not otherwise. If the man who owned the unclaimed balance left legal personal representatives, children or other heirs, that unclaimed balance would go, like any other property which the deceased had owmed, to such legal, personal representatives and the Crown would have nothing whatever to do with it, so that this Bill does not profess to deal with unclaimed balances in banks except to the possible extent I have indicated where such unclaimed balance or any part of it was the property of a man who died without heirs.

With regard to money, and there was such a case, an unclaimed balance of a considerable amount remained in the hands of a bank in Ontario, and an effort was being made to escheat that, would it go to the province the same as Teal estate or to the federal authority under this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In a case such as my hon. friend describes, if the unclaimed balance escheated at all in Ontario it would escheat to the province and not to the Dominion.

I notice in the wording of the Bill that the Governor in Council may grant 'out of the moneys or out of the escheat'. Are the words broad enough to enable the Governor in Council to grant the whole escheat or should the words 'the whole or any part' be inserted there?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the words in the third section are quite wide enough to authorize the disposition of the whole *property-may grant 'any land or other real or personal property or any part thereof'.

I quite understand this legislation is intended to apply and would apply only to cases where property was escheated to the Crown in the right of Canada, but I would like to ask whether this legislation does not affect the provinces to this extent that a question might arise as to whether a particular estate should escheat to the Dominion or the province as in the case of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, with regard to which provinces the minister said there might be some 'question as to which Crown the right would be vested in. Would1 not this legislation affect these provinces to this extent that it would confer upon the Exchequer Court the exclusive jurisdiction of determining the question of right as between the Crown in the right of Canada and the Crown in the Tight of the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the only

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: answer it would be possible to make to the question which my hon. friend has propounded would >be to say that if the property escheated to the Dominion government then certainly jurisdiction would be conferred on the Exchequer Court only, but, on the contrary, if the property did not, as a matter of law, fall to the Dominion government, this Bill would not touch it at all.

I quite understand that if it were once decided, but I am asuming a case where the escheat takes *place in a province, where, as the minister says the question is not absolutely decided whether the escheated property would fall to the Dominion of Canada or fall to the province. I am assuming the case that Canada claims that the escheat is to her. Then, under this Act, would not she be entitled, as against the province that might be claiming the right, to proceed before the Exchequer Court as this Act provides and to that extent are you not affecting the position of the provinces to the extent that you are compelling them or putting them in a position where they can be compelled, to submit the question of their right to the escheat to the determination of a Dominion court? You are putting them in a different position from an individual having a right to enforce or defend in regard to a property within the province when you are compelling them to meet the claim of the Dominion of Canada before the Exchequer Court. I am not prepared to say that perhaps it is not proper to do it, but I only want to make it .clear. It seems to me that you are, in this instance, affecting the position of the provinces.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Mr. OLIVER moved that the House go into committee to further consider Bill (No. 163) to amend the Volunteer Bounty Act, 1908.
The hon. minister received a lot of suggestions the other night. Perhaps he might just explain which, if any of them, he has accepted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The other night the Bill stood over in order that I might have an opportunity to consider a number of suggestions that were made. I have them before me, and will refer to them in detail. Before doing so, however, I may say that after giving them the most careful consideration I have not been able to agree that it would be well to add them to the Bill or to adopt them in the Bill. Taking them in the order in which they came up in the debate, there was the; amendment suggested by my Ron. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turiff). He suggested as an amendment to section 4:
That section 4 of the Volunteer Act, 1908, chapter 66, be amended by adding to it the following words: ' Every such grantee or his substitute may within six months after the date of entry, abandon the land so entered and may thereafter, within the time limited for selection and entry by subsection 1 of this section, or within six months after such date, make a second entry; provided that nothing in this subsection shall authorize or entitle any grantee or his substitute to make any further entry in place of the land abandoned as aforesaid.'
My view with regard to that is that volunteer scrip cannot in fairness to the administration be treated differently from other scrip, that is half-breed scrip, and everybody agrees that it would be entirely improper to allow a location of scrip to-day and to allow it to be exchanged to-morrow. Besides that, the amendment would practically give an additional six months, that is to say that instead of the time limit terminating at the time set by the statute it would be extended by the operation of this provision for six months longer in the cases of those who desired to speculate in this scrip. To put the matter shortly, it would he an undesirable addition to the speculative element which necessarily enters into the dealing with this scrip. Moreover, I do not think it} would be fair to the ordinary settlers that these scrip holders should be allowed to take part in a rush for entry, thereby tending to displace the ordinary homesteader, and afterwards to. have the right to exchange their location. Another suggestion was made by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) in the fallowing words :
That section 4 be amended by inserting in the second line, after the word ' Act,' the following words:
Or any bounty certificate that has been, prior to the passage of this Act, sold or transferred to any person acquiring the same for purposes of speculation or resale.
That amendment is intended to meet the view that has been expressed by a number of members that it would be desirable while giving an extension of time to the present holders of their own scrip

not to give it to the men who had 'bought scrip. In regard to that I would observe that the fundamental principle of the Act as it was first passed was to put the substitute or buyer on an equal footing with the original holder, the view being that by doing so the original holder who did not wish to locate would get a higher value. The purchasers bought in the belief that this principle having been affirmed by parliament would be adhered to. Volunteers who have sold have had the benefit of this belief on the ipart of the purchaser. This belief was further warranted by the action of parliament in dealing with the scrip of 1885 in regard to which extensions were given. On that point I might mention that there have been a number of previous issues of scrip. There were issues to the veterans of the first Red river expeditions between 1870 and 1873, of 1,559 military bounty warrants for 160 acres of land without settlement duty. There was no limitation of time as to the location of those warrants, and to-day we are advertising in the newspapers hundreds of those warrants, giving notice to the public that there are such and such warrants that have not been located which are just as good to-day as they were when they were issued nearly 40 years ago.
Because there was no limit, I suppose?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
I am very sorry that this Act has been introduced at all by the Minister of the Interior. Even now there are still some eight months within which persons who have received this bounty will have time to locate their land. It is very much against the washes of the farming community throughout the Northwest that there should be any extension of time. However, the minister seems determined to force this Bill through the House. That being the case, I think it would have been wise on his part to accept some of the suggestions which have been made on this side of the House, and especially that suggestion which was made by the hon. member for St. Anne, Montreal, namely, that the extension of time should be made applicable only to the veterans themselves, those who intend personally to locate their scrip. I regret that that suggestion has not been accepted by the minister. I would urge him especially to accept one other suggestion which has been made by the hon. member for Macleod. I hope the minister will think that over again, and that he will change his mind. The principle is generally recognized everywhere, I think, in regard to giving war medals, that the man who sets as far as the seat of war becomes entitled to a war medal, even though he never saw a single shot fired in anger. That principle is certainly recognized in the mother country, and it should be equally applicable to those men who volunteered from Canada to serve the empire in South Africa. They started in on their duty, but either through illness or through accident, they were not able to reach the seat of war in South Africa, and they or their legal representatives, in cases where they have died, are now going



to be deprived of the benefits which I think they are Tightly entitled to. I am sorry the minister has not come to the conclusion to accept the principle that those men who enlisted and started on their way, but through illness contracted owing to their service, or through accidents which have happened to them during that service, were unable to reach South Africa, should receive the benefits of the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The question as to who should receive the benefit of this bounty was discussed very fully at the time the Bill was passed. For good or bad reasons, parliament came to a certain conclusion. It was not my wish, in introducing this Bill, to raise any question of that character whatever. It seemed to me that if you raised the question, you opened a door that it would be difficult to close. There was a request made to us by certain representative volunteers for an extension of time, and they seemed to give good reasons for that. We agreed to give them only a part of what they wanted, thinking it would not be unreasonable, and would not do any great harm to any one, and might do good. But I did not wish, in bringing that position before the House, to raise any other question, nor do I desire to do so at the present time. There is no doubt that a good case can be made out for certain men whose circumstances have been brought before the Houise by different members. But I ask the House to consider the position. You have to put a limit somewhere, you have to put a limit some time, and where-ever you fix that limit, there is somebody going to be just outside of it, and somebody else going to be just inside of it. It is as if you drew a circle: somebody is going to be just inside that circle, and somebody is going to be just outside it; and the man who is just outside of it feels that he has a grievance, and his friends feel that way also. You proceed to enlarge the circle and take in a few more. Do you reach a conclusion by that means? No; the more you enlarge the circle, the more you increase its circumference, the more people you find are beyond, on the outside of that circle. You have satisfied those who are included in this enlarged circle, but you have created dissatisfaction in the minds of the larger number of people who are still outside the larger circle. I quite appreciate the feelings of my hon. friends, and I quite appreciate their arguments. But 1 want to assure them, and I ask them to realize the fact, that there is no way a line can be drawn that won't leave people just outside of it who have nearly as good a right to be inside as the people who are inside. Now, in order not to raise the question at all. I would think it advisable in everybody's interest not to open the Bill. There Mr. LAKE.
is one particular class that appeals to me very strongly, and that is those who died on the way to South Africa; but even in that case, if the House should see fit at a later date to do something for them, it would be better to do it by way of a money grant than to open the question of an increased grant of land scrip. There is no doubt that the sentiment of the country is against any further grant of land scrip for any reason whatever. That being the case, I think it would be well for us not to put ourselves in the way of increasing the number who would become liable for land grants under this.	,

Would the minister be personally in favour of such a measure as he suggests might be introduced in the future, if such a measure were introduced next year, that is to make a money grant for those who died from injuries received on the way to South Africa?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If I could dissociate my personality from my responsibility I would say yes, the case appears to me so strong; but I do not think it would be wise in the interests of these people, to change the present limitations of this Bill.

I know that in my district the rule was absolute that no young man who was married or had parents or others dependent on him was permitted to go to South Africa. In my own corps there were two or three hundred volunteers for South Africa, but they were weeded out if they were married or had any one depending on them. It seems hardly in keeping that after such care in the selection of men claims should be put forward on behalf of their heirs.

There are one or two cases in which scrip for the 1885 volunteers has not yet been located. Could not the minister under this Act provide for an extension of this scrip in cases where the volunteers are still anxious to locate?

speechtext: I do not think it would be wise to bring that under this Act. I read a list of the extensions given to the 1885 scrip. I know of one of these 1885 scrips that has not been located. The party was not aware that these'extensions had been made, and he is bntStled to every consideration. I shall draw his attention to this matter. In listening to the debate so far I think the minister is not

On section 3, extension of time.

The minister referred to the case presented by the hon. member for Hamilton the other night, although he does not appear willing to accede to the request of the hon. member (Mr. Barker). speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no provision whereby the privilege asked for could be granted even by order in council, and if my hon. friend will remember when the Bill was up for consideration in the session of 1908 that question was raised, and it was decided by the House at that time that the privilege which we gave in the case of the man who sold his scrip would have to be the consideration that he would get, that is to say, we gave liberal consideration in regard to the sale of scrip so that the man who could not himself, in his own bodily person, go into residence on the land, would be able to realize as much as his scrip was worth from the man who would actually go on the land. The principle of the homesteader being on his own land is the very foundation of our whole system in the settlement of the west, and I do not think it would be well to deviate from it.
