At the beginning of the session I introduced a Bill to somewhat limit the appeals from the Board of Railway Commissioners to the Supreme Court. After a great deal of attention given to the subject 'by the subcommittee to which the Railway Committee referred the Bill, and after consultation between the subcommittee and the Board of Railway Commissioners-(because the object was to make a piece of legislation that the board, as administering the law, could work out- the matter was sent back to the Railway Committee and reported unanimously to the House. The effect of the section as here proposed is to eliminate subsection 3 of section 56 of the Railway Act and enact the following:
3.	An appeal shall also lie from the board to such court upon any question which in the opinion of the board is a question of law, upon leave therefor having been first obtained from the board within one month after the making of the order or decision sought to be appealed from, or within such further time as the board under special circumstances shall allow, and after notice to the opposite party stating the grounds of appeal; and the granting of such leave shall be in the discretion of the board.
3a. No appeal, after leave therefor has been obtained under subsection 2 or 3 of this section, shall lie unless it is entered in the said court within thirty days from the making of the order granting leave to appeal.
Until this session there was no time limit for the making of atpplication for leave to appeal. The board passed rules from time to time which, however, they found they could not enforce very well The latest rule made a limitation of 14 days, but they found that they could not always hold people to that. Besides, we all agreed that it was necessary to have a statute fixing the time. So, it was made as here proposed that application shall be made within one month and the appeal muslt be prosecuted wjitWin thirty days

after leave to appeal is granted. These limitations were thought reasonable so that an appeal cannot be kept for ever hanging over .either the railway company or any other party to a case before the board.
Is that the whole effect of this section?

Yes, except that we make it clear-which was in doubt before that the board shall have discretion to allow an extension of time under special circumstances. The head of the Railway Commission, ex-Judge Mabee pointed out that cases might arise of delay through persons not knowing the actual result of the decisions given, or there might be other special circumstances in which they would desire to extend the time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The proposal is that section 1 of the Bill as reprinted shall be section 1 of the Bill before the committee.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Section 1 of the Bill as before the committee now becomes section 2 as shown in the reprint. The section is as follows:
The said Act is amended by inserting the following section immediately after section 59:-
59a. Whenever this Act requires or directs that before the doing of any work by the company the approval of the board must be first obtained, and whenever any such work
has been done before the	day
of	, one thousand nine hundred
and nine, without such approval, the board shall nevertheless have power to approve of the same and to impose any terms and conditions upon such company that may be thought proper in the premises.
It will be observed that there are two blanks in this section. The object of the section is to provide for cases of this kind. It has- been found that some railway companies have proceeded to locate their lines and do things which they should not have done without the consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners. And, when the board has been appealed to, the chairman has held that the board has not power to deal with the road unless it begins at the beginning and practically starts with the rails torn up. All that this section is intended to do is to give the Board of Railway Commissioners power to deal with a situation of that kind. If they see fit to make the company put the road somewhere else, they can do it, or if they like, they can approve of what has been done. I propose that the blanks should be filled in so as to make it read 'before the 31st day of December, one thousand nine hundred and nine.' [DOT]
The section will not have any post facto effect beyond that date?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
That is all. The chairman states that he has come across several cases of that kind and he really thinks he has not power to deal with them unless we give him that power.
On section 3, vice-presidents who are not directors.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is introduced in response to a request from the railway companies that they be allowed to appoint officers who may not be members of their boards of directors. They want to have vice-presidents who are not on the board of directors. I think the Canadian Pacific railway has a special Act permitting this, and one of the other companies asked for a similar Act, but I said I would introduce a general Act and permit them all to do it. They argue that there are cases in which they wish to appoint an officer to give him a title and engage him, although he is not to be a member of the board of directors. It means nothing except to the board itself.

The idea apparently is to follow the American practice of making the working officials directors, not to have figureheads on the hoard of directors. That i3 a good practice. The English practice, of course, is the reverse, and all the directors are outside of the company, who know nothing about the affairs of the company, the officials being simply servants.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
One thing I had in mind was, for instance, the case of a company with the majority of its directors living in the old country, so that it would be impossible to make a selection from these gentlemen to do some particular work requiring the man doing it to have some standing.
On section 4, orders of the board relating to crossings with telegraph and telephone companies, &c.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This clause is merely to expedite the crossing of electric or telegraph wires over a railway line where the two companies can agree and the work is done under a regulation of the board. Heretofore, they have had to get an order from the board in each case, and some small crossings have occupied a good deal of time and caused a good deal of trouble. The commissioners and the companies agree that where there is no dispute, these crossings can be made under regulations framed by the board, and both parties may agree.

The hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Wilcox) is interested in this clause. The idea prevailing was that the Railway Commission were to establish two or three standard forms of crossings and that blue prints would be supplied to parties who wished to make crossings, and if any one applied and put

in that standard form of crossing, underground or overhead, following the specifications" laid down by 'the board,_ therq could be no question about the right to cross by either company. As it- is now, the application must be made. The board has not made a standard form of specification.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Not yet.
Is it the intention of the board to make it? As it is now, every time a crossing is to be made, costing perhaps $5, there are expenses of _ $35 or $40 in connection with the application.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This section really provides for the adoption of such a standard. In 90 cases out of 100 the companies will agree, and if they should not agree, it will be going too far to say that one company shall cross the line of the other without the board saying how it shall be done
On general principles, if they do not agree, the board will decide.

I am informed that if they do not agree, that the railway company will send the telephone company to the board every time. I would strike out the words ' with the consent of the company.' Let the board establish a standard crossing, and if the people will follow that exactly, I do not think the railway company should have any kick at all.

Suppose the railway company insisted that a certain point was not a proper place for a standard form of crossing, or take the case where they persist that the usual form ordered by the board was the one to use and the municipality thought it was not, and would not agree. Would my hon. friend say that it was right that the railway company should be allowed to force the use of the standard arrangement? Should they not be allowed to do, as I advised a municipality to do in such case, go to the board and secure an order to have the work done under a special regulation? It works two ways.
The hon. member's argument would be all right if there was a standard form, but the minister has said there is not one.
The very legislation we are dealing with presupposes that there is one, and I was referring to the customary form.

I think these clauses should be carefully guarded, that these telephone companies have certain rights, and I do not think they should have to spend $30 or $40 coming to the Railway Commission every time a railway manager says: You cannot cross that railway. In western Ontario, where there are many
farmers' telephones, they have to cross the railway at almost every concession, and a standard form of specification should be adopted. I do not think that these small companies should be put to the expense of securing an order if they want to make a crossing at a country road. The proper way would be to strike out the words ' with the consent of the company.' As it is, the whole matter is still left in the hands of the company.
No.

The section reads:
An order of the board shall not he required in the case in which telephone, telegraph or electric light wires are erected across the railway with the consent of the company
That is the railway company.

-in acordance with any general regulations, plans or specifications adopted or approved by the board for such purposes.
It does not say which company it is; it may mean the telephone company.
No, it means the railway company by the interpretation clause.
There are lots of railway companies that are not half as big as the Bell Telephone company.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The interpretation clause of the Railway Act would cover that.

The clause would read just as well if that were struck out. Then it would mean that the standard specification of the board would govern unless they appealed to the board against it. If there were an appeal the Tailway company would have to appeal to the board. The grievance which exists is not righted by this Act. This clause is put in here to give a little soothing syrup to the country, but it is no good.
On section 6, section 254 amended by adding at the end of subsection 3 the word ' lands.'

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is a portion of the Bill of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), and I think if he would just explain his Bill it would apply to the different clauses as they come up.

Section 5 of the reprinted Bill is a portion of the original Bill that I introduced. However, this amendment has really nothing to do with the main portion of the amendment that I introduced. Consequently I can simply refer to this now, and when we come to section 8 I shall take that up. Section 5 simply adds the word * lands,' to section 254 of the Railway Act. Section 254 com-

pels railway companies to fence their railways. The courts have held that it simply compels them to fence their railways. The courts have held that it simply compels them to fence their frails. A very serious miscarriage of justice has occurred by reason of that interpretation. Adding the word ' lands ' does nothing more than carry out what was originally intended that they should fence their own property.
On section 6, leave to carry traffic.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
At the present time the Act reads that the Board of Railway Commissioners, to accommodate the public, may, on a road which is not completed, allow them to carry freight traffic. I am proposing to amend that by striking out the word ' freight,' so that, if the board see fit, they can ask the construction company to carry passengers as well as freight over a part of the line even if the whole line is not completed.
On section 7, warning of moving trains.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Brakesmen have been, and are compelled to stand on the rear of an engine that is running backwards. Cases do occur where light engines are sent twenty or thirty miles backwards.
Why does the engine have to go backwards?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It may be that there is no place to turn, or the engine may be ordered to go back to assist a freight or to render assistance at a wreck, and she is sent back twenty or thirty miles. Cases have been brought to my attention where men have almost frozen to death while standing on the rear of the tender. The idea of a man riding on the back of a tender is to protect the public at crossings where they are shunting. This clause protects all that because, it requires the railway men to remain on the back of the tender when they are shunting, but if does relieve them from remaining on the back of the tender when they are on these long runs.

The object of the Act has always been that people will naturally suppose that an engine is going the way it is headed, and, therefore, when they see an engine facing east, they will go west to get behind it.
I do not want to oppose it if the minister thinks it is absolutely necessary to trust the board in this regard, but when an engine is headed west people will naturally suppose that it is going west when it may be going east. It' is natural for a man to assume that an engine is heading in the direction in which it is pointing, but when he drives up he may find that it is going the other way. I can understand that there may be exceptional Mr. MEIGHEN
cases, as where there is a wreck, and it is impossible to turn the engine around, and it must be run down the line twenty or thirty miles. If this provision is necessary, I will consent to it only with the understanding that the board see that the privilege is not extended or abused.
On section 8, damages caused to or by cattle on railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is a.' portion of the amendment of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie.

This section embodies the principal part of the amendment which was contained in my original Bill. Its purpose is to extend the liabilities of railway companies in the event of their own default. At the present time railway companies may default under any section of the Act. Section 427, in addition to imposing other liabilities, renders a railway company liable for any damage that may result by reason of its default under any section of the Railway Act, that is to say, if a company violates any section of the Act, and damage is caused thereby, under section 427 the railway company is ostensibly liable for that damage; but unfortunately it has been held, and held repeatedly, that notwithstanding the provisions of section 427, there are certain sections of the Act which the railway company may violate without being under the necessity of paying the damage apparently provided for by the wording of that section. The sections I refer to are 254 and 294, more particularly section 254. Reasoning back from these sections through their history in the older Acts, the courts have come to the conclusion that notwithstanding that a railway company may be in default under section 254, and may thus be liable for damage under section 294, the class of damage to which it is liable is not as general as that to which it is liable, for violating any other section. Section 254 provides that the railway company shall fence its railway, and maintain gate's and cattle guards. The limitation to which I call attention has the effect of restricting them in the event of their violation of these provisions to such damages as result in the killing or injury of cattle by the company's negligence or wilful act or omission. Under the old law that was the only liability, and the courts have held, notwithstanding the provisions of section 427, that the company is still limited, in the case of a violation of section 254, to the same liability as it was formerly under; that is to say, it is only liable if by reason of its default- animals are killed or injured through its negligence or wilful act or omission. A large class of damages may result and have resulted which do not 'come within that old

limitation-damages occasioned by animals which have got on the track through the default of the company in failing to maintain fences, gates or cattle guards-escapes and does damage to neighbours' crops or other damage which the company escapes. In a case with which I was connected animals got on the railway track through the absence of a fence, ran down the track and were injured so as to be useless by having their legs broken on a bridge, and the railway company was not liable because the damage was not caused by their trains or engines. Many other cases occur. For instance a company is bound to fence its right of way so as to keep all cattle out, and the term ' cattle,' includes sheep. This the companies have refused to do in certain cases, and as a consequence the farmer who owns sheep has either to go out of the sheep business or run grave risk of damage, because his sheep can get through the railway fences, and do injury to his neighbours' crops. Under the present amendment the railway company would be liable for all damage done by their default in these respects, the same as under any other provision of the Act. There is a provision added at the end of section 8 in the following words:
Provided, however, that nothing herein contained shall be taken or construed as overriding the provisions of section 407 of this Act.
Section 407 of the Act has the following language:
Every person whoexcept as authorized by this Acit, without the consent of the companies, rides, leads or drives any horse, or other animal, or suffers any such horse or animal to enter upon the railway, and within the fences and guards thereof;
shall, on summary conviction, be liable to a penalty of $20 for each offence, etc.
He is also liable for various other offences, such as leaving gates open, taking down part of a fence, or turning animals loose. When my original Bill was before the Railway Committee, just at the moment when it was accepted, this provision was placed before me for my approval:
' Provided however that nothing herein shall be taken or construed as overiding the provisions of section 407 of this Act.' At the time, I read it as carefully as I could, and I could see no objection to it. However, later on my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), who has had more to do with this class of legislation than I have, and doubtless knows better the difficulties that have arisen under that class of legislation, drew my attention to a dangerous feature of the amendment. It would be quite possible under the proviso at the end of the section, in fact it would certainly be held that section 407 was the dominant section prevailing over subsection
8 of the reprinted Bill, and that wherever they were in conflict section 407 would prevail with the possible Tesult that the whole benefit of the amendment would be obviated, because if a man unconsciously allowed his animals to be on the track and, if the company then escapes liability for injuring then the real benefit of subsection 4 of section 294 would be lost. The subsection renders the company liable even if a man has suffered his animals to be on the track so long as that suffering is not due to any wilful act or neglect of his own. Consequently to the wording of the proviso of section 8 of the reprinted Bill, I cannot consent. I think, however, it could be amended so as to obviate the danger to which I have alluded. So, long as it is restricted to preserving the penalty I have no objection, but to the word ' override,' I cannot agree, because its effect would be too far reaching.

I agree in the main with what has been said by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen). This matter was referred to a special committee. and I think it was the law clerk of the Railways and Canals Committee that suggested to the minister that those words should be added. They were not really considered by the committee, but the hon. member for Portage la Prairie at the time did not think they would do any harm, and the Bill was reported. The position is this, that previous to 1901, just because of the language of the section now replaced by 407 there was no liability for animals killed. It was because of the language of what is now section 407 that we had all the trouble for three years. We finally got section 294 as it is to-day. The object of that section was to protect the owners .of animals, who without any default of their own .allowed their animals to escape and get on the railway track. My hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) rightly enough in my opinion thinks that if the railway company is in default and the animals are not injured, but cause other damage, the railway company should be responsible. While he is attaining that, I think it is proper that we do not unconsciously deprive the owner of the animals of his right to recover, as we declared after all the contest which went on for three years, and which ended in 1903, that the railway company may be liable for the animals themselves. I suggest that instead of saying ' provided, 'however, that nothing herein shall be taken or construed as overriding the provisions of section 407 of this Act ' that we say * provided, however, that nothing herein shall be taken ot construed as relieving any person from the penalties imposed by section 407.' Section 407 is two-fold. It prevented civil liability which we determined after a great deal of trouble should exist, and it also im-

poses penalties. I think the penalties should stand. I think if one is within the penalty clause of section 407, he should be liable. If he is not within the penalties of the section, we should not attempt to bring section 407 in here.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That would be acceptable, and I move that amendment.

It is moved that the words ' over-riding the provisions of section ' in the last line of section 8 be struck out and in lieu thereof the following added: ' relieving any person from the penalties as imposed by section.'

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
On section 9.

This is rendered necessary by section 8 of the reprinted Bill in order to work out the same effect. Section 295 is the excepting section, consequently it must be made to read in compliance with the new reading of section 294, which is the section imposing liability.
On section 10.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
This was part of a private Bill which I am putting in here as a government Bill. Hon. members will remember that this is a Bill which was introduced by the hon. member for Beau-harnois (Mr. Papineau). It means this: Last year we passed an Act providing that, where damage is done to property by a railway company up to their limit of liability, that is, $5,000, and that the party injured received insurance, the railway was practically relieved from paying damages to the amount of that insurance. Damages often exceed the amount of the insurance. Consequently, this section is to provide that the railway company, even though no negligence is shown, and though the injured party has received $5,000 insurance, is liable for the damage done by the railway up to the limit of $5,000. A section designed to provide for this case was passed by the Railway Committee; but, as I said before, I am merely adopting these and have the right to-amend them. I submitted the matter to the Minister of Justice, who made a little alteration in the draft which I submitted also to the chairman of the Railway Committee. It seems to accomplish the object and reads a little more smoothly. I propose the words approved by the Minister of Justice instead of the words included in the Bill. The words of the Bill on this point, as will be seen, are as follows:
_ Provided further that where there is any insurance existing on the property damaged the company shall only be liable under this subsection for the amount of such damage over and above the amount accepted or recovered by the assured by way of insurance Mr. LANCASTER.
upon the property, but where the company has used modern and .efficient appliances and has not otherwise been guilty of any negligence such liability shall not exceed the said sum of five thousand dollars.
Instead of these, I propose that the section shall read in this respect as follows:
Provided also that if there is any insurance existing on the property destroyed or damaged, the total amount of damages sustained by any claimant in respect of the destruction or damage of such property shall, for the purposes of this subsection, be reduced by the amount accepted or recovered for the benefit of such claimant in respect of such insurance

But will not this leave unprovided for the proviso of the section:
-but where the company has used modern and efficient appliances and has not otherwise been guilty of any negligence such liability shall not exceed the sum of five thousand dollars.	_
Unless we make it clear that $5,000 is^ to be over and above the insurance, I think the inference might be that the total amount must always be not more than $5,000, and that you deduct from the total amount the amount of insurance a man carries, so that his insurance is for the benefit of the railway company and not for himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that this language, if examined, will be found to cover the case that has been put in illustration. Take the case of a man whose loss is $10,000 and who has $5,000 of insurance, and consider whether or not it is covered by this language. It provides that where insurance exists on the property destroyed or damaged, the damage sustained by the claimant shall, for the purposes of this subsection, be reduced by the amount recovered in respect of such insurance. That is to say, in the case that we have been putting 'the total amount of damages sustained' is $10,000, and this amount ' shall for the purposes of this subsection be reduced ' by what? ' By the amount accepted or recovered ' in regard to the insurance. That is, the insurance recovered is $5,000, the total damage is $10,000, and the claim for the purposes of this subsection will stand as to the remainder.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is a point of legal construction. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) is clear in his opinion that the amount of the loss makes no difference as the clause has been drafted by him.

Whit we did in the Railway Committee was to make it clear, and I cannot understand why our clear statement should be struck out and that of the Minister of Justice substituted. We say in the Railway Committee that this man insures for his own benefit. Now, if

he is going to be limited to $5,000 when he is damaged $20,000, the company should pay that $5,000. II he is insured for $5,000 he should get $10,000 in all. That is what we say in the printed Bill, but the Minister of Justice strikes out that and says that the liability should be limited to $5,000. We have two liabilities in the previous part of the section. If there was no liability but the one stated in the previous part of the section, I would agree with the Minister of Justice. But there are two liabilities: the one is the absolute liability if they do not use proper appliances; the other is that if they do use proper appliances, they are only liable to $5,000. So there are two liabilities that we are dealing with in this reprinted Bill. The Minister of Justice speaks of liability. Which liability? Judges would undoubtedly differ in the interpretation of the term. I think the positive statement put in by the Railway Committee is clear and distinct and bad better remain.

The clause gave us considerable difficulty in the Railway Committee, and I think that the clause suggested bv the minister is much more clear than the one the Railway Committee put in. If I understand the amendment now proposed, it is that the amount of insurance shall be deducted from the total damage suffered; then, that the balance recoverable against the railway company shall be limited to $5,000, where the railway company have used proper appliances and have been guilty of no negligence, but unlimited where they have been negligent.
I think it says that the total damage is recoverable.

The total damage sustained; the insurance shall be deducted from that. If the company then has been guilty of no negligence, its loss is limited to $5,000; if it has been guilty of negligence or has not used proper appliances, there is no limit. I must say that the clause gave me some trouble, and when the amendment was first suggested, I did not agree with it; but after examining it I think it expresses our intention better than the clause drawn in the Railway Committee.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I may tell the committee now so as to save discussion later on, that the Government Railways Act as amended practically puts the government railways in the same position as other railways in regard to fires. I am giving notice of an amendment to be added in the Government Railways Act; so, while we are accepting the disabilities, we are also having advantages of the General Railway Act.
What good will it be if you do not give them the right to sue without a fiat?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We have passed an Act giving them the right to sue up to a certain amount in their own local court.

It will be limited to that small amount, $200.
On section 11-free carriage and reduced rates may be given in certain cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
This is another amendment, a portion of which is asked for by the railway employees. In brief this is to allow to former railway employees transportation if they wish; and also to allow Canadian companies to give the Interstate Commerce Commission reduced rates or free transportation if they desire.
On section 13-working agreements to be approved by board.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The real meaning of this is to include telegraphs in section 13. The original Act has only telephones, and I am putting telegraph companies in the same position.
Does this clause allow the government telegraph company to make an exclusive agreement with another telegraph company?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is to provide that all these agreements, agreements of telegraph companies as well as telephone companies, must be subject to the approval of the board. Heretofore, telegraph companies were not included in that section.
Does it apply to government telegraph companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I imagine not.
On section 14-safety at highway crossings.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
In passing the Act of 1909 we had a provision making it incumbent on railways to make protection to level crossings, constructed hereafter, at their own expense. In framing that Act, we used the words ' at the passing of this Act.' That means the passing of the original Act, as I am informed; and to make it clear that that clause was to be operative from the passing of the Act of last session, I am asking the committee to change the words to read ' 19th day of May, 1909.'
On section 15, rate of speed at certain crossings.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is a section which I wish to submit to the House with an explanation. My (hon. friend (Mr. J. A. Currie) introduced an amendment really to place the control of level crossings, as it was before, in the hands of the Board of Railway Commissioners.

Yes.
COMMONis

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have had representations from men in charge of fast trains, engineers, conductors and firemen, concerning the clause which we placed in the Act last year saying that no train could run over a level crossing where an accident had occurred during the preceding ten years, at a speed exceeding 10 miles an hour. That was considered very drastic. The object as I explained to the House was that there would be no difficulty in finding where the work of reducing level crossings should begin because where an accident had occurred there was a iprima facie case that it was a dangerous crossing. In its operation that is- found to be very drastic. The railway companies have instructed their employees to comply with this provision of the Act. That means that the fast trains cannot begin to make their time. I have had some experience of the fast trains on the Grand Trunk railway, and I have found that the Act works -out as contended by these men. Then I took the position with .the railways: Hurry up and fix your crossings. They pointed out that it was impossible to do that with sufficient rapidity to comply with the law.
They have had five years under the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The Act passed last year was very drastic and it was impossible to live up to it. The railway companies said:	Suppose you reduce that
irom 10 years to 5 years, tnen we will proceed with all rapidity to protect the crossings where accidents have occurred in the past^ 5 years, and then we will have to continue until all dangerous crossings are Trotected; in the meantime it will not work a hardship on us and will allow us to keep within the spirit as well >as of the letter of the Act, and at the same time hot disarrange all the traffic in relation to making time. The clause I submit to the committee reduces the time to five years so that trains can pass these crossings at a greater speed than 10 miles an hour if protected, leaving the other 5 years to he dealt with later. The proposition did not seem to me to be unreasonable, and I submit it to the House for consideration.
How much difference would it make in the running time of a train from Montreal to Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I would have to have a list of crossings. Take the International Limited, it would have to slow down to 10 miles; at every crossing where an accident had occurred within ten years. Slowing down scuh a train and getting up the momentum perhaps two or three times within 10 or 15 miles, consumes a good deal of time, and yet perhaps only one accident has ever occurred at a particular Mr. CURRIE.
crossing. Yet they have to stop or be criminally liable if anything should occur. It .places the employees in a very awkward position. They are expected to make time, and if they disobey orders and an accident occurs they will be criminally liable because the company has given them orders to comply with the Act. There is a difficulty 'both with the employees and with the company, and it struck me that it would be reasonable to reduce that period to 5 years, the company to pay attention immediately to as large a number of crossings as require. attention.

There is another aspect of this case. Consideration, of course, has been extended to the foot passenger and the driver, and the man who wants to travel on a fast train, hut no_ consideration seems to be given to the shipper. I have no hesitation in saying as a shipper that the operation of that clause has cost the shippers of this country $1,000,000 in added interest on goods delayed in transit. Take goods shipped from Sydney to western Ontario, they had been delayed nearly two weeks longer than they would have 'been under ordinary circumstances and when you ask the railway companies for an explanation they say that a freight train has to come to an absolute stop at each of these crossings, not to slow up to 10 miles as a fast passenger train does. When I came to analyse the question I found that 25 per cent of the accidents that have occurred at these crossings have occurred on crossings that would not be called dangerous crossings, most of the accidents have occurred through carelessness of the people themselves driving on the track where they could see the train openly for miles. There are carried on the railways of Canada each year 67,000,000 tons of freight, and when you stop the carriage of these goods for two or three weeks in a year the mere banking charge for carrying these goods for that time means a lot -of money. In shipping there is the haulage by the railway, there is the traffic charge, but there is a larger and more deadly charge 'because it goes on day and night, that is the interest that the banks or some one must be paying on the money value of these goods, and whilst this Bill may have benefited a few careless people, and perhaps have saved the lives of one or two innocent people I do not see why the business interests of the country should be held up on account of a section of this kind. If the section is amended so that the Railway Commission may order the train to stop at any crossing which they consider dangerous-and they have examined them all by this time I understand -and shall order that the train shall slow down to ten miles an hour until the

crossing is made right, we would have a more satisfactory condition and there would not he so much difficulty. The Railway Commission are really violating their oath of office every day. It is well known that in some cases they have given the railways (permission to cross where there has (been no protection put up, a few trees may have been cut out and the trains go on at the same speed. Some amendment is necessary. The present legislation involves a danger to the railway companies and to the men-because the man on a locomotive is as much afraid of an accident as the man driving a team on the road, because his life is in danger a man might drive a team of horses on a crossing, ditch the locomotive and kill the fireman and engineer just as easily as the locomotive might run down the team.
They never do it.

I remember a case fifteen years ago in which a horse got on the track, and upon a bridge and was struck by a locomotive, the result being that the engineer and fireman were killed. In delaying 65.000.000 tons of freight for three or four weeks in the year by this legislation it seems to me that you are taking a pretty bold, drastic stand. I am quite in sympathy with any legislation to protect what are considered dangerous crossings and to compel the railways to make the necessary arrangements to protect those crossings as quickly as possible. But why treat the subject in a blanket clause like that? There are crossings where men have been killed accidentally but where under ordinary _ circumstances, there can be no chance in the world of people being killed. They can see the train two miles away, but in some cases people try to beat the train. It is a very grave thing to stop all the traffic on these railwavs the way it is done now. A freight train has to come to a stop. It cannot slow down to ten miles an hour because the air will not apply on one of those long trains, and the train will break in two. If you have a train of fifty cars and apply the air you can stop the train, but you cannot slow it down, because if you try to, the train will part. I think the [DOT] government should consider this matter, and I believe that they would meet the case by inserting the words: ' if so ordered by the board '.

The effect is practically the same to-day as that contended for by mv hon. friend from North Simcoe. These trains cannot pass over any highway crossing at rail level at a greater speed than ten miles an hour if at such crossing an accident has happened, unless the crossing is protected to the satisfaction of the board. The board can order any protection
and in doing so it may say to the company: You do not need to do anything but clear away this embankment with which you are obstructing the view, or widening your track. We have had cases of that kind in the Niagara district. It does not cost the company more than a nitre bagatelle. By putting in their plans and showing their elevations the company mav be permitted to run without any special protection. The board have full power under this section to absolve them from any responsibility of this section under such circumstances as they see fit.
Where?'

By the very language of this section which I have just read. Trains are run as fast as they were ever run over crossings protected to the satisfaction of the board. The power of the board is nothing more nor less than the power to say what is absolutely necessary in order to protect the interests of the country.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
At six o'clock, House took recess.

speechtext:
House in committee on Bill (No. 210) to incorporate the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada.-Mr. Gervais.
On section 1,

The parties who are asking for this incorporation are a very important class of people; I think they represent the largest amount of capital of any class in Canada. I understand that they do not intend to go into business a3 an association; but if we allow this Bill to go through and give them incorporation,' it will combine all the retail merchants throughout this country, and they will be able to control prices, the number of stores, and everything of that kind in every town in Canada. They will be able also to control the wholesale people. Suppose there are five or six stores in a town, and a man wants to start another store. These people will have such power that they will be able to go to the wholesale men and say: We do not want you to sell goods to this store; if you do, the retail dealers throughout the country will not buy goods from you. In that way they will be able to control the retail business from one end of this country to the other. The great excuse they are giving for wishing to have this Bill passed at the present time is that the retail merchants will be able to compete v ith the great departmental stores of the coun-

try. It is true, the great departmental stores, such as Eaton's and Simpson's, are doing a great injury to the retail trade; but I maintain that this is not the proper way to deal with them. The retail dealers should go to the various provincial legislatures and get them to pass laws whereby each municipality could put a tax on all goods coming into the municipality from these departmental stores. I wish to protest against this Bill going through.

I fail to see the point our good friend is trying to make. Why should not the Retail Grocers' Association be entitled to the same rights and privileges as the Wholesale Grocers' Association or the Manufacturers' Asso?iation or the Shipping Federation, for which I had the honour of putting a Bill through this House, and it went through unanimously? If any of these associations could be said to represent a monopoly, as my hon. friend suggests, surely it "would be the Manufacturers' Association. I hope this Bill will go through, and with the unanimous assent of this House; there is no reason why it should not. Do not let us do injustice to the Retailers' Association, because there may be some little feeling against them. I do not think this House will stoop to that.

I wish to say, in reply to the hon. gentleman, that the people in western Canada know how much the Manufacturers' Association has hurt them. That association is taking undue toll from the people there to-day. Because we have put through other Bills, and allowed other combinations to work hardships on the producers of this country, is no reason why we should continue to do the same in this case.

When this Bill was before the House two or three days ago, I put myself on record as being opposed to it, and I want to do the same now. My hon. friend wants to know how it would be unreasonable to pass legislation in this House in favour of the Retail Grocers' Association when the Wholesale Grocers' Association has had Dominion legislation. Well, it seems to me that there is a good deal more necessity for wholesale business to receive Dominion legislation than retail business. Retail business is local, distributed all over this country; but wholesale business has necessarily to have its inteT-provincial connections in order to operate and to provide and distribute its supplies all over thi3 country. It does seem to me that this is purely provincial local legislation. I would like to call the attention of the committee to this institution which is asking for incorporation. In the last few days, a convention has been held in the Mr. W. H. SHARPE.
city of Toronto by the manufacturers of food products in this country, combined with the Wholesale Grocers' Exchange, at which representatives from the Retail Grocers' Association were present and dis->
cussed the food-supplying trade of this country; and what happened at that convention? This very association, which today is asking for powers from this parliament, entered into discussion and came to conclusions with the other parties _ represented, to arrange and maintain prices of food products in this country, and went further than that-intimidated the manufacturers who refused to enter into what they called the contract-selling system. All this happened in the last few days, and has been reported in the daily press. Now, my opinion is that what this institution wants is power from this parliament to combine with these other Dominion bodies for the purpose of fixing and maintaining high prices.at the cost of the consumers of this country. I think the evidence of the convention which has just been held, if the members of the committee have read the correspondence, will convince them that this is a very dangerous power to place in the hands of an association which, aftefi all, is simply a local institution doing business all over this country under local con-* ditions. There is not expressed on the face; of the Bill any necessity for Dominion legislation for the purpose of carrying on that business. Therefore, so far as I am concerned, I -want to put myself on record,) for those reasons, as being entirely opposed to the Bill.

I desire to reiterate my objections to the Bill. I took exception to it the other evening, and I have seen no reason to change my opinion. It is true that the promoter of the legislation claimed the other night that this was a purely benevolent institution which did not mean to go into any trade or business whatever. If that is the case I think they are coming to the wrong shop. I do not see why they should not secure their legislation from the provincial legislatures and the suspicion in my mind is that these gentlemen under the guise of this Bill are seeking powers that they feel confident they could not secure from the provincial legislatures. That is the reason they are coming to the Dominion parliament. It was pointed out by a former provincial secretary the other evening, one who ought to be conversant with the legislation of the province of Ontario, that all the powers necessary for this company could be secured under the Ontario Company Act. The only objection offered to that is that they wish to spread their business beyond the confines of the province of Ontario. What is there to prevent them doing exactly what the insurance companies or other companies do, and

registering, taking out a license in the other provinces. There is no reason whatever why they should not do that, and we may view with suspicion an association coming to the Dominion House to seek such wide powers as we find in the various clauses of this Bill, when the proper sphere to secure that legislation from, is the provincial legislature. Now the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Ralph Smith) has referred to the danger there is of those gentlemen associating together for the purpose of combining and raising prices. We are pointed to the fact that there is a combines Bill which has been amended and passed through this House. But, I think that Bill will not be of very much service to those who may invoke its aid, and I do not think it is at all necessary to impose upon the people of this country the burden of calling into requisition a combines Bill in order to strike at a possible combination of retailers. The hon. member from the St. Lawrence division of Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike) said why should we object to incorporating the retail groceries association any more than the wholesale grocers. Yes, and why should we object to incorporating the consumers of this country, such as members of this House did the other day. The very association which is now seeking incorporation were the principal objectors. They might not have been the cause of the defeat of the Bill, but they were represented there by their counsel to oppose it and they would have opposed it if that counsel had been heard. If they had shown a less selfish spirit and allowed the consumers to be incorporated to do business with their neighbours, their case might have been treated a little more leniently at the hands of the members of this House to-night. I think the retailers have no more reason for seeking incorporation here than the consumers, who were simply asking for poweT to do business among themselves. That was denied because the promoter of this Bill says it was detrimental to the public interest. Fancy the consuming population of this country, the masses, enacting legislation on their own behalf that would be injurious to themselves. It is a preposterous proposition and I take the position taken by some hon. gentlemen who have spoken on this subject that the legislation necessary should be sought at the hands of the provincial legislature and not here.

May I point out that this is a Dominion association and that it is a Dominion Act, an Act to incorporate the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada. Now, I ask, can such an association go to the province? It is said that because the promoter of this Bill, or some other gentleman appeared before this committee and asked that the Co-operation Bill be 267
thrown out, that this Bill should be thrown out. Surely we are not going to prosecute the retail grocers of Canada simply to have revenge on the member for St. James division (Mr. Gervais). Surely that is not the intention of this House.
That is not the idea.

I find myself on this subject in hearty agreement with my hon. friend from Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike). I can see no harm whatsoever in the principle of this measure. I greatly enjoyed the other day the banter which my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) addressed to the promoter of .this Bill on his inconsistency, but I fail to see that because the promoter of this Bill was inconsistent, my hon. friend (Mr. Smith) does not suffer a little the same way. Because, if he says that a member is inconsistent who opposed co-operation a little while ago and supports a similar principle now, I think inconsistency can be traced equally to him who supported co-operation a little while ago and opposes it now. I think there is a fallacy lying at the root of all that has been said by those who are opposing this measure. It is assumed that the retailers are asking for powers which they intend to exercise against the consumer. Now, that is not at all a safe conclusion. The wholesalers are now organized. May it not be that the retailers are seeking the powers in order to arm themselves against the wholesalers and in the interests of the consumers. But the elementary proposition is the one which was pointed out by my hon. friend from Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike) that every class of the community in the British empire has the right of combination. My hon. friend who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Roche) is a member of the medical profession, a profession to which I have the honour to bejong, myself, and we have both in this country and the old country our medical associations, whereby medical men combine for the protection of their legitimate interests. In my few remarks on the Combines Bill the other day, 1 pointed out that one of the struggles of the Liberal party in the last century in Britain, was for the right of workmen, and my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) knows it well, to combine in their trades unions. Legal gentleman have their combinations, employers have their combinations, in fact all men are to have their combinations except these retail grocers. I do not think that is a position which will be seriously taken up and maintained by any one in this House. I think it the more easy to support this measure because of the Act that was passed by parliament the other day. I pointed out at that time that there was no harm in combination, that combination was only harmful when it



acted in restraint of trade and in the raising of prices. But, all that is now perfectly safe in the hands of my hon. friend the Minister of Labour, and if this retail association shows that it is endangering for one moment the rights and interests of the consumers, we can safely leave it to be dealt with by the piece of legislation which went on the statute-books a few days ago.
Can my hon. friend point out to the committee any benefit that would accrue to the community by this Bill being passed?

Suppose the wholesalers are charging the retailers too much, will the retailers not have a better chance of buying well from the wholesalers if they are combined in a union. We all know that union is strength. I should think my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) sees that that is_ a perfect answer to his question. And if they buy better, they will sell cheaper to the consumers.

It is somewhat of a surprise to me to see that this Bill, which was considered some days ago, and the first section of which was defeated by the committee, is before the committee once again. When the promoter of the Bill asked that the vote on clause 1 be reconsidered, I understood that he wished merely an opportunity to withdraw gracefully when he found that the committee was not in a mood to sanction the passing of the Bill. Otherwise, as one who voted against clause 1 of the Bill, I certainly would not have given my consent-and I think others who voted as I did would not have given their consent-to the reconsideration of that vote. I thought the promoter of the Bill understood the action of the committee according to its true intent.
My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) thinks that those who are opposing this Bill are arguing from false premises. I do not agree with him on that point. In the first place, he draws a parallel between the trades unions of this country and the Retail Merchants' Association, and argues that because combination does good in one case it will do good in the other. There is no objection on my part, nor, I think, on the part of the committee, to the retail merchants of Canada having a voluntary association such as they have at the present time for the advancement of any interest that they may think it their duty to advance. But I would call the attention of my hon. friend from Red Deer to the fact tliat, as far as I know, not a labour or trades union in Canada is incorporated by an Act of this parliament or any other.
They are all incorporat-" ed by the general law.
My hon. friend (Mr. Gervais) says they are all incorporated
I think my hon. friend (Mr. Neely) was in the House when I introduced the Bill incorporating the Shipping Federation. If he was not, he should have been here.

I think not. But I still fail to see why this committee ought to assent to the incorporation by Act of this parliament of an association of the retail merchants of Canada. They have their association to-day, and they have the privilege of going to the various provinces and being incorporated under the Joint Stock Companies Acts of the provinces. I should think that they could secure all the powers they require in that manner. So far as I can see, all the names given in this clause 1 are names of people from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
What objection is there to that.

I do not find the names of any from any other provinces of the Dominion. Yet these gentlemen must be incorporated by Act of the parliament of Canada. Now, it is true that the medical men of the various provinces of Canada have their associations, but not under Dominion Act, their powers are obtained from the provincial legislatures. And I want to say to my hon. friend from Red Deer that, so far as the medical profession at least is concerned, there is no parallel between that case and the case of the retail grocers of Canada in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Will the hon. member (Mr. Neely) allow a question for information? With regard to the medical men, is it not true that a large number of them have been anxious to get Dominion incorporation, but cannot agree among themselves as to the terms?
This House has refused it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I thought they were unable to agree.

I have always understood that they have never been able to secure such incorporation. But, in any case, there is this difference between the case of the medical profession and that of the retail grocers, that, whatever protection is furnished by law of the provinces to the medical profession is furnished with the primary object of protecting the public from quacks and quackism. and not for the protection of the profession.
That is the object of our Bill exactly.

So far as the consumers, the public, are concerned, the incorporation by Act of this parliament of this association is certainly not intended primar-

ily for their benefit. That is the great and essential difference between this and the case of the medical profession-in one case, the statute is for the protection of the public, while in this case, if there is any benefit, it is purely and solely for those who are interested in having this incorporation brought about. I say, as I said when this Bill was before the committee on a former occasion, that very many possible evils lurk in this legislation should it come into effect. We should be giving to these gentlemen the prestige of an association incorporated by Act of the parliament of Canada. That would enable them in many ways to bring about a certain measure of coercion in so far as securing membership is concerned. They would be able to bring pressure to bear on the men engaged in the retail trade who are opposed
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question?
One momenG-who are opposed to the
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question?
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gervais) will not let me finish the sentence, I will give him the opportunity to ask the question.

I would ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Neely) to point out to the committee any word in the Bill to support his contention that the Retail Merchants' Association is seeking for power to establish a combine which will produce any of the many evils of which he speaks, but which he has not stated definitely. Let him mention one woTd in the Bill in support of his contention.

No matter what the ulterior object of the promoters of this Bill might be, we certainly do not expect them to state on the face of the Bill any such object. Most assuredly the Bill is drafted so as to appear on the face of it as innocent as possible. But 1 am simply stating the fact, that we are placing in the hands of these gentlemen, if we incorporate them by Act of this parliament, certain powers which they might very easily use to the disadvantage of the consumer, and the public. I have said that we give them the prestige of incorporation by Act of this parliament. By the aid of this prestige they would have great influence in coercing into their membership many of those in the retail trade who might not be willing to enter. Here is one way in which that might be accomplished. This association, let us say, is incorporated; it has its president, its executive and its secretary. Its representatives the towns and cities of this country, and we will suppose that they 267i
secure a large proportion of the retail tradesmen as members of the association. But there were some independent tradesmen who did not see it to their advantage to join this association. They see no need of it, they are getting along very well as it is without paying tribute to this association. Sir, this association in a very short time will be strong enough to go to the wholesalers of this country in a certain city or a certain town, and say to them: There are certain tradesmen who will not join our union, who will not come in as members of the Retail Grocers' Association. Now we say to you that you must not do business with these men. We have a right to protection the same as other trades unions, we have a right to have our association recognized by men who are occupied in that particular trade, and we say to you wholesale men that you must not sell those tradesmen unless they consent to become members of the Retail Grocers' Association. I am nqt saying that that appears in the Bill, of course it does not, but that is a power we will be putting into the hands of this association if we incorporate them by this Bill. There are other ways by which men might be coerced to become members of the association. It is a very simple matter, when a man is in business difficulties and finds himself hard pressed, for rumours to be circulated that he is getting into deep water, that he is not in the best financial circumstances, and it is an easy matter to undermine his credit. If a man is obstinate and refuses to join this association, I say there is another method by which his financial standing and his credit with the wholesalers, and with the public might be undermined.
Now, there is another consideration. I cannot for the life of me see why these retail grocers cannot have their local associations if they require them for the discussion of the betterment of trade conditions, and their own individual affairs, without incorporation by Act of parliament. When my hon. friend was introducing this Bill the other night he told us of many things that had already been done by the voluntary Retail Grocers' Association. Well, so far as the cities and towns of this country are concerned, I think they can very well look after their own interests by their organizations. For instance, there is hardly a little town in western Canada, and I understand it is so in the east, but has its board of trade, and I think the boards of trade in the cities and towns are quite capable of looking after the local commercial affairs of their respective centres. In the Bill that sets forth the objects of this association, nor in the remarks of the promoter of the Bill, have I found one single substantial reason giv.en why this Bill should be put through, why these

retail grocers associations should be incorporated. Let me call attention to another way in which the public of this country might be injured by this incorporation. Here is an association of a Dominion character having a membership in >every town and city in the Dominion of Canada. A certain individual in a certain town is unfortunate, he is in poor financial circumstances, he cannot pay his grocer's bill. What happens? That grocer refuses to give him credit. Is that all? I conceive the possibility that a man in straitened circumstances might seek to benefit himself by moving to another part of Canada, and by reason of this Dominion-wide association that man might be black-listed by every retail grocer from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I say that is a possibility. Does my hon. friend deny that that is one of the objects? Of course it is not so stated in the Bill, but does he deny that that is one of the objects? Of course he will deny it, he will sav that the obiect is to secure protection from poor creditors. But it may be protection in the way of a black-list against men who are unfortunate, and who cannot pay their grocer's Bill. I conceive that that will be one of the primary features in the incorporation of this association. Of course mv hon. friend will say that that is not in the Bill, and I am willing to agree with him.
But it is, in subsection 2, clause 2.

Whether it is or not, to my mind there is not a doubt but what the association would benefit its members in the way I have indicated. I hone I need not say anything more. I do not think that the sentiment of this committee has changed much from the last time the Bill was before us, when the first section was defeated. I do not want to block the Bill in any way, I am perfectly willing it should go to a vote.

Did my hon. friend say that the Medical Association of Canada was not incorporated?
Mr.. NEELY. No, I said that the medical nrofession had provincial protection. There is no Dominion law dealing with the medical profession.

I only wanted to direct my hon. friend to a slight inconsistency in his position. Let me remind him that he sat in the House last session and assisted in the incorporation of the Medical Association of Canada.
That was purely pro forma.

I have under my hand the clause of that Act which empowers the Medical Association to hold exactly the Mr. NEELY.
same value of property, $50,000, that is to be found in the Act under discussion.

The intention of the medical profession in applying to this parliament for incorporation, as alluded to by the Minister of Public Works, was to allow a professional man who had passed his examination to practise in any province in Canada. It was not to create an association for any purpose other than that.
That is not the Bill to which the Minister of Public Works referred.

The minister spoke of the application which it was the intention to make to this parliament this session, but which was not made. I was here the other night when the Bill now before the House was under discussion, it was put to a vote and voted down almost unanimously.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Then it was reconsidered.

I do not know how, in the face of the vote of the other night, there can toe a sufficient number of members present to-night to make a majority in favour of this Bill without any reason being advanced in the meantime to induce them to change their minds. If any one reads over the objects of this association he cannot "but come to the conclusion that it is a combination for purely commercial reasons, in so far as the retail merchants themselves are concerned, and must result in a combination to raise prices in Canada. We as a parliament have hitherto been rather favouring the interests of the corporations as opposed to the general public, and it is now time that the general public had some little show in the legislation passed by this House. It is time that the ordinary consumer comprising the great mass of the people, had some one to stand up for their interests as opposed to the corporations. I have seen no reason, I have heard no argument offered, to induce me to change my mind from what appeared to be the general opinion of this committee when this Bill was up before.

T have listened to the discussion on this Bill, and have come to the conclusion that the only reason the Bill is being opposed is that the retail merchants came down here in a large body and opposed the principle of co-operation.
Oh, no.

My hon friend says no, but I heard my hon friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) the other night use that as his main argument, and I heard the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) to-night, use practically the same argument.
No, you did not.

I was present in the Committee on Banking and -Commerce when the question of co-operation was discussed. There were no retail merchants there. A vote was taken and I voted for the principle of co-operation myself, because I am not opposed to it; if it will assist the people to buy more cheaply, I.am in favour of it. The Bill was defeated on a vote of 10 to 8. I supported the measure, because I wanted to hear it discussed in the House of Commons, as I am not unfavourable to that principle. The objects of the proposed Bill seemed to me to be very harmless. It: has been argued by various members that the association should ask incorporation from the various provinces. If I understand the principle of granting incorporation to various organizations, prima facie, where a body of men are carrying on business in various provinces, this is the proper place for them To come, and it is only* a question for us to consider what rights we shall give. I fail to see anything very harmful in the objects of this Bill. It has been argued that they will create a combine. If that is the case,'they can be prosecuted under the Criminal Code. The great majority of the arguments against the proposed measure seem to me, to be very hazy, and to depend on something that may occur in the future, so that they do not constitute any objection to the Bill at all. Clause 2 of the Bill says:
The objects of the association shall be the promotion of the industrial and commercial interests of the retail merchants of Canada, the collection and publication of information and statistics, &c.
So with the rest of the section^ there is nothing with respect to the carrying on of business. This association is being formed for the purpose of obtaining information which will be beneficial to its members, and if I understand the proposition, it is similar to a Bill which we passed the other day respecting the Dominion Millers' Association.

If the object of this Bill is not to form a combination and to affect prices, what object would a merchant in the province of Quebec have in common with a retail merchant in Saskatchewan in joining the association?

I can only refer to clause 2 of the Bill and say that the object in joining the association would be to get information. I cannot see any argument in stating that this association is going to increase prices. No information has been placed before the House as to that. It does not say so in reciting the objects of the association. My hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) says it would not say so in any
case. But we must find within the four corners of the Act the object for which an association is incorporated, and I fail to see anything that would lead me to oppose the Bill. I have heard clause 8 discussed, which says they may accept, endorse and become parties to promissory notes and bills of exchange. That might lead us to think they intended to carry on commercial operations, but I find that this is to be for the purposes of the association, and in clause 2 I fail to see anything which will lead me to believe that they are going to carry on a large retail business ot attempt to enhance prices.

After an experience of 25 years in the retail business, I am satisfied that you cannot get that harmony and unanimity amongst retail men that will bring about an enhancement of prices. I do not fear at all that any such combination can be brought about amongst retail men even if this Bill is adopted. I would support this Bill if it were nothing more than one clause-clause (d), section 2. I think it is a good clause:
The procuring and furnishing to its members information as to the solvency of persons who deal with any of its members.
To my mind that clause is worth all that is in it.	i

The hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Henderson) thinks that there would not be unanimity enough to enable them to accomplish any of the objects of a combination, but if my hon. friend had read the proceedings of the meeting of the Wholesale and Eetail Grocers' Association in Toronto during this week he would have found that they have a great deal of power to do that very thing. They are proposing now that the manufacturers should make a price at which any particular article should be sold to the consumer, that neither wholesaler nor retailer shall be able to compete one with another. subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: I would like to know if this Bill takes the control of these water-powers from the local government and transfers it to the Dominion government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: What is called the railway belt of British Columbia is a strip 20 miles wide on each side of the Canadian Pacific railway from the eastern boundary of the province to nearly its western boundary. This is land that became the property of the Dominion by reason of the agreement made with the province of British Columbia in regard to the construction of a Pacific railway. The ownership of the land is vested in the Dominion. Until comparatively recently the administration of water rights within the railway belt was carried on by the provincial government. The provincial government administered the water rights in the railway belt as well as in the other parts of the province. There was always 'Some question as to whether the right of administration of water in the railway belt properly rested in the province or in the Dominion. However, the province was exercising the right and the Dominion was not contesting it, but it was so uncertain that the right was in the province that on several occasions, where large works were being carried forward, the parties who were interested in the -water rights in connection with these works, having received authorization from the provincial government, came to the Dominion government for a confirmation of their rights. In certain cases where large amounts of money were involved, the parties who secured the water-rights from the British Columbia government, in order to make themselves secure in their title, came to the Dominion and got a quit claim from the Dominion. ' I point this out to show that the question of title was always in doubt. At last, the issue was raised. A case was entered in the Exchequer Court, and that court gave a decision to the effect that the right to water in the railway belt was vested in the Dominion and not in the province. The case was then appealed to the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court has given a decision confirming that of the Exchequer Court. The case is again being appealed to the Privy Council, and until the Privy Council has decided, the question is not settled.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: Did that decision go to the length of holding that after the land was alienated, the Crown by virtue of the Dominion would still control?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

I cannot answer that question. I am merely stating the facts as I understand them. As soon as the decision of the Exchequer Court was given the province ceased granting water rights within the railway belt. They took for granted, whether wisely or unwisely, that that decision set aside their Jurisdiction

for the time being. The result of that decision is that the water rights which were granted by the province within the railway belt have no standing in law.
