speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: Does it strike the minister to be a wise thing to legislate in that state of affairs, with the question of our authority being liable to disappear as a possible effect of the judgment of the Privy Council?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
That is what I am trying to convince the House of. Let me repeat that, as I am advised, from the decision of the Exchequer Court the rights granted by the province within the railway belt have no legal status, and will not have any unless and until that decision is reversed by the decision of the Privy Council. That means that rights of serious importance 'within the railway belt, which should be maintained in legai status, have not that legal status. There is a chaotic condition, then, in regard to water rights
within the water belt. That is a very undesirable condition, and what we want to do by means of this Bill is to say that these rights, which have been invalidated by the decision of the Exchequer Court, shall be, under the conditions set out in the Bill, re-established by the authority of this parliament, so far as this parliament has authority to do that.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: I am informed that there is a possibility of the Privy Council taking up this case next fall. Has the minister any information as to that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
I understand that leave has just been granted for the hearing of the case by the Privy Council. I cannot say how soon a decision will be reached; no person can say that. There is good hope that it will not be interminably delayed. But it makes no difference whether it is one month or six months or six years, during the interval these important rights have not that legal status to which they are properly entitled, and I conceive it to be the duty of this parliament not to allow that condition of affairs to continue. So long as this parliament has jurisdiction, it is its business to re-establish those rights. That is one proposal of the Bill. The other proposal is this: There are large investments of capital at present and in prospect. There is the work of irrigation, which is necessary throughout a large part of the railway belt, and neither tlm investments of capital nor the work of irrigation should be hampered if it can be avoided. The Bill, then, in another part assumes that the decision of the Exchequer Court will be upheld, and authorizes the Governor in Council to grant licenses for water rights within the railway belt.
It may be said that it is not wise for parliament to take or give that power when the power may shortly be taken away by a reversal of the decision of the Exchequer Court. But on the other hand it does not seem to me to be wise that the development of (power or the work of irrigation in the railway belt should for any reason be delayed, certainly not because of any lack of legal right in the matter. Now, so long as the legal right was assumed to rest with the provincial government, the provincial government granted 'all rights that were required, and when 'the parties got those rights they came to thisi government andi got a quitclaim. The British Columbia government not now being in a position as I am advised to grant rights, this parliament may assume to itself the power to grant rights. And persons coming to this government under the proposed legislation and getting rights may go to the province of British Columbia or to the provincial government of British Columbia and get a quitclaim

of the provincial rights., just as under the former conditions an applicant went to the .provincial government and came to us_ and got a quitclaim. The abject of this Bill is to validate existing rights, and to provide for continuous development of the water privileges in the railway belt. Notwithstanding the litigation that is now in progress, that is the whole purpose of the Bill. That is all we have in view. We consider it [DOT]absolutely necessary in the line of good government and for the safety of capital, and for the continuous development of the railway belt. For that reason we ask the House to agree to it.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
If what has just been described by the minister in his last few sentences were the scope of the Bill I do not think it would be open to very much objection. But unfortunately the Bill goes very much further than that. I have had occasion to look into it with more care than I would usually bestow upon a matter affecting rights in British Columbia, by reason of the fact that I happen to be acting as solicitor and counsel in a rather heavy case, now pending before the Exchequer Court of Canada in regard to certain water rights in British Columbia. On account of the case no doubt my attention has been drawn particularly to the various clauses of this Bill. I think the object of the minister is a most laudable and proper one in seeking to. give definite confirmation to rights which may be more or less in jeopardy owing to the uncertainty of the matter as it now stands, as between the jurisdiction of the province of British Columbia and of the Dominion of Canada. But I would point out to my hon. friend the minister that the decision of the Exchequer Court was given in the month of May, 1909, just a year ago. The case went to the Supreme Court, was decided in the Supreme Court last December, the judgment of the Exchequer Court being upheld, and it has now gone to the Privy Council. Leave to appeal was granted the_ day before yesterday, and in all probability the matter will be argued and probably decided by the Privy Council at its sittings in mid-summer, probably in one or two or, at most, .three months. I should think under the circumstances it would ibe reasonable for the minister to allow this measure to stand over until the next session of this House, some time next fall. By that time 1 nave no doubt we will have the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and we will know just what the rights of the respective governments are in regard to the waters in the railway belt of British Columbia. I think if the only object of the minister is to confirm existing rights that can be done in a single clause and capital Mr. OLIVER.
will not be left in uncertainty or jeopardy. A single clause will be all that is necessary by way of confirmation of rights granted by British Columbia or of rights granted by the Dominion of Canada. But my hon. friend the minister has. gone much further than that in his Bill. He has sought to wipe out common law rights, the rights of riparian owners in British Columbia, a matter which I should say this parliament has nothing to do with. He has sought also to introduce a licensing system to be carried on under regulations which are not laid down in the Act, and which are to foe hereafter prescribed by orders in council. He has given other rights in regard to expropriation which particularly affect the case in which I am interested in the Exchequer Court.
Now, if these matters are to be legislated on in this Bill, I can only say to my hon. friend the minister that at this late hour of the session, he has stirred up about as contentious a measure as we have had before us this parliament, and certainly one of the most intricate measures. The interests involved are almost innumerable. In the first place there are those people who own land in the railway belt, who acquired their land before confederation. I know of the case of one man who is now a suppliant in the Exchequer Court, and who got his land from the old Crown colony before British Columbia entered confederation. He claims common law rights as a riparian proprietor which this Bill seeks to take away from him. There is another class of persons who obtained their land from British Columbia after confederation, _ but before the conveyance in 1880 from British Columbia to the Dominion of Canada. They have rights to be protected. There is a third class who obtained their land after the transfer from British Columbia to the Dominion of Canada, by patent from the Dominion government. That land has been alienated by the Dominion government. And then there is a balance of land remaining now, so far as proprietary ownership goes, in the Dominion of Canada. These various rights have to be safe-guarded in this Bill. Then there are other interests to be looked after. There are persons who have obtained water rights in the province of British Columbia and unconfirmed by the Dominion government. There are others who have obtained water rights which have been confirmed by the Dominion government by way of a quitclaim deed as my hon. friend the minister has announced. And there are others such as my clients, the city of New Westminster, who have both land and water rights in the railway belt granted to them by order in council, not by a quitclaim deed, but by an order in council.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: By which government?

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
This government, and it is now the subject of litigation in the Exchequer Court. I understand from a conversation with my hon. friend, the minister that he is quite willing to put a clause in this Bill protecting the rights of litigating parties. That is usually done and I am content with that. But, there is another clause in the Bill which might wipe out the effect of any judgment which the Exchequer Court might give. I mention this case because it is a case of a good deal of prominence, and of a great deal of consequence in the province of British Columbia. It is a case in which the city of New Westminster acquired by an order in council, a grant of 18,000 acres of land and the water on the land, as we maintain, in the railway belt. The water was procured for a special purpose and the land was granted for the protection of the lake where the water came from. That was done by an order in council by this government in 1902. After the decision had been given by the Exchequer Court last summer, the Vancouver Power Company came to Ottawa and made application for rights in that same water and upon that same land. The order in council of seven years ago was cancelled and a new order in council issued granting the rights that formerly belonged, as the city contends, to the city ot New Westminster to the Vancouver Power Company. It is upon that question that the city have on a flat obtained from the government entered a petition in the Exchequer Court.	But the point is this. If
the action succeeds, if it be declared that the city of New Westminster is entitled to hold its land and is entitled to the waters which it obtained, any power company having a license from this government under the present legislation can immediately expropriate New Westminster of all its lands and all its water.
That is my own particular interest in regard to this pending legislation. But I also look to the broader question, and I submit that the broader question is one of too great intricacy to be dealt with in the closing hours of the session; there are too many interests to be looked into, too many interests to be safeguarded and very large interests too. I am told that some of the power companies of that province have investments of $20,000,000 and others have large though not so large, amounts. It may be that the title of all these com-.panies is more or less uncertain under the "decision of the Exchequer Court. I agree that some confirmation might well be given, but let it be by some simple enactment without attaching a licensing qualification which this Bill seeks to attach, without interfering with riparian and private rights, as this seeks to do, and with- [DOT] out prescribing regulations by order in council, which no one knows anything about as is proposed under this Bill. These are all proper matters for legislation, I admit, but I do not think that this is the time for that legislation. If the excuse is to confirm doubtful or uncertain rights, I say, by all means confirm them, but do not go further pending a decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. If that decision upholds that of the Supreme Court and I am bound to sav that I believe it will-there is no doubt that this government has power to regulate the waters in the railway belt of British Columbia. I think a comprehensive measure should then be brought forward and passed, proper regulations framed, licenses issued, and the government should take control of rates and tolls; but to do all that for the purpose of holding it for three or four months until a decision can be reached is, ,1 think, absurd. I would urge the minister to pass, in one clause, the confirmation he speaks of, and allow the matter of his Bill to rest until the Judicial Committee has decided this question. Next session we shall have the. decision one way or the other, and when that decision is reached, we can legislate with some intelligence on the subject. For, I am free to say, that I do not know when a more difficult question has come before this House. Far greater lawyers than I am, or can ever hope to be are very much puzzled as to the respective rights in these matters. The province of British Columbia conveyed a large block of land to the Dominion of Canada, there is no doubt. The Dominion of Canada obtained proprietary rights in that land. Did it obtain legislative rights? I doubt it very much. Could the Dominion, for instance, establish a municipal institution there? I say they could not; such matters are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the province.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: You say the Dominion became land-owners?

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
Yes, they have pro-priatory as distinct from legislative rights. But the decision of the Exchequer Court is that, on the Dominion's own land, at all events, they have the right to regulate the waters flowing therein. I know a case where a stream rises outside the railway belt, flows through a portion of it and then on into private property. Can it be said that the government has the right to pass legislation affecting the flow of that water, and the use of it though only a small portion of its flow is within the railway belt? These are some of the questions that come up. I would urge upon the minister, for the sake of peace, and for the sake of this legislation and do justice to

all concerned, that he should, as he proposes by the statement he has made introduce some legislation by way of confirmation, and nothing more. It would be only a provisional Bill in any case. It may be upset in a few months. I understood the confirmation was to last for two years. But I think the minister is on dangerous ground if he goes further, and it is hardly a proper time to bring in legislation so intricate and comprehensive as the present Bill.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
A large portion of this territory is in my own riding, so this. Bill is of great interest to me. I have a good deal of sympathy with the view put forward by my bon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), and I think the minister, if he could see his way to it, would do better to put through a Bill with a simple clause validating existing rights and providing a modus vivendi until the matter is settled. In the dry belt of British Columbia, in which this land is largely situated, there would be many complications if this Bill is put through in its present form. Many of these difficulties have been pointed out by the hon. member for South Wellington. If we look forward even to the Privy Council confirming the decision of the Exchequer Court, there are many sections of the Bill which, to my mind, call for serious consideration. For instance, there is the validation of the records since 1880 and up to May, 1910. But, under this clause, they are validated only for two years, and, after that, practically all the provincial records, as I understand the Bill, would be wiped out, and the decision as to private record holders would be left to the Dominion government. From our point of view of the question of jurisdiction, it would be wiser to leave all these things to the province. The question arises.: Will they confirm the private records as they passed, or will they confirm them as we are doing now in the province, because we have recently passed a comprehensive Act in which we are going to alter the records and apportion the water in a fairer way, and give the users the benefit of the somewhat limited supply that exists in some districts. So far as irrigation is concerned, as the hon. minister knows, nearly every creek in the dry portion is recorded up to the full, that is as far as low water is concerned. Then, there is the question concerning water arising outside the railway belt, and a lot of similar questions that, it seems to me, would give rise to complications under this Bill. I confess, as I have said, that I think the suggestion of the hon. member for South Wellington, if the minister can see his way to accepting it, would be a happy solution of the difficulty-a simple Bill with a validating Mr. GUTHRIE.
clause, and providing a modus vivendi pending the settlement.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: I cannot see the clause which has the effect spoken of by the hon. member for South Wellington of taking away private or riparian rights.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: Section 4.

speechtext: It certainly preserves them.

speechtext: I have read it-it certainly preserves them. The last clause relating to riparian rights merely refers to riparian rights in Crown property, not in respect of property already granted by the Crown. And, in any case, the saving clause to which, as my hon. friend intimated, the minister has expressed his assent, that the Bill should not interfere with vested rights or pending litigation will cure any danger of that kind. It seems to me that it is necessary not merely that existing rights should be confirmed, but that there should not be a hold-up of all business in that belt by reason of the want of power in the Governor in Council of Canada to act. We must take it that at the present time, these rights are vested in the Governor in Council. Having considered the matter, I cannot see that, while the case is pending before the Privy Council any one would make a large investment under a grant made under regulations of tbfi Governor in Council. He certainly would make no large investment under such a grant without getting it confirmed by the province of British Columbia. It seems to me also that my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) is a little too sanguine when he expects a decision of the Privy Council in a week or two. I have had some experience with the Privy Council, and I know that it is not the custom of that body to give a decision within a month of two after leave to appeal has been given. If a decision comes within a year, it will exhibit the usual activity of the Privy Council in respect of such matters.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: They hear these cases in July.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
Leave was only granted yesterday, and it would be impossible that that appeal should be brought on in July. With respect to the other question that has been raised as to water outside the belt, this legislation cannot interfere with that. With respect to the rights of the Dominion within the twenty mile belt as to streams passing through it, this Act does not increase in the slightest the rights of the Dominion, or take away from the rights of the province. The Dominion can only exercise those rights with due regard to

the rights outside, as an ordinary proprietor could. They can divert the water, but they must return it to the stream exactly as it was before. It seems to me it is essential that this Bill should apply not merely to the confirmation of existing rights, but to make sure that 'any one can act who receives something in the nature of a confirmatory grant from the province of British Columbia. There may be some objectionable features in some of the sections of the Bill; I do not know about that, but at all events, they can be dealt with as we reach them.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend has misapprehended the meaning of clause 4 in regard to riparian rights, which says:
Also saving the right of every riparian owner in the use of water for domestic purposes as that expression is defined in this Act.
But domestic purposes is not the only right of a riparian owner, that is one of the purposes that is saved to him, that is his common law right, and he can do what he pleases with the water provided he returns it to the stream and does not interfere with the man below him. But the only right preserved to him under this section is to use water for domestic purposes. He may run machinery, he may do what he pleases with it, so long as -he returns it, and allows the joint proprietor the natural flow of that water uncontaminated.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: I do not understand that the Act intends to take away from any present riparian owner any of those rights which he now has; it merely provides that in grants of that land there shall be preserved to him in the ordinary manner the riparian rights as defined by this Act. This Act can never be interpreted as taking away any personal right which he has already. It can only be interpreted as limiting the rights which a riparian owner will have under the rights hereafter granted by the Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
Well, I w'ould be very much surprised to learn that after the Exchequer Court of Canada had decided that the British Columbia government has no property in, or right to deal with, water rights within the railwav belt, and after that decision has been confirmed by the Supreme Court, I would be surprised to learn that the British Columbia government was still continuing to act as if it owned the water rights, and as if such judgment had never been given. The law to-day, notwithstanding an appeal to the Judicial Committee, is that these water rights are vested in the Dominion government; that is the law, and until the judgment of the Supreme Court is reversed, all inferior courts are bound to take notice that this is the law'. If, on appeal to the Privy Council, the decision should be reversed, of course, then the law would be different from what we must all understand it to be to-day. While upon my feet, I desire to say that I feel that my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) who has had occasion to give close attention to the rights of parties who might possibly be affected by this legislation, has approached the discussion of the subject in the fairest possible spirit. I do not think he and the minister are very far apart in their view of what is really the object to be aimed at. I understand that what the minister seeks by this Bill is to preserve the status quo so far as any'rights have been granted by the British Columbia government. He recognizes, and my hon. friend from South Wellington recognizes also, that an enormous amount of capital

has been invested, upon the idea that the British Columbia government had power to deal with these water rights. Now, the minister desires, and I am sure my hon. friend from South Wellington, and no doubt every hon. member of this House, would desire that those rights shall be preserved as far as possible, and that the capital wdiieh has been invested in these great undertakings should be protected to the fullest possible extent. I think all will agree with the Minister of the Interior upon that point. Now, the minister seeks, by section 6, to safeguard the interests of the capitalists; in that particular. The next question is as to whether all existing rights are preserved. It is desired, I think by all, I am sure it is desired by the minister, that no existing rights should be interfered with. As to that, I am bound to say that it is just possible that the new section 4 is not quite as broad as it should be. I am inclined to think myself that it would be only right and proper that the rights of every riparian owner, whatever they may be, not simply to the use of water for domestic purposes, but whatever those rights might be, should be preserved and not interfered with in any way by this Act. Then I understand the only other serious objection which myf hon. friend from South Wellington raises is that if the Governor in Council were to issue a license under section 9, the licensee might have power to expropriate land under the provisions of the Railway Act, and so in that way interfere with vested rights. I think myself the suggestion of my hon. friend is well worthy the consideration of the Minister of the Interior. I know he does not desire to have any provision in the statute which would at all imperil or jeopardize the rights which already exist in the city of New Westminster or in any other municipal or other body. It seems to me we might well enter upon the consideration of this Bill, and as we come to different sections suggestions might be made which I have no doubt will be carefully considered by the minister, and it may be that we could get together, knowing that we all have practically the same object in view, to protect the status quo, to protect capital, pending the final decision of the Judicial Committee, and also to safeguard existing rights. Having these objects in view, it should be possible in the different sections to so safeguard the Bill as to carry out the views which we all, I think, entertain.

herfei the judgment of the Exchequer court. I do not read that judgment as declaring that this parliament has legislative .power. Mr. PUGSLEY'. I am inclined to think it would too.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
He might pay me the compliment of believing that I would not advance such a foolish argument until 1 have stated my position. The court has not decided that the Dominion has sole jurisdiction to legislate for these lands. What has happened is that the government as owners of property, just as .they own the Welland canal, have a right to object to that property being interfered <with or confiscated. The judgment of the Exchequer Court is that a certain grant which the Dominion government was asking them to hold invalid is invalid and conveyed no interest to the defendant company. Why? As being an interference with property subject to the exclusive authority of the Dominion of Canada, that is property over which the Dominion government has a right to exercise rights of ownership. Second, 1 bev cause the diversion of water-power therein will be a serious interference with the navigation of the river and thirdly because it is not in accordance with the Water Concessions Consolidation Act of the province of British Columbia of 1897. This implies that if there was any legislation of British (Columbia which had undertaken to properly deal with this matter it would have had some force and effect in the opinion of the judge of the Exchequer Court because he says it is not authorized by a certain statute of British Columbia. The judgment continues. :
And this court does therefore order and adjudge that the beforementioned grant of the 7th of April, 1906, be cancelled.
It seems to me we are undertaking to assume that legislative authority has been given to us, but on that judgment that matter has never been decided. The judge merely gives to the Dominion of Canada,

as to any other owner of property, a right to object to interference or trespass or confiscation of that property and says that the province of British Columbia had not legislated to interfere with such ownership. Therefore, the person who claimed those rights had no standing for want of that legal authority from the statute of British Columbia and because the Dominion of Canada was the owner of property affected by it. As the hon. member for South Wellington has said, legislative power to control a title t-o lands is one thing, but the ownership of land, say the Intercolonial, does not give the Dominion government the right to legislate in New Brunswick in respect to matters not within the jurisdiction of the Dominion. I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Guthrie) that -this matter is full of very serious complications, and I do not think it is wise for the government at this stage of the session to press such a controversial matter as this, which will be very far-reaching in its effect from one end of Canada to the other. It will affect every province, and every interest of every province.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
No doubt the question is complicated, but it is the duty of parliament to deal with questions, whether complicated or otherwise, if the public interest requires that they shall be dealt with. Our duty is to bring to bear the best intelligence we have, and the best methods we have of dealing with these difficult, 'complicated and) important questions. As to the legislative authority in regard 'to this matter, if there is any doubt about that the sooner that doubt is set at rest the better. Every one will agree on that point, and the way to set that question at rest is to exercise legislative authority and then the matter is brought to an issue forthwith. This question of water rights in the railway belt of British Columbia is, we all agree, of such great importance that we cannot afford to leave a particle of doubt in regard to the jurisdiction, either as to property rights or legislative jurisdiction. It is in the interest of every one that the question should be brought to an issue as quickly and plainly as possible. The question of legislative jurisdiction will certainly be raised by the passing of this Bill; I believe that the sooner it is raised the sooner it will be settled, and the sooner it is settled the better for British Columbia, and for everybody else. The Deputy Attorney General of British Columbia was here some time ago in consultation with the Department of Justice in regard to matters affecting the province and this question was under discussion between the Department of Justice and the Deputy Attorney General of British Columbia. The Deputy Attorney General of British Columbia and
the Department of Justice at Ottawa agreed that certain amendments would be right and proper. I shall read these amendments;
I	assume that the Attorney General was satisfied that they safeguarded the interests of the province, and I assume that the Department of Justice was satisfied that the interests of the Dominion were fully represented in them. The first amendment is to strike out section 3 as it stands at the present time and substitute the following:
This Act applies to all lands within the railway belt in the province of British Columbia as herein defined: Provided that nothing in this Act shall be construed to affect any riparian rights or rights to water in or appurtenant to those lands described in section
II	of the terms of union between the Dominion of Canada and British Columbia as held under pre-emption right or by Crown grant, or to affect any riparian rights or rights to water in or appurtenant to lands which haying been heretofore granted by the Crown in the right of Canada are not now vested in the said Crown.
I think it will be agreed that this proposed change of section 3 covers a number of the important points raised by the hon. member for South Wellington. When we come to the consideration of the section I will move that this be substituted. It was agreed that section 6 should be amended by striking out the words between the word ' issued ' in the fifth line and the word * two ' in the eighth line, and substituting therefor th.e words ' prior to the passing of this Act '. The effect of this would be that all rights granted up to the passing of the Act would be confirmed, or would be eligible for confirmation, whereas, as the Act stands now, it is only rights granted up to the date of the decision of the Exchequer Court. Then, I woujd further propose as section 11:
That nothing in this Act contained shall affect any vested right or pending litigation.
With these amendments the Department of Justice of Ottawa and the Deputy Attorney General of British Columbia were both satisfied, and I would ask the committee to accept them when we come to their consideration.

I think that the amendment just proposed by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) with

regard to the question of riparian rights probably gets over the difficulty I referred to. I am quite satisfied that the difficulty did exist in that acute form under the Biil as drawn, and I am also quite satisfied that this will protect the rights and property of the riparian proprietors. But the other sections remain, to my mind, just as objectionable. The minister knows much better than I do what the view of the government and the Deputy Attorney General of British Columbia may be, but my information is that so late as the day before yesterday telegrams passed objecting to the Bill-I do not know with what department-but the objection came, as I am informed, from the British Columbia government, accompanied by the request that nothing be done pending the appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. However, as to that my information may not be accurate. Clause 4 certainly is 'one of the most objectionable clauses in the Bill, and they do not seek to alter it. I have not been able very clearly to find out what the latter half of clause 4 really means. If it is intended by that language to establish all rights that have been granted by British Columbia or by the Dominion parliament heretofore, they 'have gone about it in a very clumsy fashion. The particular language that I refer to is this:
Unless, and until, and except only so far as some right therein, or to the use thereof, inconsistent with the right of the Crown, and which is not a public right or a right common to the public, is established.
These two last words certainly imply that the owner of a private right has to do something to prove and establish that right either before my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior or before some court. He may have his deed or order in council, but it is of no use to him until he takes some subsequent step to establish that right. I know of instances in British Columbia where parties have both orders in council from this government and from the British Columbia government and quit claim "deeds from this government. These rights are not established by that clause, but these parties must come to the Department of the Interior, submit their proofs and establish their rights if they can establish them. As the minister says that it is his intention to confirm rights, I ask for a substantive clause that such rights be and the same are hereby confirmed. Then, if the clause suggested by the minister is placed in the Bill I do not think the Bill can be very much objected to, particularly if the clauses with respect to regulations, licenses and defining the rights as to water he stricken out. That would limit the Bill, merely in the first place, to declaring the rights of the Dominion government, and, secondly to the confirmation of rights heretofore granted, and thus protect the rights of the riparian owners.

speechtext: I have a good deal of difficulty in seeing what is the purpose of this Bill, by section 4, declaring that these things are vested in the Crown which I understand to be the Crown in the right of Canada. Is not that precisely the question that the Privy Council is going to decide one way or the other? Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: Yes, that is correct.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: Then, what is the purpose of our declaring that these things are vested in the Crown in the right of Canada while we have a pending suit as to whether they are or are not? Upon this question at the present time we stand in the same position as any other litigant, and we are trying to make a title unto ourselves by declaring that these things are vested in the Dominion of Canada, a declaration which the Privy Council may make in a few months, or which the Privy Council may deny in a few months. I am at a loss to see what we gain by making a declaration of that kind when the question as to whether that declaration is true or not depends upon the interpretation to be put upon the effect of the agreement established by the statute, as I understand it, of British Columbia. This question will have to remain open until the Privy Council decides it. It may be that I do not grasu the effect of this legislation, but perhaps if I do not grasp it that is a reason why it may be inferred that there are other members of this House who do not quite grasp it. If this legislation cannot go over, as this has been our first opportunity of dealing with it, it might be well for the minister to give members of this House an opportunity of looking into it so as to place themselves in a position to deal with it intelligently. If the minister is not prepared to let the legislation absolutely go over, I would suggest that he at least let it stand for the time being until we can have an opportunity to look into it and get an understanding of it. I admit that it is only this evening that my attention has been called to this Bill, and in the examination that I have been able to give to it I have had difficulty to grasp its significance. I am unable to see the wisdom of passing legislation declaring that we have a title when the question whether we have one or not is pending before a court whose decision we can reasonably .expect to have in a few months. I think the minister might at least consider the advisability of letting the Bill stand over until to-morrow or the next sitting day so that we can look seriously into it.

Yes, very real. In evidence of that I find that in the Irrigation Act there is a parallel clause, and for exactly that reason; and one reason why we have so little litigation in regard to water rights on our western prairies as compared with the prairie states, is because of this declaration of ownership on the part of the government in these water rights. As I understand the situation, the water rights of the railway belt in British Columbia are not in possession of either government at the present time, and what is wanted is a declaration by this government that so far as it is concerned, it has the right to these waters, and that any right acquired must be acquired from this government. That begins a title, and without such declaration there is a possibility of title being acquired by possession or occupation, or other means, which only tends
to litigation and to confusion. That is the reason for this section.

speechtext: Does not the hon. gentleman think that the very litigation which he wants to avoid will be multiplied by our acting now, pending the decision of the Privy Council? speechtext: No, it is a Bill to avoid litigation. The only question is in regard to the assumption of possession by the Dominion and the granting of rights under that assumption. I maintain that it is just as necessary that the Dominion should make this declaration, and that means should be taken that Tights might be acquired under the authority of the Dominion, as that the rights now existing should be affirmed. Unless there is a foundation for the title which this section proposes to establish, a title may be acquired in the present condition of affairs by- mere occupation, by possession, by various means, which tend not only to litigation, but to hamper legitimate development.

If in the end the Crown in the right of the province is declared to be in possession, it is true no harm is done; but if in the end it is declared that the Crown in the right of the Dominion is in possession, then the man who has entered into occupation since the decision of the Exchequer Court, and before the Dominion takes the authority that will come to it, if it does come to it, by the decision of the Privy Council, has established a squatter's right to the water, has found an impediment in many cases to proper development, and has laid a foundation for litigation and for trouble that is absolutely desirable from every point of view that we should try to avoid. gard is just as necessary to the benefit of the railway belt of British Columbia in regard to its water rights.

Before the committee rises, I would like to call the minister's attention to a point which he has not yet discussed. First of all, I come from the railway belt in British Columbia and from New Westminster where they are seriously concerned with this Bill. They have sent me a very urgent protest against the provision in the last clause which I will not discuss just now, as I will have another opportunity. But, I would like to point this out, that so far from there being any confusion in British Columbia because of the existing conditions of the law, I as a resident in the railway belt know that there is no confusion at all. There is nothing to indicate there that the province of British Columbia is not in possession of the water-powers within the railway belt,

and is not exercising it the same as it has exercised it during the 39 years we have been in confederation, exercising it without any question on the part of this government up to this day. The case now on appeal to the Privy Council does not set out in plain terms that the Dominion government does possess the rights which we are asked to declare by section 4 that the Dominion does possess. I would like to point out to the minister that while he proposes to put all the holders of water rights upon their defence at once, to see that they have those rights, his authority in the premises is not nearly so extensive as is set out here, and as I will show by reference to the judgment of the Exchequer Court. That judgment states that whatever right he has disappears, with respect to any portions of the railway belt, so soon as he sells that portion to settlers. Now a large proportion of the railway belt has been alienated already, sections of the railway belt are being disposed of to settlers right along, so that day by day or year by year, whatever right this government has there is vanishing and in the course of a short time the rights of the Dominion will cease altogether. Now, I ask the minister in view of that condition whether it would not be much better to come to an arrangement with the province of British Columbia that that province should continue to exercise the right which for 40 years has been exercised, rather than to make all the confusion that will be created by the passing of this Bill. I have not heard the minister refer at all to the section of the judgment which says that his right disappears with the alienation of the property to settlers. It seems to me that he could not have given attention to that. In view of the vanishing of whatever right he has there, it is all the more neces-cary that we should not do anything so drastic as pass a Bill, the effect of which will be to put every water owner there on his defence.

speechtext: Without passing it to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: Why could not the government submit a stated case to the Supreme Court, and get a decision on the rights of the federal and provincial powers? To hear and give judgment in such cases that was one of the great reasons for establishing the Supreme Court.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) was not in when some of the discussion was going on. A certain side of the case has been settled by the Supreme Court and is on its way to the Privy Council.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: I desire to make a suggestion to the minister (Mr. Oliver), which he can think over. Would it be possible to appoint a joint committee or commission, one member representing this government, one representing British Columbia, and they to appoint a third, this body to administer this matter pending a decision in the litigation now in progress? That would enable business to go on, for the minister is anxious to see water rights granted, and I fancy that the province is granting some too. Everybody would be satisfied with some arrangement for management in the meantime by a commission if a commission could be arranged. As the minister says, there is no body in possession. I merely throw out the suggestion for him to think over. Possibly if the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and all concerned were to take the matter into consideration, they would w'ork out a plan on that basis.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext: I do not think that suggestion would quite answer. It is not -a question of administration, but of law that is at issue.

subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
The minister has two things under consideration, as it seems to me. One is the question of such pro



perty Tights as have been granted by the province, and by the Dominion. But there is another part of this Bill which proposes to give the Dominion government the right to grant rights pending the decision. It is just possible that the Dominion government, whilst in temporary possession, might grant rights which would not be recognized by British Columbia, so that further litigation would ensue. But if rights were granted by such a commission, both governments being interested would immediately confirm them, and there would he no difficulty in the title.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: WATER AND WATER-POWER IN RAILWAY BELT, B.C.
speechtext:
There is great merit in that suggestion, but we are not able to deal with it at the moment. It is necessary that we should have the position established.
