speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: House in committee on Bill (No. 166) an Act respecting insurance.-Mr. Fielding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There were several
clauses allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think No. 59 was the first of these.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under paragraph 3 of subsection (b) of section 59, dealing with the investments of the companies, it is provided that a company may invest in:
The preferred stocks of any company which has paid regular dividends upon such stocks or upon its common stocks for not less than five years preceding the purchase of such preferred stocks, or the stocks of any company which are guaranteed by a company which has paid regular dividends upon its preferred or common stocks for not less than five years preceding the purchase of such guaranteed stocks.	*
The point was raised, I think by my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Perley), that a small company might guarantee a Mr. J. A. CURBIE.
large amount of bonds of another company, and that would defeat the intention of the clause. It was suggested that we should put a limit upon the amount to be guaranteed in that way. The point seemed well taken, and I propose to add to this paragraph 3 these words:
Provided that the amount of stocks so guaranteed is not in excess of 50 per cent of the amount of the ordinary or common stocks, as the case may be, of the guaranteeing company.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wish to call up again section 14.

Section 14 provides that Canadian companies should make a deposit with the minister to the amount of $50,000, and that foreign companies should make a deposit of $100,000. There are some Canadian companies doing 'an insurance business in some states of the American union who say that this provision interferes with their business, they say that the state of California, for instance, is discriminating against them in California because we in Canada discriminate in this way against foreign companies; and they say that within the last few days they have received advices that the state of Kansas also threatens to discriminate against Canadian companies for the same reason. Therefore, these Canadian companies ask that section 14 be amended to the effect that Canadian and foreign companies should be asked to make the same deposit, and they, therefore, ask that the word 'Canadian' in the second line of subsection 1, and the whole of subsection 2, be struck out, which would have that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How would it do to make them both $100,000 instead of $50,000?
I think that would answer the same purpose; there would be no discrimination.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is only fair to say that the Canadian companies would probably complain of that. There is something in the argument that if we do discriminate in this way we provoke retaliation on the part of the United States companies. I think under the circumstances, however, I would prefer to make both $100,000. I do not feel like resisting strongly the view of my - hon. friend from Grey (Mr. MilleT), but I would ask the sense of the House upon it.
Perhaps the minister might compromise and make it $75,000.
Should not the deposit have some relation to the amount of business that they do? $50,000 would be a small deposit if they do a large business.
The department will see to it that they have to keep a reserve proportionate to the amount of business that they do.
I am in favour of the suggestion to make them all $50,000. If you discriminate against foreign companies you provoke retaliation.
I think if $50,000 is enough to make a Canadian insurance company safe towards its policy-holders, it ought to make it equally safe for the policy-holders in any company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am disposed to accept the amendment of my hon. friend from Grey.
Further consideration of section 59, subsection 3, other securities authorized by Treasury Board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We provided that a company might purchase securities not strictly within the scope of this clause in exchange for other securities which they wished to get rid of it. But it was pointed out that if they should buy these securities or take them in exchange for others, some provision should apply as to disposing of them within a reasonable time. I think that is a fair suggestion, and I propose that the following words be added to subsection 3:
But the bonds, stocks or debentures and other acceptances so authorized shall he absolutely sold or disposed of within five years after the acquisition thereof, or within such further time not exceeding one year as the Governor in Council shall, on report of the minister, fix and determine.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
On section 60, subsection 2, custody of securities abroad.
FIELDING. There is a provision there that m case it is necessary to exchange securities they may be entrusted to a responsible person residing out of Canada. The point was taken that this ought to be done by a bank or trust company, and while we do not want to discriminate to the extent of indicating the particular kind of companies, we propose to say that instead of being entrusted to a responsible	person,	they	may	be entrusted to 'a bank, trust company or other *corporation	carrying	on	business	outside
of Canada'.

Would it not be possible that they would be entrusted to a corporation	carrying	on	business	outside
of Canada, say in the United States, to which it would not be desirable to entrust them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was not thought that any change should be made in this section.

Then I am to suppose that the minister has not approved of the suggestion I made that this section is objectionable as being retroactive to this extent that it imposes on companies with regard to policies issued before this legislation was enacted, obligations which do not come from the contracts they entered into in accordance with the law in force at the time the contracts were made and creates a right or protection in favour of the insurer to which he was not entitled. That would be avoided if the section were not made applicable to policies issued before the passing of this legislation. As a general principle retroactive legislation is not looked upon with favour and unless substantial reasons are given, this-section seems to me to be open to those objections.	->

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand this point was fully discussed in the Senate Committee and representations made concerning it. After full consideration the conclusion was reached that this was the better way of dealing with it. I understand that the companies generally are quite satisfied with the clause. One outside company objected, but after hearing representations from that company the committee agreed that this was a wise provision. It is sometimes unavoidable in .making a law that you have a retroactive clause, but it is necessary in order to carry out the general policy. For instance in this Bill we give the policy-holders the right to vote. Some companies had decided to give that and others had not, but we give them all that right, and in that sense it might be called retroactive legislation.
On section 95, subsection (b) incontestability after two years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The point was in regard to military service. I find on inquiry that some companies already specify that the policy-holders may engage dn war for the defence of Canada without any extra charge, but if they leave Canada and go abroad to engage in war they have to pay an extra premium which could not be very well fixed by law as various circumstances may change the nature of the risk. I doubt if we could by legislation make any improvement on the provision.
On section 11, assessment life insurance companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I desire to say that all the sections under the head of assessment life insurance companies are repetitions of

the present law. We are not proposing any change in the law respecting these companies.
On section 123, notice of intention to maintain a reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I desire to make a change in conformity with a change made elsewhere in the Bill. I, therefore, beg to move that in line 3 of the section the words ' office of the superintendent ' be struck out and the word ' department ' be inserted in lieu thereof.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 139, insurance in unlicensed companies.

I think there is a misprint in this section. There is evidently a contradiction of the previous clause. It was understood that no broker from the United States would come into Canada and do business here. It was provided in the amendment that any man in Canada might insure his own property, but he could not become a broker for that purpose. I suggest that we change that clause so as to provide that a man shall simply insure his own property. I therefore propose that the section be made to read:
Notwithstanding anything in this Act contained any owner of property situated in Canada may insure such property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the clause as to which there was the most discussion when we had the Bill before us a year ago. and as to which there has been the most contention. I have already explained the change desired there. In substance it was decided by the Senate, which I am willing to accept, that these outside insurance companies might under certain circumstances be permitted to do business when the business was offered to them, but they could not send here to solicit business or employ agents. Roughly, that is the substance of it. I do not know whether the words suggested by my hon. friend will carry out that purpose or not. My hon. friend means to distinguish between the owner and the broker?
Yes.

Would not that, if it were adopted, prevent a man who had an insurable interest, other than a broker, from insuring his property? Any person might as the principal to the contract insure his property, but when a broker insures, he acts only as the agent of the person having the insurable interest. He is not insuring the property, he is procuring insurance for the person who employs him.

That has been the objection all along, and I do not see how this got into the clause. It is not the in-Mr. FIELDING.
tention of the Senate. It was understood that no outsider should be allowed to come into Canada and do the business of insurance.

No person can insure a property unless he has an insurable interest in it, and it appears to me that th^ words ' any person may insure any property ' should be followed by the words ' in which he has an insurable interest.' It is not to be supposed that this clause can bd interpreted as meaning that a broker may start out and insure property wholesale.
That is what we1 want to make clear, that no man can go around and insure other people's property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he made a business of it he would be liable to the penalties of the Act. But suppose my hon. friend want3 to take some outside insurance, and he has not time to attend to it, and asks his neighbour to do it for him. The neighbour in that case would be acting as his agent. Would there be any objection to that?
It would open the door, and I do not think that was the intention.
How could any one insure except through an agent who would act for the company, and give the company's official receipt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Any man who acted as agent for a company would violate the Act, but the case suggested by my hon. friend was the case of an agent acting, not for the company, but for the owner.

As the clause reads, it says: ' Any person may insure any property situated in Canada.' I am afraid that is a contradiction of what was originally intended. I think it might be worded in this way: ' Any owner of property situated in Canada may insure it.'

It is necessary to make a distinction between the owner of property and one who has an insurable interest in it. You permit the owner to insure his interest, but the hypothecary creditor has not the same advantage. Why not provide that any person may insure any property in which he has an insurable interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the words ' may insure his property or any property in which he has an insurable interest,' would meet my hon. friend's view.

When a creditor, say a bank, requires a certain amount of insurance as collateral security for an account, and the insurance must be obtained within a limited time, unless there is an agent of the company to give an official receipt that

would be accepted by the bank as evidence of the insurance, the account might be impaired.

A company does not wait until the last moment to place insurance. If they are insuring outside of Canada, they will have an agent outside of Canada who can provide for any additional insurance at any time by telegraph.

The amendment suggested by the hon. member for fit. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) might interfere considerably with the grain business of the west. There is a large amount of insurance carried on the grain in the elevators at Fort William, and it is often carried by the elevator company or by the brokers to whom the farmers consign their grain. The Bill as it is now provides for that, whereas if the aimendment of the hon. member for St. Lawrence division is adopted, it will hamper the elevator companies in handling the insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the words suggested to be added ' or any property in which he has an insurable interest ' will meet the objection of my hon. friend.
Will the minister kindly explain what effect the Bill has in relation to the canvassing for insurance by foreign or unlicensed companies by means of circulars or other literature?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My attention was called to that the other night. We in general terms (forbid} advertising, but the word ' circular,' is not used, and we propose to submit an amendment to include the circular as a form of advertising which should be forbidden.

This is the clause regarding which I have received a great deal of correspondence from my constituents, and I would like to know what changes have really been made. I understand that outside companies have hitherto been allowed to come to this country, and get business, and that you are now preventing that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the spirit of the insurance law in the past has been that these outside companies should not do business in Canada, otherwise there would be no excuse for having an insurance law. It would not seem to be reasonable that we should require all our Canadian companies, and all other companies that desire to do regular business, to take out licenses, to make returns, and submit to penalties, if outside companies could come in, and do business without putting up any deposit, without any license or without making any returns. I think the spirit of the law always was that these companies
should not do business in Canada. However, the law was found not to be strict enough, and they did business. When the Insurance Act was being revised that question received a great deal of attention. The conclusion we reached before the committee of the House of Commons was that it would not be wise to forbid the business altogether, even although the spirit of the law seemed to contemplate that, because it was held both as respects the volume and the cost of insurance that large owners of property ought to have some liberty beyond that of dealing with licensed companies. Sometimes the licensed companies could not furnish the volume of insurance required at short notice, and sometimes thought they might indicate their ability to furnish the volume of insurance required, they quoted rates so much in excess of the mutual companies rates that the large owners of property felt very much aggrieved. Therelore the conclusion reached by the Banking and Commerce Committee was that we would permit them to do their business, but that we would impose a tax upon them for doing it.
What was the tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The tax was 15 per cent on the premiums collected, with the qualification that in certain cases it should not exceed a certain limit. We regarded that as a fairly good compromise. However, it was one of those compromises I regret to say which pleased nobody. The insurance companies complained because they said we should not allow those companies to come in at all, and the large property owners complained, because they said we were preventing them from obtaining the insurance they desired. The Senate Committee devoted a great deal of attention to it. They heard gentlemen both for and against it, and I understand the representations made were both full and effective. The end of it was that the gentlemen on the Senate Committee, man>
ot them insurance men, came to the conclusion that it would be fair and reasonable to permit what might be called overflow insurance, that is insurance that cannot be furnished or obtained at home except at excessive rates, that property owners might be allowed to go out and obtain insurance from the foreign companies, but that the foreign companies should not be allowed to come in and seek it. And so the Bill comes to1 us in that form. As it stands now, an owner of property who is not content with the arrangements at home can get his insurance in these mutual companies, taking his own risk, making his contract in the United States, and bringing his suit, if he has to bring a suit, under American law. But the foreign company cannot come into Canada, and seek the business

br solicit business in any form. They cannot send agents in, they cannot open an office, and they cannot advertise, and we will have it so that they cannot issue circulars. In other words I can go out, and take insurance if I care to take the risk, hut the company cannot come to Canada, and solicit business from me.
Did these unlicensed companies not pay anything before for a license or make a deposit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Did the insurance men who appeared before the committee admit that they were unwilling or unable to^ take any amount of insurance that might be offered to them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think in some cases they did, though somewhat reluctantly, but there were some cases in which they stated that they were not able to supply the volume of insurance required at short notice.
They are not admitting it all over the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I am safe in saying that they did admit it to the committee.

They certainly did. One man stated in the presence of the representative of an insurance company that he had admitted that he could not take it. I think $450,000 was the amount. J was going to say with reference to prohibiting the distributing of circulars and advertising, that it might make it very difficulty for a great many of those who desire insurance to know how they can get it. Suppose I wanted to insure and I [DOT]am not in touch with any insurance men, and do not know the name and address *of any insurance company, how am I to find out if they are not allowed to advertise.	i	j i

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Business men who have a large amount of insurance to take out usually inform themselves on these matters. Every manufacturer or merchant, or .large owner of property, is well acquainted with the system commonly called the New 'England Mutual and he knows he can get insurance in that way if he is willing to take the risk involved in it. But I think if we can give our Canadian companies and the foreign companies which come and take our licenses and submit to .all the conditions of the law, if we are giving them any measure of protection at all, I do not think we should allow outside companies to come in indiscriminately.

Not indiscriminately. But suppose the Finance Minister himself wanted to insure, and I asked him which Mr. FIELDING.
company he was going to insure with, 1 venture to say that offhand he could not tell me.

How will the minister prevent circulars coming in? Suppose I am a manufacturer in St. Catharines and some company sent me a circular soliciting business, how are you going to stop them doing that. Who is going to punish them?

I may be excused from speaking upon this clause of Bill (No. 139), from the fact that the- insurances of the corporation with which I am associated are all carried in the unlicensed companies referred to. Now some of these companies are in the habit of sending out monthly statements showing the result of each month's business, and if I understand the construction some of my brother members are endeavouring to place upon this clause I would not be able to receive these statements without incurring the risk of paying a penalty, for they come under the heading of circulars.
Again, suppose I desire to place additional insurance upon our premises tomorrow, I would be obliged to go to Boston or Providence to do this, as I understand I am debarred from allowing any agent of these unlicensed companies to visit our works, inspect the same, and fix the rate at which the insurance can he carried. This appears to me to be both unfair and embarrassing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The inspector is allowed to come, that is provided for.
And the statement also would be allowed.
The monthly statement that I have spoken of comes as a circular.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would not be a circular advertising for business; it would be the rendering of an account in a transaction already made. All that we can hope to prevent-and I know that there are difficulties in the way-would be the sending of circulars to solicit business. But the difficulty of carrying this into effect is rendered less by the fact that, as hon. members know, these companies, as a rule, do not come with offers of business; you have to go to them. Knowing that to be the general practice, I do not think we shall have any difficulty in working it out.
If that is the practice, why do you need the clause at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You have to prohibit all from doing it, otherwise, somebody might do it.

I have followed this clause as it was in the old Bill, and as we have it now from the Senate. It seems to

me that this clause which has been so much debated in the House and the Senate, has nothing in it. It is simply declaratory of what the law was before the Act was introduced. The Bill would be just as effective if the clause were struck out, except for the fact that the insured has to make a return to the department. 1 do not think the Act would be either better or worse if the clause were struck out. It is a fake, pure and simple.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In that case, it might just as well be allowed to stand. I am informed that, after very great discussion, the representative manufacturers and merchants who discussed the question on one side and the insurance companies on the other side, though neither party was fully pleased, agreed that this was about as wise a conclusion as could be reached.
It does neither good nor harm.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If that could be said of all legislation, the world would be much better off than it is.

There can be no question that the main purpose of insurance legislation is sacrificed by the arrangement, whoever may .havg agreed to it, that is, there is no protection for the public who may insure in these foreign and unlicensed companies. I would like to understand two things: first, do we as a committee proceed upon the assumption that, if the insured goes and seeks the company and is not made the subject of a canvas by agent or circular, he is entitled to no protection against a company that, possibly, is not in a financial position to meet losses? Second, in arriving at the 15 per , cent tax that was formerly proposed, was it estimated that this' would represent an equally onerous burden on the licensed companies to that which is imposed upon the licensed companies in the way of putting up a deposit and complying with the other obligations imposed upon them by the statute ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would not say it was
mathematically adjusted. It was regarded as a certain measure of protection which might fairly be given to the home companies. I suppose that the companies would claim that it was not equal to. the burdens imposed upon them. But, as I say, it was not intended to be a mathematical adjustment of burdens.
Do I understand that the present clause does not contain the provision for a 15 per cent tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is struck out; there is no tax. That is the material change that was made in the clause by the Senate Committee.

I am surprised that we should allow that to go through here.
I did not know that the Senate had proposed that. I enter my protest on behalf of those I represent here. I think it is exceedingly unfair. The 15 per cent tax was a very slight tax under the circumstances. Our companies have to take out licenses, put up deposits, make reports and comply with all the conditions of the law, while the outside companies can do all the business they like quite free from these conditions. 1 say it is exceedingly unfair, and I protest against it.
Is it not clearly in the interest of the insured public of Canada?

There are two classes, the insured and the insurers. The insurance agents do not seem to think that it is in the interest of the companies that they represent, or in their own interest, for they protest against it earnestly. I do not' know what the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Fowke) means by saying that it is in the interest of the insurance companies, when the agents of those companies protest against it. I agree with' the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaff-ner), and I think the Senate went a long way when they struck out this clause. I believe they should have left it in.
My view is the same as that of the hon. member for Souris. I have had many representations on behalf of insurance companies and their agents against this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the old question whether we shall protect one class or the other.
The manufacturers want protection in big things and free trade in the little ones.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought there was some force in the argument that this was unfair to the licensed companies. It is, however, a vexed and complicated question. If the parties chiefly concerned-of course, the whole public are concerned- the insurance companies on the one hand, and the representatives, so far as they can be assumed to be such, of the large inw suring public, the owners of large manufacturing establishments and the great merchants, have accepted this as, on the whole, a fair compromise, I do not think the House will make a mistake in assenting to it.

I cannot understand why we should go on in this country continuously giving^ everything to the manufacturers. That is about what we are coming to as fast as we can. I am exceedingly sorry to think this fifteen per cent tax has been removed and, I say again, I enter my

strong protest against the clause as it stanch. The manufacturers are getting nearly everything in this country now, and it is about time that something were done to curtail their privileges.
Fifteen years ago it was worse.
I am following the policy of Sir John Macdonald, who held that when these manufacturing industries ceased to be struggling infants we should cease to protect them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is only fair to say, that thh is not a manufacturers' question. The large merchants were represented also. For instance, Mr. Green-shields, of Montreal, representing one of the largest importing houses in Canada, I am informed, made one of the most effective speeches before the Senate committee in support of the view that they should be allowed to get outside insurance. Every large importer, every large manufacturer, every large merchant, or handler of produce is interested in this. Petitions came in in reams, not only from these people, but also from the agricultural interests, from the cheese and butter factories, complaining that if the fifteen per cent clause remained they would be severely pressed. I am not always supposed to be too favourable to the manufacturers, but it is only fair to say, as I have already said, that this is not a manufacturers' question, nor is it a merchants' question, but it covers practically all classes, including the agricultural.
The policy of self-interest will come into play.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In all these cases selfinterest is the moving principle. It is only the few gentlemen who sit in this House that can be impartial.

It seems to me the chief danger is that the public is not protected against companies that may not be warranted by their financial standing. Another thing is that while the House has forbidden companies to solicit insurance by agents, it has so framed the conditions that there will be no need of a foreign company advertising or soliciting business, business will be forced upon it. They will be able to get business, or to offer business, at a so much lower rate that as soon as it is known that Mr. A has insured at such a low rate in a certain company in the states, his neighbour will at once apply to the same company for insurance, and before long the poor local agent will be completely out of business. I do not think this House should too hastily accept the amendment of the Senate. It should be the duty of the House Jo see that whatever Mr. SCHAFFNER.
tax may be imposed should be such that the burden will be not less than upon the Canadian company.

I may say that the insurance companies were not satisfied with the conditions imposed by the Senate, but they made up their minds to accept the conditions imposed by the Senate rather than discuss the Bill any longer, and if it did not work out reasonably satisfactory, they could come back again to the House, and get' it amended. That was their idea, I speak frankly, in accepting the conditions imposed by the Senate. There is no doubt that clause 139 is more or less of a farce, as it has been called, because it will be evaded, no matter what you do. I would like to say that it was not the so-called New England mutuals that were being kept out by the insurance companies so much as it was what we call the underground companies, the companies without any standing which are allowed to insure throughout the country, and of course the people that insure with them have to take their own risk. They do here now by this clause. There is a preventive to a certain extent. My own idea about the insurance business in this country is that there should be no exception or excuse, every company should be licensed, what is fair for one is fair for another, and if we are to have licenses at all, every company should be licensed without regard to where they come from. But the licensed companies tried to get that in the Bill for two years, and as I said, made up their minds they would accept the Bill as it is rather than continue the agitation, and see what could be done.

I think we should try, and make the legislation in the true interest of the country. The insurance people felt that they were suffering an injustice, and the fact that they gave in, and said they would go without their just rights for a couple of years, does not concern me. What concerns me is whether this legislation is fair to the whole country. I agree with the hon. gentleman that they, all ought to be licensed, but we should not say that a company must continue to submit to an injustice, because they are afraid of the powers that be, or afraid of the Senate. If the thing is wrong we should say it is wrong, and if it is right we should put it there. I say again that there should be some license, or some tax imposed upon these companies that come into this country, and interfere with our domestic companies. I believe in the principle of protecting Canadian industry in every way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At the end of subsection 1, to meet the criticism about circulars and so forth, I propose to add:

Provided further that no such company, underwriters or persons shall, within Canada, advertise their business in any newspaper or other publication, or by circular made in Canada or elsewhere, or maintain an office or agency therein for the receipt of applications or the transaction of any matter or thing relating in any way to their said business
I would understand that advertising by circular would not mean a statement of business.
What is the use of passing legislation if we cannot enforce it? How can you stop a man from sending me a circular from New York?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You could not prevent him sending it in, but you could punish the inspector who came here to inspect the risks of the company which violated that condition. By a special clause we allow these companies to send inspectors to examine the risks; but if we found that these companies were violating the intention of this Act then we could have recourse against the inspector.
Do you mean to say that you could punish the inspector for some one else doing something in New York, for sending a circular info Canada ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We would try, but we might fail.
You could get after the insured. If the company sends him a circular, he has no right to insure in that company.

Why all this sumptuary legislation? I am very much surprised. This House started out to make an insurance Bill for the people, to try and get them some rights which they were not getting from the insurance companies in the first place. We have landed up by giving the bulk of the rights entirely to the company; every particle of It is for the company except these two clauses. I think the least said about this the better. Because a man sends me a circular from New York, and if I get insured in a New York company, why should I be punished? I think that is very drastic legislation. _ I think people should have a few liberties left to them in business matters in this country. I think that is most absurd legislation. If you look over all the statute-books of every country, even Turkey, you would not find such foolish or sumptuary legislation, and I am surprised to find members asking for more of it.

I have very serious protests against this clause from my portion of the country, and I would be prepared
to vote against clause 139 if I had an opportunity of doing so.

It strikes me that you canno.t prohibit any one from sending a circular from ' elsewhere '. You cannot prevent a man sending a circular into Canada from any American city. How you are to prohibit that by putting in the words ' from elsewhere ' in this clause I am not able to comprehend.

And I do not see how we are going to prevent the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Harty) from going to Boston or New York, making a contract there and getting all the insurance he wants. The contract is made in that country, and he has to enforce it there. I do not think this parliament has any jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Sometimes you prohibit the doing of certain things with a fairly good knowledge that somebody will do them, and all you can do is to provide a penalty. I think in this case it is a measure of protection to our own companies. You cannot prevent a man issuing a circular in New York, and sending it through the mails, but if a company is discovered to have done that it violates the provision of this clause and we can go after it by proceeding against the inspector.
For what crime?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We would consider that the company doing the business had violated the law, that his inspection did not come withing the law and therefore he could be proceeded against.

What would be his offence, before what court would he be tried, and what would be the penaltv? I challenge the Finance Minister to say what is to happen to a man if he does this. Let us have no such nonsensical legislation as this is. I think I see the reason for this legislation. Men who have obtained standing in communities, who have used energy and skill in building up a business as insurance agents, who are thoroughly honourable men, and who know how to carry on their business have had their living interfered with, and this is done as a sop to them, they are led to believe that some one is going to be punished for sending a circular,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only refer my hon. friend to the penalty clause, section 70.

How' is he going to get the man into Canada who sent the circular and does he believe that when an inspector comes in on another piece of

business entirely he can punish him for what some one else did in New York? The inspector can say he did not know any, thing about it. Let us not humbug the people.
Mr. SPROULE We should not lose sight of the important educative work carried on by these companies in instructing individuals how to prepare their risks so as to minimize the danger of fire. That is antecedent to the insurance, and the inspector must come there before the insurance is affected. This educative work was never done to the same extent in Canada before. Why will a Canadian company ask me eight per cent to carry insurance, when this company will carry it for one-quarter of one per cent after they have given instructions how to prepare a building so as to minimize the danger of fire and to reduce the cost of insurance? It is the individual who wants the insurance who should be considered, not the company. They are not coming here soliciting business, the individual, who wants insurance and cannot get it in Canada without paying an exorbitant figure should be allowed to get his insurance where he can get it.
The risk is all hig own.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think we can do better than take the clause as it is.

I think the word ' circular 1 should be left out. They send circulars giving instructions as to what shall be done and a statement of the standing of the insurance from time to time. Perhaps that might be construed as coming within this clause of the Act, and it might be said that they were sending circulars for advertising purposes.
On section 148, by-laws.
I understood the minister to say that these were all provisions of the old law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Where there is any material change I will call attention to it.
On section 150, capital stocks, calls, and increase of capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That the heading before section 150 be changed so as to read ' the capital stock and calls thereon/

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
On section 153, forfeiture of shares for default in paying calls.

A, CURRIE. Where a company is approaching a point at which it is ver-tually in liquidation the directors might Mr. LANCASTER.
call and cancel the unpaid shares and thus relieve themselves from liability in case of disaster.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the law as it has been for years and I think there has been no trouble about it.
On section 166, arrears prevent voting.

I would ask the minister to make provision, the same as that which is in the English company's Act, that where two or more persons are registered for shares as joint trustees, the one whose name is first on the roll shall cast the vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the existing law, and I am advised that there has been no difficulty arising under it.

I think it is not the law. Where two parties are down for the same stock or where executors are down as holding stock in trust, the one whose name is first upon the register casts the vote That is the English law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe it is in the English Act, but I hope my hon. friend will not feel it necessary to press it this evening. I am told that no difficulty has arisen under this clause.

I do not wish to delay the Bill; if I had noticed it sooner I would have called the minister's attention to it.
On section 179, actions against shareholders.
CU*RRIE. Did the companies make any representations to the government in reference to this question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am advised that the matter was not specially considered. No attention was called to it.
It is a very dangerous provision. I do not think you will find it in the Companies Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the existing law and it is in the Companies Act.

Not in that form.
On section 184, cost of incorporation chargeable to shareholders.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This section is designed to make the cost of incorporation chargeable to the shareholders and not to tile policy-holders.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.

speechtext: Before the orders of the day are called I would like to ask the Minister of the Interior if he has inquired into the matter I referred to the other day as to the delay at Halifax in connection with a ship that arrived there.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have a memorandum on the subject, but I have not it in my desk at the moment. But I would be glad to hand it to my hon. friend or lay it on the table at any stage.
Perhaps on Monday you could do it.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: House went into committee to consider certain resolutions respecting the granting of subsidies in aid of the construction of lines of railway therein mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I may say that all the subsidies granted in this respect have been voted before. There are two or three cases where the subsidies apply to different parts of the line, but only in two cases is there any different mileage, and in both cases I think the measurement was found to be incorrect, in one case by three and a half miles, and in the other by one mile. The other subsidies are all taken from the statute and revoted in the same terms for the same distances and to the same amounts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the necessity for re-voting these? Was there a time limit in the statute which made provision for these subsidies?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The time limit in all these is two years unless construction has begun and four years if construction work has been started. But under the statute they all run out at the end of two years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Unless the work has been commenced.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Unless the work has been commenced.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Section 4 has that I think. What is the reason that they are put in? Are we voting them for the second time only, or for the third time, or for the fourth or fifth or sixth time?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I would not like to say positively, because I have not gone back through the statutes further than 1906. There are two or three which were voted in
1906, but the great majority we revoted in 1908. Possibly some were renewals at that time, I would not like to say. In the statute they do not appear as renewals. I have had representations with reference to all these subsidies, and it is the usual statement I imagine with respect to a great many of them that during the past two years or four years, as the case may be, they have not been able to get into position to proceed with the work, but they think now that if the subsidies are revoted, in fact they assure me that they think they will be able to proceed within the two years extended by this statute. In some cases the work has been started. I have not included any new ones at all.

The Minister of Railways will remember that a deputation from Manitoba waited on him two or three weeks ago. On that deputation there were representatives from Brandon, Hamiota and Birtle, and probably some other towns, asking for a subsidy for a line between Hamiota and Birtle. The Canadian Pacific railway was considering the question of constructing a branch line there. It is a portion of the country that is badly in need of facilities and the Canadian Pacific railway promised with the usual assistance, to construct this road this summer. I understand the deputation left here very hopeful of receiving this assistance after their interview with the Minister of Railways and his colleagues, but I do not notice any subsidy for this road in the list presented to the House. Does the minister not sympathize with the aspirations of the people in that important portion of the country? What is the reason for refusing it?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have a good deal of sympathy with the proposition that the gentlemen referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) placed before me. As he says there is considerable need there for railway facilities and for a connection between these two points. The Canadian Pacific railway representatives also discussed the matter with me. As he will understand, however, there are scores and scores of applications for new subsidies, and after investigating them the government thought that for this session at least, they should not recommend the granting of any new subsidies; but in order that no person who was in a position to proceed with the work might suffer, it was decided to renew certain of the old ones that had been already voted. I assure my hon. friend that if any new subsidies had been voted at all, the one to which he refers would have been included, as they put up a pretty strong case.
Are all these renewals made upon representations of the parties interested, or are they renewals as a matter of form, in some instances ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
There have been requests made for every one of them, or they would not have been renewed. There are scores that have not been renewed that were on the statutes before.
On resolution 1,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As I understand it, every one of these is a renewal of a subsidy granted in 1908.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: As I said, there are exceptions, three or four of them were granted in 1906-7, but the majority are of 1908.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Did those of 1906-7 expire ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes.
M. R. L. BORDEN : Could the minister tell us which of them are of the year 1906-7 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
They are named in the resolution as we go along. For instance, No. 5 was granted by chapter 40 of 1907 ; No. 12 was 1907; No. 13 was 1907. The chapter and the year of the statute are indicated.
On resolution 2,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are these and the following paragraphs exactly the same as those which have been enacted by the House in such matters in the past ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, they are an exact copy of the statute.
On resolution 8,
Is section 8 the same as in all the railway subsidy Acts?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
An exact copy.
Resolutions reported, read the second time and agreed to.
House went into committee to consider the following additional proposed resolutions for subsidies to railways :
45.	For a line of railway from Montreal to a point on the National Transcontinental railway in lieu of subsidy granted by chapter 63 of 1908, section 1, item 48, not exceeding 200 miles.
46.	To the Little Nation River Railway Company, for a line of railway from Papi-neauville on the Canadian Pacific railway towards Lake Nominingue, in lieu of subsidy granted by chapter 63 of 1908, section 1, item 70, not exceeding 30 miles.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: These were passed in 1908, but after my resolutions were prepared it was called to my notice that I had not included these. I had included them in the Act, but not in the other list of resolutions. They are an exact copy of the statute of 1908.	'

Resolutions reported, read the second time and agreed to.
Mr. GRAHAM moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 226) to authorize the granting of subsidies in aid of the construction of the lines of railway therein mentioned.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, Bill read the first and second time, and House went into committee thereon.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The Bill contains nothing that is not in the resolutions.
On section 5,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The section of the resolution is different from that of the Bill. The resolution contains these words :
And the said board shall have absolut* control, at all times, over the rates and tolls to be levied and taken by any of the companies, or upon any of the railways and bridges hereby subsidized.
In the Bill the words ' and bridges ' are omitted.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The reason is, I think, that there are no bridges subsidized under the Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then, it should not be in the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is superfluous in the resolution. There are no bridges covered by the Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Except in so far as these may be part of the railway lines ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: But there are no special subsidies to bridges.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 5 stand as part of the Bill? Carried.
Could the minister tell us the total amount of the subsidies we are authorizing to-day at the maximum and minimum rate, and the total mileage subsidized?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The total mileage is 3,277-4 miles. At a subsidy of $3,200 per mile that will amount to $10,487,680; at a subsidy of $6,400 per mile that will amount to $20,975,360.
On the preamble,

Is there any intention on the part of the government to grant the subsidy to the Ontario government railway which has been granted to all the colonization roads? I understand that this railway is to be an important link in the Transcontinental. The next time the minister brings down his subsidies for railways, I suggest that he should propose and pay a subsidy to the Ontario government railway, such as the ordinary railway company have received.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The government at present has no intention of granting a subsidy to the Ontario government railway. That road did not get any subsidy when it was inaugurated. It has now been largely constructed by a very rich province, and I think it would hardly be wise for this government to interfere with the government of a province in that way, particularly under all the conditions. Then if we were to grant a subsidy to that line I would be inclined to say that the line should come under Dominion jurisdiction, under the Dominion Board of Railway Commissioners, and the government of Ontairo would not care to permit that.

If I were discussing the question of jurisdiction, I should say that the Dominion government railways ought to come under the jurisdiction of the Ontario government, and then they would be able to give a profit.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
will give me the rate the'Ontario road charges I will give a profit of $2,000,000 each year on the Intercolonial railway.
Why do you not take it?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The people get the benefit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have heard so much about low rates on the Intercolonial railway as compared with other railways that I really would like to have some information on the subject. I would invite the minister to bring down, before the close of the session or before his supplementary estimates go through, a table comparing the rates on the Intercolonial railway, both through and local, with the standard rates on the other great railways of Canada. I have not understood that the local rates on the Intercolonial railway were so much lower than. those on other railways as the minister would have us imagine.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It might take some weeks to prepare such a table. The rate sheets, unless in the hands of an expert, do not show the income from freight. The classification of freight has a great deal to do with it. As a matter of fact, the location and the classification of freight of the Ontario government road is suoh that if its rates on a sheet were exactly the same as on a sheet of the Intercolonial railway its income would be much lower on account of the higher class of freight it has to carry. They are in a much better position per mile.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That does not mean that the rates are higher, but that they are favourably situated in respect to the particular description of freight that forms the bulk of their haulage.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is one reason.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have made a statement before the House as to passenger traffic. Their passenger rates are higher than the Intercolonial railway.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should not imagine that they are very much higher. I realize that the through passenger rate from Halifax to Truro or Montreal is a very reasonable one, but the local passenger rates on the Intercolonial railway in Nova Scotia are about the same as on any other railway in Canada, so far as I am aware. I am rather tired of hearing about these rates. It is creating in impression throughout the country that the people of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Quebec, are getting a sort of pauper rate on the Intercolonial railway. I do not think that that is the case; I think they are paying the usual rates, in respect of local traffic at least. If I am wrong, I want to be corrected. If the minister cannot give that information before the close of the session, I would like to have it after the session, or at all events at the commencement of the next session.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The information my hon. friend has asked for is on ' Hansard ' either this year or last. We took the local rates on the Canadian Pacific railway in the maritime provinces and compared them.

The'question was asked last year if these figures were on a ton mile basis, but the minister said they were never calculated on a ton mile basis on the InteTcolonail railway. The only statistics the people will accept in the United States are the statistics published in the manuals and based on a ton mile basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: These returns are placed on the table of the House every year.
If we had the information we could tell what the rates are. You can juggle the other figures in any way you like.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The information published in reference to the Intercolonial railway is the same as the sworn statements in regard to other railways, and the hon. member has a copy in his desk.

I had occasion to look into the freight rates on coal to ascertain whether the rates in the west were higher than in the east. I got the freight rates for coal on the Intercolonial railway and found that whereas in the west we are paying a much higher rate to carry coal 400 miles than the Intercolonial railway was carrying it for 800 or 900 miles. I think it is absolutely unfair that the Intercolonial railway should haul freight for one

half the price charged by the other roads. We in other parts of the country do not get any part of the cheap rates on the Intercolonial railway. We have to pay our own high rates and have also to put our hands in our pockets and pay taxes to get cheap rates for thos& who happen to have the advantage of living along the Intercolonial railway.

In inland towns we pay a good rate. From Stellarton to Truro, a haul of 40 miles, we pay 80 cents a ton, although the through rate to Halifax is the same. So in making up their rates it is hard to strike an average.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And there is a low rate, established many years ago, from the coal mining centres to Montreal. This was done advisedly with an idea of assisting in the development of the mining properties of Nova Scotia. I am not prepared to dispute that that is a fairly low rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, it is.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I say that so far as the local rates in Nova Scotia are concerned, they are not materially lower than rates on other railways. Take the case mentioned by the hon. member for Colchester, 80 cents a ton for 40 miles, that seems a fairly substantial rate, and I doubt whether the rates in Ontario are higher than that. My hon. friend (Mr. J. A. Currie) tells me that for such distances in Ontario the rates are lower.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
On all these things my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie) is not a strict authority. There are special cases. The question of freight and passenger rates is very complicated, and the study of a freight or passenger sheet is a science.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: AID TO CANADIAN NORTHERN ALBERTA RAILWAY COMPANY.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, That it is expedient to provide:
1.	That the Governor in Council may aid and assist the construction of the line of railway of a company to be incorporated under the name of ' Canadian Northern Alberta Railway Company,' from a point at or near Edmonton or Strathcona, in the province of Alberta, thence, in a generally western direction, to the coal areas, situated at or near the Brazeau river and the headwaters of the McLeod river, for a distance not exceeding one hundred and fifty miles, by guaranteeing the principal and interest of the bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other securities, hereinafter called securities, secured as hereinbefore mentioned, of the company, to the extent of thirteen thousand Mr. TURRIFF.
dollars per mile for the first fifty miles of the line so aided, and, for the remainder of the said line, to the amount of twenty-five thousand dollars per mile, not exceeding in all one hundred and fifty miles, the interest upon the said securities to be at the rate of three and one-half per cent per annum, payable half yearly, the principal to be payable in fifty years; and that the aid granted or authorized by chapter 25 of the Statutes of 1908, intituled: ' An Act respecting aid for the extension of the Edmonton, Yukon and Pacific railway,' be cancelled:
2.	That the said securities so guaranteed shall be secured by a deed or deeds of trust, by way of mortgage or charge, to a trustee or trustees, approved of by the Governor in Council, and such deed or deeds of trust shall respectively grant a first mortgage or charge upon the said line of railway so aided, and the right of way, station grounds, or other real estate and interest therein, buildings and other structures and improvements, rolling stock and equipment, plant, machinery, tools, supplies, materials and other personal properties, present and future, acquired for the purposes of the said line so aided, and in connection with operating, repairing and maintaining it, and the tolls, incomes and revenues of the company arising and to arise from the said line, and the right9, privileges, franchises and powers of the company now or hereafter held with respect to and in connection with the said line and the operation, maintenance and repair thereof.
3.	That the kind of securities to be guaranteed as aforesaid, and the forms thereof, and the form and terms of the deed or deeds of trust securing them, and the times and manner of the issue of securities and the disposition of the moneys to be raised thereon, by sale, pledge, or otherwise, pending the expenditure of such moneys for the purposes of the line of railway so aided, and the form and the manner of guarantee, shall be such as the Governor in Council approves, and such terms, provisions and conditions may be included in such deed or deeds of trust as the Governor in Council deems expedient or necessary.
4.	That the said guarantee shall be signed by the Minister of Finance or such officer as is designated by the Governor in Council to sign it; and upon being so signed the Dominion of Canada shall become liable as guarantor for the payment of the principal and interest of the securities so guaranteed according to the tenor thereof, and the said payment shall form a charge upon the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
5.	That any moneys paid by the Dominion of Canada under any guarantee herein provided for shall be held to be paid in discharge of the liability of the Dominion and not in discharge of the liability of the company under the securities guaranteed, or under any deed of trust securing them, and the moneys so paid shall be held to be still secured by the said securities and deed of trust, and the Dominion shall be subrogated in and to all the rights of the holders of such securities, the interest upon or the
6rincipal of which has been paid by the ominion, and the Dominion shall, with respect to all moneys so paid, be in all respects

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
in the position of security-holders with respect to whose securities default has been made in payment to the extent of the moneys paid by the Dominion.
6.	That the decision of the Governor in Council as to the length of the mileage of the said line of railway so to be aided shall, for the purposes hereof, be final.
7.	That the books of the company shall at all times be open for inspection for and on behalf of the government by any person named in that behalf by the Governor in Council or the Minister of Finance.
8.	That the Canadian Northern Railway Company shall, by guarantee included in the said deed or deeds of trust, or in some other instrument agreed to by the Governor in Council or the Minister of Finance and the last named company, in such form as the Governor in Council shall approve, guarantee to his Majesty the due payment by the company of the principal and interest of all securities issued and guaranteed under the provisions hereof, according to the tenor and effect of such securities, respectively, and in accordance with the terms of the said deed or deeds of trust, and shall also guarantee to His Majesty the due payment by the company of all loss or costs which His Majesty may sustain or be put to in enforcing, after default, the provisions of the said deed or deeds of trust against the line of railway and premises thereby mortgaged and charged.
9.	That the company may acquire the line of railway constructed or partially constructed or located by the Edmonton, Yukon and Pacific Railway Company, or by the Canadian Northern Railway Company as its successor by amalgamation, between the points set forth in paragraph 1 hereof, and all properties, works, surveys, plans and locations, held, made, approved or established in connection therewith; and the same shall, for the purposes hereof and the guarantee hereby authorized, be taken to form part of the line of railway hereby aided. The deed of transfer or acquirement (which the respective companies interested are hereby authorized to execute) shall be executed and deposited in the office of the Secretary of State of Canada before any securities are issued or guaranteed hereunder in respect of the line of railway and incidental properties so acquired; and the said deed upon being so executed and deposited shall, without further formality, be taken to vest in the company all the properties, works, surveys, plans and locations held, made, approved or established by or for the transferring companies, or either of them, in respect of the line of railway or portions thereof so transferred, with the same rights, privileges and priorities as were at the time of the execution of such deed held by the transferring companies respectively.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: AID TO CANADIAN NORTHERN ALBERTA RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
This resolution is somewhat unusual, but under the conditions that exist the introduction of such legislation seems to be imperative. In 1908 certain lines of railway were guaranteed by the Dominion government. The Edmonton Yukon Pacific was given a guarantee of bonds of $13,000 per mile for fifty miles, and $25,000 per mile for the balance of 100 miles, the length of the road being 150
miles with the proviso that the Edmonton Yukon Pacific should become part of and amalgamate with the Canadian Northern. When the amalgamation came to take place, and the securities were about to be issued a difficulty arose. The Canadian Northern itself has practically two sets of securities, one Dominion guaranteed or provincial guaranteed, as the case may be, for I think it is $15,000 per mile, and these securities become a first lien on the roads to be constructed, and a second or third mortgage on the lines already constructed. But they have another class of security called consolidated debenture stock, extending over their entire system, and in the Act giving them authority to issue these securities it is provided that there shall not be more than $15,000 per mile of an underlying security. That being the case, when the amalgamation took place, the portion of the guarantee by the Dominion for $25,000 on its 100 miles was found to come in conflict with the other Act of the Canadian Northern. It was impossible Tinder existing conditions for the Dominion to get its first mortgage on this 100 miles for more than $15,000 per mile, although the guarantee was for $25,000 per mile. In order to overcome that the solicitor of the company, Mr. Phippin, after consultation with the Justice Department, and the Finance Department decided to introduce a Bill to really incorporate a new company. This new company is to be called the Canadian Northern Alberta Railway Company, and the guarantee is to be given to this company and executed. Then after this is done, and the guarantee provided for, and the road constructed, they are to amalgamate with the Canadian Northern, and the securities would then run for the $25,000 per mile, for the 100 miles, no Act interfering. That is all the Act is intended to cover, and it is what the Justice Department, and Mr. Phippin assure me is provided for by the Act. If asked if the company gave up this guarantee given under the Act of 1908, I say that they do release that absolutely. I have submitted this to the Justice Department, and to the Finance Denartment. Some little changes were made, and it was approved of by Mr. Phippin.
Mr. HENDERSON Perhaps the minister can tell us what the estimated cost of this road will be, whether the $13,000 and the $25,000 will be sufficient to build the road or whether it will be more than sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
