1 take this opportunity to ask the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) if he has ever had his attention called to the idea of allowing women to homestead. I noticed, some time ago, an article in one of the city papers of Winnipeg commenting upon a letter by a reverend gentleman in Saskatchewan, in which letter this idea was advocated. I have seen also a great deal of comment upon the subject in the press of western Canada. I think the minister might do worse than allow women to take up homesteads. Undoubtedly, there are men who have families of girls who would move to the west if their girls had the privilege of homesteading. And the minister knows also that in the west we have a surplus of bachelors. The change suggested would not only allow our ladies an opportunity to acquire some property, but would afford the male members of the population an opportunity to find helpmeets. As the letter I have referred to puts the case better than I can do, I take the liberty of reading it:
Let Women Homestead.
Editor ' Telegram/-I wish to call your attention to the remedy for one of the serious problems in our western world.
It is everywhere conceded in the province of Saskatchewan that there is a great dearth of marriageable ladies. In almost any of our new districts you will find ten young men for one young lady.
It seems to me this could he remedied by allowing girls over eighteen to homestead. I have just returned from a trip to Toronto and meeting an old friend down there I said to him, ' Why don't you come west? ' He said, ' Oh, if my girls were only hoys I would have been west long ago.' I told him we needed him more with his girls than if de had boys. He had four grown-up daughters.
Now, I ask you. why that man had not just as much right to homestead and get a quarter section for each of those girls as the man who happened to have four grownup boys ?

I claim, sir, that the west has more need to-day to allow such a man to come in with his girls and give him every right that a man with boys should get, than we have to encourage the single man. Again, in conversation, on the train, with a Norwegian from North Dakota, I got more information on the subject. He said down in the Dakotas and Minnesota, there are many men with large families of fine, strong, healthy girls, who would come to Canada if their girls could homestead, but because they cannot they are moving on down into the new country in Montana, where they have the privilege.
Now, sir, we all know what fine blood we have received from the Norwegian and Swedes; should we not encourage them to come?
We look forward to a big year in the growth of our population in this year 1910. But if it is going to receive the stimulus which will make it a red letter year in the history of the growth of Canada, our government cannot too soon grant the ladies the privilege of homesteading. For it would bring fathers and mothers, sons and daughters, lovers and sweethearts that we could never get in any othef way.
REV. R. W. BEVERIDGE. Watrous, Sask., Jan. 15.
I was unaware before reading that letter that Montana had land laws permitting ladies to enjoy the same privilege as the men, that is, the privilege of homesteading. Apparently, it is quite an attraction in that state, because Norwegians and Swedes go there from Minnesota and the Dakotas on that account. I would like to know if the minister has ever had his attention drawn to that, and if he does not think that it is worthy of serious consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This matter has been brought to my attention frequently, as it was no doubt brought to the attention of preceding ministers and preceding governments. But it has never appeared to them, and does not appear to me, mat it would be in the interest of the settlement of our country. I am aware that that law is the law of the United States, but I am not aware that it is an advantageous law, even there; so far as my judgment goes, I do not think it would be advantageous in our country. The purpose we have in view in our homestead law is not merely that people may acquire land which will mean money to them; the purpose we have in view in giving free land to homesteaders is that the land may be made productive; to secure the productiveness of the land is the reason of our homestead laws. Our experience, and I have had considerable experience, is that in order that a homestead may be made fully productive, there should be, not a single woman upon it, nor even a single man, but there should be both the man and the woman, in order that the homestead may be made fully advantageous to the country. The idea of giving homesteads to single women would tend di-269
rectly against that idea; the idea of withholding homesteads from single women, as my hon. friend will see, tends strongly in favour of that idea. I do not know that I need emphasize the point that the single man on a homestead is not in a position to bring that homestead up to its full measure of productiveness.
Because he has not got the woman with him.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Exactly. Then it is for him to get the woman, and for the woman who wants to settle on land in the Northwest to get the man, rather than that she shall have land of her own, simply to hold it down. The single woman cannot bring the land into productiveness under ordinary circumstances, even as well as the single man. We have provision for granting homesteads to women under certain conditions, and the princple underlying that system is this, that where a widow has children, although not of age to enable them to take homesteads, they are yet of sufficient age to help her satisfactorily to improve a homestead, then under those conditions, the woman is allowed to have a homestead. Having once given the privilege to widows with dependent children to secure homesteads, we find that it is used as a means of acquiring land by women who are not in a position to make improvements, and who were not in the position that was contemplated when the provision was first made. Our experience is entirely against the idea of women homesteading.

One or two questions have been asked across the floor of the House during this session in regard to the duties of Mr. Leach, inspector of homestead agencies, and whose salary I presume, is provided for in this item. I would like the minister to give us some idea of what those duties are, and why it is necessary that Mr. Leach's office should be at Brandon. Looking through the Auditor General's Report for the last two years, I find that Mr, Leach appears to have drawn an extraordinary amount of money for board and lodging, and for travelling. I have calculated that during the two financial years of 1908 and 1909, he drew for board and lodging $2,135.90, or an average of nearly $3 per day for the whole time, or nearly $3.50 per day exclusive of Sundays. His travelling expenses during that time amounted to nearly $3,000, or upwards of $5.50 a day for every travelling day. It does seem to me that that is a very large sum of money, and either that Mr. Leach's office should not be at Brandon, or that he is charging very high amounts for board and lodging and travelling expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Leach's business is that of inspector of land agencies at the



present time in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I think until a year ago he was inspector of all the land offices in the four western provinces. He is also employed at times in the adjustment of difficult cases that arise in regard to land, and his duties therefore require a good deal of travelling. It does not matter where the office is, because he is not supposed to be in his office any more than is necessary for the compilation of his reports, and generally to give him an opportunity to look over the field of his inspection. There are in the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan four land agencies and 32 sub-agencies. I need not enlarge on the amount of business that is done or the intricate and complicated nature of the business that is done in these agencies, and the disputes that are continually arising. But I can assure my hon. friend that Mr. Leach's duties should occupy all his time, so that he would have very little time to spend in the office at Brandon. It makes little or no difference whether he is located at Brandon or anywhere else, inasmuch as Brandon is 130 miles west of Winnipeg, and as his duties extend westward to the boundary of Saskatchewan, his travelling expenses are lightened by his residing in Brandon rather than in Winnipeg.

Does not the minister think that an average of $3 a day for board and lodging for every day in the year, for two years, is somewhat high charge when compared with the usual prices for board and lodging in those two western provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, I could not answer. I am sure it cost me more than that for board and lodging when I travel. It would depend upon the number of days that Mr. Leach was absolutely away from his office whether it was a fair charge or not.
' Mr. LAKE. Has the department any check on the number of days Mr. Leach was absent. It struck me as a very large 'charge, indeed, and I think the department should have some means of checking it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Leach puts in a fnonthly account to the department, and it is checked there. I presume the account is all right, although I agree with toy hon. friend that it seems a large amount. However, travelling is not inexpensive in that country, and Mr. Leach is supposed to be travelling pretty nearly all the time.
Protection of timber, forest reserves, &o., $146,250.

Is it the intention of the minister' to take any portion out o the Riding or Duck mountain forest reserves and throw it open to settlement. I have had sent to me a petition largely Mr. OLIVER.
signed by those living along the Canadian Northern railway, not far from the town of Roblin where it is said there are two townships with very little timber on them and which would make splendid agricultural land. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no intention, so far as I know, of taking any portion out of the reserve, except at its northwest corner where the main line of the Canadian Northern railway cuts a little into the reserve. I was discussing that with the officer in charge with a view of deciding if it would not be well to cut that out of the reserve so as to leave the Canadian Northern railway outside the limits of the reserve entirely. We have had no discussion so far as I know about taking two townships out. I would certainly advise the people who are looking for occupation of these townships not to depend on It, because the matter has not been under my consideration yet. What the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) said is the first I have heard of it.

I think the Minister of the Interior should take into consideration the question of opening to homesteading a portion of the Turtle Mountain reserve south of my town. There is a township, or probably there are two townships there that we will never be able to do anything with as a forest reserve. The government is sDending money all the time on it, but the growth of the trees has not been satisfactory, and we will never be able to make it a forest reserve. That fact can easily be ascertained from the officers of the department, and if it cannot be made into a reserve why should we not throw it open to homesteading. I think the minister understands what I mean.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Schaffner). We have no wish to hold land in reserve simply for the purpose of having it under reservation. But' of course these reserves were created on the supposition that it would be possible to improve the source of water supply by securing the growth of timber, and we are trying to do that in that locality. If we fail the reasonable thing will be to abandon the effort, but we cannot abandon it without having made a fair attempt to succeed. I will ask the hon. member to I have patience to give us an opportunity

to make good fair test, and if we fail we will no doubt have to take the other course.
Is the Department of the Interior having any considerable amount of printing done outside of Canada at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have still a very large amount done in the United States, and especially the atlases that we print for circulation for immigration purposes.

Why should not those be printed in our own counry?
Mr. OLI\ ER. Since I have been minister, I have made several attempts to get these atlases printed in Canada, but so far without success. I presume the reason is because, in order that such an atlas may be turned out in good quality and style and at the lowest price, it must be done by a well equipped establishment which carries on a very large business in that particular line. There did not seem to be an establishment in Canada which was willing and able to take hold of the work in the same manner as this institution in the United States can do it. The hon. gentleman understands that when we want immigration literature we want it at a certain season of the year, and unless we get it at that season, its value is largely lost. One of these establishments we were dealing with took an order at a certain price, but they did not make delivery within anything like the time stipulated, and while it was not a dead loss, it was not an advantageous commercial transaction.
Was that a Canadian company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, one of the largest in Winnipeg. However, I managed to get some of this work done in Canada, and we have recently given a trial order for some atlas work that will be used for distribution at the Brussels exhibition. We are having that done in Canada as an experiment, and if we get satisfactory results we will be glad to give further orders.' In view of the necessity for getting quality, and prompt delivery, at a certain price, the printing of this atlas cannot be handled as in the case of an ordinary printing contract. Now, as to the printing which we require for use in the United States, if we printed it in Canada the United States customs charges would make it an altogether disadvantageous transaction for us. The hon. gentleman may take it for granted that for any printing we want in the United States, we will have to get it done in the United States, because of the customs duties. I am anxious to have any printing we want in England, or Canada, or on the continent of Europe done in Canada.

I want to direct the attention of the Minister of the Interior to the necessity for taking greater care of the immigrants arriving at the Union station at Toronto. The minister himself must be thoroughly conversant with the condition of affairs in that respect. Any person who passes a few hours of any day during the summer months at the Toronto Union station will see congregated there a very large number of immigrants, including some of our own people from other parts of Ontario, who are making ready to go to the west. Among the immigrants are also to be found a considerable number who intend to locate on farms in various parts of Ontario. I heard the minister state the other day that it was not the duty of the government to make provision to detain the immigrants in the cities, but rather to send them out to their destination as soon as possible, and I do not at all criticise that idea. But, I would point out to the minister that money expended on employing one or two extra immigration officers at the Union station at Toronto during the summer months to look after these immigrants, would be money well expended. These officers could direct the immigrants how to get to their destination; they could give them information as to the conditions which they would be likely to meet with, and they could communicate with the farmers who are coming into the city every day looking for these immigrants to engage their services. I believe that the government could wisely expend a sum of money for the employment of one or two capable and intelligent officials who would counsel and advise the immigrants and look after their comfort. If this were done by the government it would be in the interests of the government themselves, in the interests of the farmers of Ontario, and it would be especially in the interest of the new immigrants who are very susceptible to first impressions. and who should receive some special attention from the government when they arrive in great centres of population like the city of Toronto.

To pay expenses connected with waterpower investigations and reports in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and the railway belt in British Columbia, $20,000.
Is this a new vote, and if so, what is its purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The question of water-powers is attracting more attention than ever before, and it is thought well that the department, in order to administer the water-powers that come under its jurisdiction in the prairie provinces and presumably in the British Columbia railway belt, should have advance information as to the character of all these powers and their possible value for development purposes. If a person comes to the department and makes application to develop any water-power, the department has either to delay the application until it ascertains what the possibilities of that water-power are, or accept the statement made by an interested party. We want to gather information so that when applications are made we will be able to deal with them on their merits. This, of course, will cost some money, and the information may not be turned to account immediately, but I think it is in the interest of the country that the department should have that information.

Naval service - including the purchase, construction and maintenance of ships, the maintenance and upkeep of dockyards at Esquimalt and Halifax, and the establishment and maintenance of training schools, $3,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
On a previous occasion I stated to the House that it was our intention, as soon as the Navy Bill passed, to ask for tenders for the ten ships with which we propose to commence our navy. It is not probable that any portion of the $3,000,000 for which we now ask will be applied this year to that purpose. Tenders will be called for, and the first thing the successful tenderer will have to do will be to put up a plant, and therefore I do not think we shall be in a position this year to spend a single dollar of this amount. I will explain to the committee how we propose to deal with this appropriation. I stated on a former occasion that we had entered into negotiations with the imperial government for the purchase of the steamship ' Niobe.' Those negotiations are practically completed and are only awaiting the assent of parliament. The amount of the purchase money agreed upon, as I have already stated, is $1,075,000. This will be taken out of this appropriation. The ' Niobe,' it is expected, will reach Canada early in the season and will form the first nucleus of our navy. We propose to appro-Mr. OLIVER.
priate for the maintenance and upkeep of this steamship the following amounts: Pay of nucleus crew and training personnel, $174,000. We estimate that the crew will be composed of 27 officers and 324 men, including sailors, mechanics, etc., a total of 351. For the victualling of the crew, $38,000; this is based upon an estimate of 30 cents per day per man. For medicine, $1,000; this is an estimate based upon the experience of the admiralty. For clothing gratuities, that is, uniforms, $10,000. For the upkeep

hull, machinery, sea stores and fuel-$140,000; this is based upon the calculation of the admiralty. For alterations in fitting the ' Niobe ' as a training ship, $50,000. These appropriations total $413,000.

that Capt. Macdonald, though not yet appointed, has been designated for the command of the ' Niobe.' He is a Canadian, a son of Senator Macdonald of British Columbia, and has had considerable training and experience in England.

speechtext: It will be stationed in the gulf and will be used as a training ship. Coming to the ' Rainbow,' I may say that it has already been purchased. We estimate that the crew will be composed of 16 officers and 163 men. For victualling the crew, $20,000. For medicine, $500. For clothing, $5,000. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has any estimate been made of the expected expenditures at the two places? Could the Prime Minister give a statement of what is to be done, for example, at Halifax? As I understand it, the dockyard at present is simply used for storing certain articles belonging to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. As one of my hon. friends from British Columbia said of the dockyard at Esquimalt, it might be regarded as no more than ' a glorified junk shop.' I understand that it is to be something more than that in the future, and I would like to know just what.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry to say that I am informed that the dockyard is in rather a dilapidated condition. It is proposed to establish there the naval college, with houses for captain and college director, barracks, drill shed and so on, and to spend something on dockyard construction, making a total of about $590,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
^This is to put the
dockyard in good condition?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, the dockyard at Halifax.
I understand that the dock at Halifax is owned by a private company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The dock-yes.
Is any of this money to be spent to enlarge the dock so that it will take in the ships of the new navy?	*

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: None of this expenditure is for that purpose; it is for the preparation of the dockyard.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is to be spent, I understand, on what was formerly the imperial dockyard at Halifax. I may explain to my hon. friend from North Sim-coe (Mr. Currie) that the Halifax graving dock and the imperial dockyard are entirely distinct things. There is no graving dock in connection with that dockyard. The graving dock is owned by a private company which has had assistance from the imperial government, from this government and from the city of Halifax. I would like to ask the Prime Minister how it is that this very great expenditure is necessary? The imperial government as I understand, handed over that dockyard in perfectly good condition. I do not know to what extent it was dismantled if at all; I never understood that it was dis-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
mantled. I brought to the attention of the government in January last the statement of an English gentleman of experience, Sir. Wm. White, who spoke with authority on these matters. He had visited the dockyard at Esquimalt, and he gave an exceedingly bad report of it. In effect he said that it was in very poor and ineffective condition. He stated, further, that he had not visited the dockyard at Halifax, but understood, from information that had been given him, on what he conceived to be reliable authority, that it was about in the same condition. I received from the government a rather reassuring reply. True, like many replies that we get from the government with respect to such matters, it was not very definite, but, so far as it was definite, it was reassuring. I cannot understand how it is .possible, if that dockyard has been kept up by a proper system and by reasonable expenditure in the meantime, that it should be in a condition necessitating the expenditure of about $600,000. If the expenditure is necessary, I am not objecting to it; but I think that before the committee votes the amount, we should have a very clear and definite explanation as to why that enormous sum of money is necessary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As to the dockyard at Esquimalt, that has been like Mahomet's coffin, which was suspended between heaven and earth-the dockyard has been in the possession neither of the imperial government nor of this government, and so it has got into a rather dilapidated condition. Of course, I have never seen it. But I have seen the dockyard at Halifax, and I must say that it is not in so bad a condition. There is a splendid property there, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) knows better than I do. I do not know that there is much to be done in the way of repairs, except what might be expected in a property of that kind. But the expenditure I have spoken of is made necessary because of the character of the new navy and the works and buildings in connection with it that are to be put there. For instance, in this expenditure is included the naval college. It is impossible to say how much that will cost until we have, seen the plans and specification prepared by the architect, but I understand it must be a fairly expensive building.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has this expenditure of $590,000 anything to do with the naval college?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It includes the college. Let me give the items covered by this expenditure of $590,000-naval college and furnishing of the same; workshops in connection with the college; houses for captain of college and director

of studies; barracks for men; battery for heavy and light gun drill (this is something new, and I do not know what expense may be involved in it); arming of battery; drill shed; alteration of admiralty house for officers of barracks; dockyard construction.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is that- dockyard construction?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That covers the repairs to the building and the wharf. All this expenditure cannot be very definitely estimated until we have the plans and specifications from the architects. But this is the nearest approximate that the officers of the department have been able to give us.

I had the pleasure of going through the dockyard at Halifax last year. The epithet applied by Sir William White to the dockyard at Esquimalt applies to some extent to the Halifax dockyard. This plant is there, but it is not modern. Of course, there are some modern tools, but, in order to carry on the work of the navy under modern conditions, fully three-quarters of the appliances and tools might as well be cast into the sea. There are no air tools, the power is not applied by electric motors, and there are none of the economies that ought to appear in a modem dockyard. Everything there is substantial, but old-fashioned, and evidently intended more for the repair of ships built of wood than for the repair of modern steel vessels. The condition of the tools and machinery, I must say, speaks well for the staff, for everything not in use was carefully oiled and in good repair. But I have not the slightest doubt that it would take a couple of hundred thousand dollars to put modem tools and appliances in that dockyard so that ship repairs might be made economically.
As to the admiralty house, that is to say, the quarters and that sort of thing, I think they are very good quarters, some slight repairs might be needed. Another thing in connection with this college, if it is^to be in Halifax, is that it should be placed where the cadets of the college can be given practical employment in the yard where 'these tools are used, and then there would be no necessity of duplicating the tools at the college. I cannot understand why the government does not renew that dock and enlarge it. An expenditure of possibly $200,000 would lengthen that dock, and by means of concrete piers and widening the bottom, it could be made a first-class dock. It will also be necessary to provide the necessary crane equipment to handle the heavy steel and cast iron bars and ordnance, and everything of that kind to be placed on those ships. That is expensive, but if the government is going to
do this work, I would strongly urge that they make it up to date, and not do it by piecemeal, and be coming down here every year for additional small items. It is better to go right on and tear out what is old, and put in what is necessary to make it an up to date shipyard. Riant of this description becomes antiquated very quickly. Labour-saving appliances and inventions are brought into use so rapidly now, that of the men who were well acquainted with these things some years ago, you could hardly find one man in a thousand now that knows how to use them. However, I am glad that the dockyard is to be fixed up, because it is a magnificent site. I do not think there is a harbour in Amerioa that is equal to the Halifax harbour. There is no situation equal to it in the world for a dockyard such as is proposed. I have also been out to Esquimalt, and I think that the opinion of it given by Mr. White is corrrect.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not know anything about Mr. White's opinion except that he is supposed to be an eminent authority on these matters. But I think some of my hon. friends from British Columbia *who are familiar with the conditions, would be much inclined to agree with him. So far as Halifax is concerned it was a naval base up to about five years ago, when we had a very considerable squadron on that station. About ten years ago one of the largest battleships in the navy was in that squadron. Up to the time that Halifax ceased to be a naval base that dockyard was sufficient for t-hfe purpose, and it was handed over to this government, as I understand, in that condition. I still desire to express surprise that it should be necessary, if proper care has been taken, to expend so large an amount for the purpose of making it effective. There may be some conditions I do not understand. Certainly the government were not lacking in one respect, for they have put a considerable number of men at work in the dockyard from time to time, and more especially at the time of general elections, when more than 400 unnecessary men were put on according to the sworn evidence of persons in Halifax who were interrogated with regard to that by Mr. Justice Cassells, and by the counsel attending that commission. Except when a general election was imminent the ordinary staff seemed to be-reason-ably adequate for the purpose. We shall have, I suppose, at another session some information as to what has been done with this money, and perhaps some fuller information as to the conditions which make the expenditure necessary. It would have been better if the Prime Minister could have found it convenient to print and distribute among us the memorandum from which he

reads, as it is not easy to get a definite idea of what the expenditure contemplates merely hearing it read.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is typewritten, but I will send it over to my hon. friend. The condition of the Halifax dockyard is very much as it has been described by my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie). The building and constructions are all of a very substantial character, every one who has been in the dockyard is impressed by that fact. I think also that it has been kept in very good condition of repair, and perhaps this explains the extraordinary number of men who were employed at election times. It shows that they did not lose their time, they oiled the machinery very well and kept it moving.
BORDEN Did they spend much of their time in oiling the election machinery?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At Halifax it is probably necessary to do what has been suggested by the' hon. member for Simcoe in order to put the works in modern condition. When the dockyard was first established many years ago it was prepared to handle wooden ships, now we have to get in a new plant to meet modern conditions, and the establishment of a navy. That will also necessitate a new building. I think my hon. friend from Simcoe is quite right in saying that we should have the naval college in close proximity to the dockyard. We must also have barracks for the men, and houses for the officers, we must have a battery, and all the conditions implied thereby, also a drill shed. We shall probably need many new constructions, as well as repairing wihat already exists there. My hon. friend from Simcoe suggests that the dock itself ought to be lengthened, and I understand that the same idea has occurred to several others. But I am informed that the officers of the admiralty, who are expert in matters of that kind, think it cannot be lengthened, they have made an examination, and found it impossible to lengthen the dock.

I understand that the gov-ernfent are to borrow officers from the imperial navy. What is the plan proposed to substitute them for those men who have been in the Canadian service, and how is the exchange to be effected, and for what period?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The officers would be borrowed for three years, and a skeleton crew will be brought over for five years. This will be the nucleus upon which we propose to build our own navy.

Is it the intention to employ some Canadian sailors at once to work with the nucleus of the British sailors?
Mr. R, L. BORDEN.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. ,
How many?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We propose to begin at once to train 400 recruits.
How many imperial officers will remain on board, and how many Canadian officers will go on board at once?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have no Canadian officers at the present time. All the officers on this boat must be brought over from England But we propose to train our own men as fast as we can.
The intention is to man the ships with imperial officers until such time as you can educate Canadian officers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear; that is it.
Are these to be educated in tlie Canadian college?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is the intention.

The Prime Minister stated that the intention was to place the Halifax dockyard in a modern condition. Has he an estimate of the whole expenditure required for that, because obviously the appropriation taken this year will not be sufficient for the whole work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is intended, as I understand it, to rejuvenate the dockyard at Halifax, but, of course, it is not possible to do it in one year, and it must be done gradually.
What is the amount for that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The estimated expenditure under all these headings will come to nearly $600,000.
How are the 400 recruits which are to be taken on at once, to be selected?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: By recruiting officers and advertisement, I presume.

Is it the intention to make Esquimalt the naval base for the Pacific squadron, and if not, where will the Pacific naval base be?	.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Esquimalt is intended to be the naval base. We have not yet had a full transfer- of Esquimalt, but as soon as we have, it is proposed to do there exactly what we are doing in Halifax, barring, of course, the naval college. We will not have a naval college on the Pacific, but everything else will be the same as at Halifax.
This item speaks of the establishment and maintenance of naval schools; what other schools are contemplated besides the naval college?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It should be school; there will only be one school.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The following table shows the pay in the British and the American services, and the proposed payj in the Canadian service. Of course, it must be understood that those rates are not definitely fixed yet.

In additian to above, men in United States navy receive $6.36 a month extra on first re-enlistment, and $4.36 a month extra on each subsequent re-enlistment. It is proposed to grant men in the naval service of Canada an allowance of $1.50 per month for each re-enlistment if the term of service is 5 years, or proportionate rates if enlisted for a longer period.

At what rate is it proposed to pay the officers from the imperial service for the time they serve in the Canadian service?
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, The same as the Canadian, the rate of pay I have just stated.
Can the minister give us the minimum ages in the British and Canadian services, for the admission of midshipmen?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The proposed age in the Canadian service is from 14 to

16 years. I understand that in the imperial service it is from 12i to 13 years.
Will members of skeleton crews from the imperial service be paid at the Canadian rates?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What expectation has the government with respect to recruiting? The Minister of Militia stated some time ago that in the permanent force not more than 20 per cent are Canadians born. I do not know how the rates of pay compare or what greater attractions the naval force presents, but assuming that they are about the same there might be the same difficulty in securing Canadian recruits.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know that we have any expectation upon this. It is a matter which must be governed by experience. We may have some difficulty on account of the smaller field to draw Strom as compared with Great Britain.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: One has to take into consideration the fact that there are perhaps greater opportunities in a country in process of development for an active and enterprising man, and therefore men who in Great Britain would enter the navy would here be diverted into some other form of activity and occupation. However, as the minister says, we will have to learn that by experience. Is any, and if so what portion of the $3,000,000 now proposed to be expended in the construction of ships?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I stated before my hon. friend came in that we did not expect to be called upon to spend a dollar of this. I stated it was our intention as soon as the Bill received the sanction of His Excellency to ask for tenders. We have no plant at present which is prepared to go into construction of ships. It may be some months before we are in a position to accept a tender, and if a tender is accepted the first thing the tenderer will have to do will be to put up a plant. It is not expected, therefore, that within the present fiscal year we will be called on to pay anything out of this appropriation for construction.
It appears that at the last conference of representatives of this government and the admiralty, the question of the flag was raised. What flag is this navy to fly?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That question has not yet been considered or determined. The suggestion has been made to us, and no opposition has been made to it, that we should fly the white ensign with the Canadian coat of arms on the fly. As to the uniform of the officers, it ha3 been suggested that we should adopt the uniform of the imperial navy, simply substi-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
tuting the maple leaf for the laurel leaf on the buttons.
When is it expected the ' Niobe ' will arrive at Halifax?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: About the month of July.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do I understand that $50,000 is to be expended on the ' Niobe ' and $27,600 on the ' Rainbow.' That of course is speaking approximately. Where are these repairs to be effected?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the admiralty yard in Great Britain.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Where are these two ships to be stationed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The ' Niobe ' will be stationed in the gulf of St. Lawrence, and the ' Rainbow ' in the northern waters of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Where will their headquarters be?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At Halifax and Esquimalt.

On the Great Lakes there are between three and four thousand sailors, seamen, artificers and officers possibly as well disciplined and intelligent a class of sailors as can be found in the whole world. They are well trained, pilots and expert machinists, most of them understanding machinery of all kinds such as they would encounter on a warship with the possible exception of the guns. Will any steps be taken to provide training for these men? Will a naval militia be attached to the navy so that these men may spend their winters at sea so that they can learn the only other accomplishments they require, gunnery and ocean seamanship such as taking astronomical observations? They are all men of fine physique. They are employed under modern mechanical conditions, and among them you could get stokers, engineers, electrical men and "all kinds of men who would be required by this government to superintend the navy in time of war. All you would require to do would be to teach them gunnery.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It seems to me a very good suggestion. If we could take some of those voters down and put them on the ships, I can see no objection. They are good seamen and I am told a very fine population.
I think some arrangement might be made whereby they would get three months' training a year, and arrangements could be made that their expenses to Halifax and back in the spring should be paid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear
I understand there is such a naval reserve in England and an officer on the lakes, who could pass an examination, should be entitled to fly a special flag, as in the English merchant marine.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Fisheries protection service, $281,500.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is nothing new in this appropriation; it is the same as we have had year after year; but I would like to amend this item by adding ' including cost of vessels engaged in fisheries inspection for the Department of Marine and Fisheries.' Hereafter the protection service will be under the Naval Department, while the inspection service will Temain under the Marine Department.
How -will you apportion the expense between the two departments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At present we have several ships which are doing both inspection and protection service. We have certain vessels policing our waters and preserving them from poachers; these are the protection service. Then we have a certain number of smaller boats, with very small crews, employed for the inspection of the fisheries, distributing provisions, and so on, and reporting to headquarters. These will remain in the Marine Department, while the others will go to the Naval Department. It is intended that in the course of time the vessels engaged in the fisheries protection service shall be replaced by vessels of our navy, which will be of a very much superior character.
Then I understand that those in the protection service will be charged to the Naval Branch, and those in the inspection service will be charged to the Marine branch?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
Will the men in the protection service be under the naval discipline and uniformed like the men of the fleet?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is the intention in the course of time, but not at present. I think I can safely say that the intention is to replace all the _ ships that we have at present in the protection service with ships of the Canadian navy; but so long as our present ships are in service, it is not intended to change them from their present condition.

When the navy is in existence^ I understand that the protection service at present given by the Marine and Fisheries Department will virtually disappear, and the line of cleavage will be between what may be called the
customs revenue or protective service and the naval service. I should think that the local service might be better undertaken by the Customs Department, as is done in the United States with their revenue cutters, so that the other department would be clear and promotions would go direct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Owing to our geographical position, I do not think that our coasts would be sufficiently protected by revenue cutters such as they have in the United States. It has been found that a particular class of men have to be trained for our protection service, and I think it is better managed as it is than it w-ould be in the way suggested by my hon. friend.

My idea is that the men who are at present in the service should have a chance to be absorbed into the navy. These ships are doing the same kind of work that naval vessels are doing in Great Britain and other countries, and if you leave them in a separate category, you will give cause for a certain amount of jealousy and disagreement, whereas if you have just the one service, with a chance for the officres to gain naval promotion, I think it would work more smoothly than it will if you have two departments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend confounds the protection service with the inspection service. The inspection service is done largely in our inland waters, for which vessels of the protection service would not be suited.
No, I mean the protection service. The crews, I understand, will be absorbed into the navy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should imagine so.
To provide for the construction of a steamer for surveying the Gulf and River St. Lawrence to replace ' La Canadienne,' $75,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The steamer is under contract, being built in England. It is ready now.
BORDEN- What has become of ' La Canadienne '?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: ' La Canadienne ' is rather a veteran, and will have to be placed under another service-not absolutely put out of commission; but 3he is not suitable for this service.
What is the new boat going to cost?	*

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: When did the construction begin?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: About a year ago.	>

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Ig there any difficulty about having a steamer of that size built in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, I do not know. It was built by tender, and the lowest tenderer got the contract.
I understand there was very little difference between the tenders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon friend is right. There was not much difference. The tender of Swan and Hunter was $177,653 delivered at Sorel, and that of the Collingwood Ship Building Company was $181,462.

That is a very small difference, and last year the Finance Minister said that if there was only a difference of 5 per cent or 10 per cent the government would not hesitate to give the preference to a Canadian shipbuilding concern over a British shipbuilding concern. The difference is so very small in this case that I think the government should have hesitated before they gave the contract to the English firm, especially bearing in mind that the customs department would have received considerable benefit from the material that went into the building of the ship and that the railway companies and Canadian workmen would also have received benefit. I do not like to criticise the department in the absence of the regular minister, but I hope that in another case of this kind the Prime Minister will bear in mind what I have said and recall the promise made last year by the Finance Minister that if there was only a difference of 5 or 10 per cent the Canadian firm would have the benefit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I agree altogether with my hon. friend. I am surprised that the Collingwood Company did not get the contract when the difference was so small. But knowing the mind of the minister, there must have been some other reason. Not only he but the cabinet as a whole would have been disposed to give it to the Canadian firm. I am delighted to find that there is such a small discrepancy between Canadian building and British building. It is a hopeful sign and I will be only too glad to remember the suggestion of my hon. friend.
Hydrographic surveys, including survey of Hudson bay, $320,000.
Have you a vessel now making a hydrographic survey in the Hudson bay?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, we have not. We have a vessel doing hydrographic survey work in the gulf. But we intend to send shore parties to the Hudson bay Sir WILFRID LAURIER,
this year to commence a survey of the bay. We have no vessel there yet.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is that the explanation of the increase?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
What does the Prime Minister mean by saying he will send two shore parties to the Hudson bay if they have no boat?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We will have to charter a vessel to send them up to Hudson bay, to both the Nelson river and the Churchill river. Then in small boats they will carry out the survey of the bay 20 miles from the shore, the object being to ascertain exactly what are the conditions for navigating purposes on both the Nelson and Churchill rivers.
Tidal service, $42,500.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is being done-?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that the study of currents is a work that never ceases. We have at the present time a steamer in the Gulf of St. Lawrence which is stationed there during all the seasons taking surveys at all times of the day. We are doing some similar work on the coast of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I suppose these observations are tabulated and published.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, published every year.
Is any hydrographic survey work being carried on in Hudson bay. They are talking about building railways up there and establishing grain elevators and grain routes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is the service which we commenced this year. We have taken an appropriation for this purpose. I repeat that we intend to send two shore parties to Hudson bay where, it is proposed, they will apply themselves to surveying 20 miles fifom the shore, at Nelson and Churchill. The object is to ascertain, in view of the early construction of the railway to Hudson bay wdiich is the better harbour. We have been under the impression that the only good harbour in Hudson bay was Churchill, but an impression has grown up recently that in certain respects Nelson harbour would be the better one. The object in sending the two parties this year is to secure as accurate information as we can collect to enable us to determine that very point. It will only be a preliminary step, for we will have to survey the bay as accurately as the St. Lawrence and the great lakes.

I understand that a great deal of money is spent every year on these surveys, and that they are simply duplicating the work done by the British admiralty years ago. I understand that the admiralty charts are very complete.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The admiralty charts are certainly very complete and the chart prepared by Admiral Bayfield is as good a piece of work as has been done in any part of the world. But in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the river St. Lawrence there are displacements all the time and the hydrographic survey cannot stop. It must always go on because every year there are displacements which have to be recorded for the benefit of navigation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What kind of displacements?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Boulders in ihe river St. Lawrence especially. I understand that the currents at the bottom of the river are different from those at the bottom of the ocean and all the time you have to keep a detailed survey going on. New maps are published every year also.

Rewards for saving life, including life-saving stations, $40,000.

With regard to this item, the minister may recall the facts of the case that took place in connection with the wreck of the steamer 'Hestia.' He will remember that the seamen were on board that steamer from Sunday night, or about 1 o'clock Monday morning, until the afternoon of Tuesday, without any one coming near them to rescue them from that wreck. There is a life-saving station not far away, and a lighthouse only about three or four miles distant. It will also be remembered that this steamer sent off continuously rockets and bombs, and also lighted a large bonfire on the deck of the ship on Monday night. It was an absolutely clear night, all shore lights were yisible, and that light should have been seen at a very long distance. But apparently no notice was taken of it by the lighthouse keeper at Gannet Rock, and as a matter of fact, the wrecked seamen were not relieved until the afternoon of Tuesday. I think the minister will also remember that when the court of inquiry took place on that wreck, the chairman, Captain Lugard, said that it was the intention of the government to make a further inquiry into all the circumstances of the case, because the court refused to go into anything that occurred after the stranding of the ship. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, also, when I brought this matter up early in the session, stated that he would hold a further inquiry into the matter. If any other inquiry has been held it has certainly not been a public one. I have kept a lookout for such an inquiry, and I have seen nothing of the kind, and no reference to it anywhere. I think it was due to the department, it was due to the shipping interests, that a further and more searching inquiry should have been made into the circumstances attending that wreck, and why these wrecked persons were left so long almost within sight of help, without any assistance being rendered them. I think some explanation is due to parlia-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
rnent and to the public from the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
The lighthouse and life-savtng service is most important, and it is growing in importance all the time as the commercial marine increases in numbers, and tonnage. One peculiar circumstance was stated with regard to the absence of the lifesaving crew coming to that wreck earlier, and it was that the life-boat could not be manned, because the crew refused to go in her owing to the fact that a considerable amount of back pay had been withheld from them. The correspondence brought down in answer to my motion demonstrates that, and it is a serious condition of affairs. The allegation that the light-keeper at Gannet Rock took no notice of these wreck signals, and bon-fires, is another thing we are entitled to have information about. I would suggest to the minister that in the appointmejit of lighthouse attendants, especially on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts, only men should be appoint-ted who have been formerly at sea, who know the anxiety which is caused to navigators approaching land in hazy weather, and who know how important it is that everything in connection with the lighthouse and signals and appliances should be in proper order. I would therefore urge that only men be appointed who have experience as mariners, and who have been accustomed to keeping watch at sea. I hope the hon. minister will give us information as to the condition of that life-saving station, and as to the reason why the further inquiry promised by Mr. Brodeur and by the [DOT]chairman of the commission which investigated the wreck of the ' Hestia,' was not had.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The wreck of the ' Hestia,' was discussed at very great length, and very fully in the earlier days of the session, and the minister explained the facts and the result of the investigation which appears on ' Hansard.' I am advised that the minister came to the conclusion that a further investigation would be of no service.
Mr. DANIEL He promised it from his place in the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The minister was later on advised that a further formal inquiry would not be productive of any good results. The department has been very active since that time, and a new and modern life-saving station is nearing completion on Wood island in the neighbourhood where the wreck occurred. A very competent man has been brought out from England to take charge of the life-saving stations on the Bay of Fundy in order that a better service may be Tendered in the future, and the steamer ' Stanley,' has been

placed in service on the Bay of Fundy to take care of the life-buoys, and beacons, and to keep them in, proper order. This is all a decided improvement over former arrangements, and I suppose it is largely due to the unfortunate wreck of the ' Hestia.' The department has since that time done everything in its power to meet the requirements of the situation. A modern gasoline life-saving boat manned with a good crew and supervised by a competent man brought out from England for that purpose, will be placed on the station. I agree with my hon. friend as to the advisability of employing seafaring men in the lighthouses. I understand that on the Atlantic coast fishermen and ex-sailors are generally if not always selected for positions of that kind.

Not always.
Mr. TEMPLEMAN My experience is that they are about the only class of men who will take such positions in these isolated stations. The great difficulty is to get good men, and my own opinion is that the salaries of the light-keepers are very low indeed and probably do not command the salaries of the light-keepers are very estly hope that the policy of the department in initiating a system of classification of lighthouses, and increasing the pay of the lighthouse keepers will be extended.

The statement of the minister as to the improvements that have been made since the wreck of the ' Hestia,' are reassuring, and satisfactory, but at the same time the further investigation promised by the minister, and by Captain Lu-gard during the inquiry, has not been held. We have no information as to whether the lighthouse keeper at Gannet Rock did his duty on the night of the wreck. There have been statements made in the press as to his seeing this vessel coming in too near and giving no warning signals. I do not know whether that is correct or not, but it is due to the department as well as to the shipping interests, and to the passengers who travel on these ships that a real investigation should have been held. If the lighthouse keeper was not at fault he certainly should be freed from blame. The promise of the minister that a rigid inquiry would ho held has not been carried out.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The investigation showed that the light was burning.
It is not denied that the Gannet Rock light was burning.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The investigation made by the commissioners was considered to be complete, and I understand the minister promised further inquiry by himself, but he concluded afterwards that nothing further could be ascertained.

The investigation stopped short at the moment of the stranding of the vessel. The delay in taking these men off the ship occurred after the stranding, and Captain Lugard and his associate commissioners would not allow evidence as to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The minister ascertained afterwards that the life-saving station was not in the best place, and I presume that it is in consequence, that he is building a better station in a more suitable location.

Templeman) now that I think the increase given to the light-keepers was not in proportion to the advance in the cost of living The duties of the light-keepers are very important; upon their faithful attention to these duties the lives and property of many people depends. In many cases, their duties are of such a nature that it is impossible for them to engage in any other calling. The salaries paid are too meagre altogether. Of course, lighthouses need not be visited so often as beacons and buoys that have no personal attendants, but they ought to be visited by the steamer practically once a month.

I am glad to hear the
minister's statement, for the evidence in the case of which I have spoken shows that, although that light had been out, and the buoy defective for nine or ten months, the fact was never reported to Ottawa until after the wreck took place. I am glad the department is waking up to the necessity of looking a little more carefully after these things than it has done in the past.

The minister has placed in the estimates this year $1,000,000 for lighthouses and aids to navigation. This is an increase of $200,000 over the appropriation for last year. I have no criticism to_ offer of the increased expenditure in this branch, for I think this a very im-270}	!
portant service. But I hold also that the aids to navigation should be properly distributed. Some time ago, I brought to the attention of the department the need for a ' Fairway ' whistling buoy at Grand Passage, Brier island. The Lighthouse Board have said that they did not consider there was any need for a buoy at that particular place for the safety of navigation. That is not the opinion of mariners who navigate those waters. That is not the opinion held by Mr. E. C. Bowers, a former member of this hon. House, a lifelong resident of Brier island, and a man largely interested in shipping at that port. I am going to add that for the lack of this urgently needed aid to navigation, there may be a serious marine casuality at that place, and I wish to be on record as having stated this danger. I understand an application was made for this aid to navigation some years ago, but was not granted. The real trouble, I think, is that the Lighthouse Board does not fully understand the situation, because if they did, I do not believe they would decline to grant this 'Fairway' buoy. There are a great many of these automatic buoys lying about the marine agency at Halifax, when they should be in use, and this is one of the cases where they are needed. The harbour at Westport is a very important harbour, and is much in use by a large number of vessels, but it is almost impossible in a fog for a vessel to safely make that port lacking this ' Fairway ' buoy. I am going to make a request now to the hon. the minister. If he will, during the coming summer, send an officer of the board to visit Westport and make a personal examination of the locality, I will be glad to accompany him myself, and if that i3 not possible, I will place him in the hands of people who know the situation thoroughly, and I am convinced that if he does make an inspection, he will report that there is a need for this whistling buoy.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I understand my hon. friend is speaking about Westport. The department built a lighthouse there last year. I have suggested to the deputy minister that the request of my hon. friend is a very modest one, and if he is content with a buoy, I promise that we will send an officer of the department to make an inspection, and if he finds it is necessary, I promise him that the buoy will be placed there.
To provide for breaking ice in Thunder bay and Lake Superior, and other points deemed advisable for the good of navigation, $40,000.

Has this all been used up at Thunder bay?
MT\ TEMPLEMAN. A part of this money was spent last year. The department hat

a contract with the Canadian Lake Towing Company for breaking the ice in Port Arthur and Fort William. The contract price is $30,000 a year, and was made for three years, to expire in 1911. Other contracts were made for breaking the ice in Parry Sound, Depot Harbour, Midland and Col-lingwood. In these cases the water is kept open by tug boats.
Signal service, $9,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: These are signal stations for signalling passenger vessels, largely in connection with the lighthouses. There are five stations: Quebec, 6t. John, Brier island, Partridge island and Pointe Bleue.
How do these stations. Brier island, for instance, signal? By means of flags, or in what way?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: They report by wire and by telephone.

I saw a complaint some time ago that a steamer belonging to the Canadian Pacific railway line tried to communicate, and hoisted her number for the Brier island man to signal her, and he did not do it. I know that the steamer reported the remissness afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The department has no complaint from the Canadian Pacific railway about that, and they would be apt to report any mistake of that kind.

I do not suppose the Canadian Pacific railway made any complaint to the government, but I saw the complaint in the press, and it showed that the vessel endeavoured to get a signal from the Brier island man, and he did not signal her.

I happen to know the keeper of the signal station at Brier island, and he is a most trustworthy man. I think there must be some mistake, and that my hon. friend perhaps has read a report in a newspaper that is not correct. I know that mariners have the utmost confidence in the fidelity of the signal keeper at that port. I notice that the minister is only paying him a salary of $250. That salary is altogether too small for the duties this man has to perform. He is stationed on a bleak hillside, away from all houses and human society, and he has to live in quarters which are not the most cheerful. I am told by people living at Westport who know the situation, and who know the life he has to lead, that the salary he receives is not sufficient. When the minister makes a readjustment of the salaries, I hope he will bear in mind the keeper of the signal station at Brier island.
Amount required to pay pensions of $300 each to fifteen pilots, $1,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

speechtext: Why does the government pay pensions to these pilots? I do not suppose the government pension system applies to pilots all over the Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Some years ago there was a corporation of pilots on the J3t. Lawrence. They had the right to pilot on that river, they were a close corporation. The department thought it necessary to make an arrangement with them, many of them were getting old, and had to be retired, and the whole pilotage system of the St. Lawrence was put on a new basis some few years ago. An arrangement was then made that when the pilots retired they would get this allowance of $300. They are compelled to retire from the service at a certain age.

In the other ports pensions for pilots are provided out of the pilotage fund made up from the earnings of the pilots. That is the case in St. John, and I do not think they make any more money than the pilots on the St. Lawrence.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The formation of a fund of that kind is purely voluntary with the pilots. I do not know whether that has been done on the St. Lawrence river. I know that on the Pacific where there is a pilotage authority they have no such fund. It is a matter for themselves, they receive good salaries, but I doubt if they put much away for a rainy day.
Purchase or construction of a lighthouse and buoy steamer for River St. Lawrence to replace the ' Shamrock,' $175,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That i3 to build a new steamer to take the place of the old ' Shamrock,' which is out of date, and practically out of use.	[DOT]
What will it cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The estimate is $175,000. Plans are being prepared, but no tenders have yet been called for.
Purchase or construction of a lighthouse and buoy steamer for the Pacific coast, $200,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That will have to be built by tender. On the Pacific coast the department practically owns only one steamer, the ' Quadra,' for lighthouse service, and as a result in the last few years the department had to charter two steamers to aid the ' Quadra.' It is absolutely necessary to have another steamer there, in fact we may have to get two.
Will these be built in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
They ought to be,
and probably on the Pacific coast if price is satisfactory.
