I wish to enter a protest against these estimates being brought down and put through to the extent of millions of dollars in the dying moments of the session, especially the estimates for this department, which are between $6,000,000 and $7,000,000, and w'hich, I can say from my own experience, is one of the departments of the government which is not being run in the way it should be. For instance, it takes over a year to get a little return from this department.. On February 4, 1909, I asked for a return in regard to the Pembina river in the province of Manitoba, and I did not receive that return until February 14, 1910, one year and ten days afterwards; end before I could get it I had to visit the department several times. I also took it up with the Prime Minister, who promised to have it brought down, and even after that, I had to -write a letter reminding him of his promise before I received the return. The Pembina river runs through my constituency into North Dakota. In the early days the farmers who lived along this river were able to get all the fish they needed for their own use; but some years ago some people in North Dakota built a dam at a town called Walhalla, which is just across the line, and since then the fish have not been able to come up the river into the province of Manitoba. I visited that town last year in company with Mr. R. N. Lee, who has always taken a great interest in this question, and we found that a dam 14 feet high, over which it would be impossible for any fish to get. We saw plenty of fish below the dam, and if there had been a fish ladder put in the dam, there would have been no difficulty in getting all the fish we needed in that part of the province of Manitoba. I may say that the settlers along the Pembina river have been trying to get this government to do something that would afford them relief ever since they have been in power. My predecessor, _ Mr. Greenway, took it up a good many times with the department, as the return will show, and he was unsuccessful in getting the department to act. The commissioner of fish and game of North Dakota, from whom I have a letter here, did promise to have this done, and if the matter had been followed up by this government there would have been no difficulty in having it done. I will not take up the time of the House to read this letter, but I wish to say that though this matter may not be of much importance to the Marine and Fisheries Department of this government, it is a very important question to the settlers who live along that river in my constituency, and I would respectfully ask the
acting minister to take some action in regard to this matter. All. that is necessary is either to write or to send a man to the commissioner of fish and game of North Dakota to show him the conditions that exist at Walhalla, and I am sure that he will be only too pleased to comply with the wishes of this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The explanation given to me in regard to the delay in bringing down the return to which my hon. friend has referred-and I think the explanation was made to him by letter-is that the delay was due to the fact that Prof. Prince, the Canadian commissioner of fisheries, had with him when in California the particular file of the department bearing upon the question about which my hon. friend asked for the return, and it was not returned to the department until after the close of last session. But I do not know why my hon. friend did not get the return immediately after the file was returned to the department. With respect to the dam on the Pembina river. I am advised that the question has formed the subject of some correspondence between the Marine and Fisheries Department and the officials of the state of North Dakota. I understood my hon. friend to say that he had a letter from the game warden of that state pointing out a way in which this matter might be remedied. I would suggest to my hon. friend that he send a copy of that letter to the department.
They have got it, It is No. 30 of the return.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: If it suggests a way of overcoming the difficulty, I think, without knowing anything about the facts, that the difficulty ought to be overcome. I can understand quite well the great value of the fishing streams to the farmers along the Pembina river; and if a 14-foot dam prevents the fish ascending into Canadian territory, and if a mere fishway, which is not expensive, could be erected, I would assume that, being in American territory and controlled altogether by the people of Dakota, it would be built altogether by the state of Dakota.
They built a mill there, and made this dam.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
If our department can facilitate the building of a fishway, I would suggest to the officials of the department that they ought to try to accomplish the object my hon. friend has in view. I am a very strong believer in conserving the fish in every river in Canada and in seeing that no natural or artifical obstructions are put in the river in the shape of dams. I know particularly in the province of British Columbia these dams prevent the salmon from spawning and so

means should be taken to overcome these difficulties and to permit the fish to ascend the rivers. The expense of doing so is not great. 1 am glad that my hon. friend has called the attention of the department to that particular matter. The officers of the department are here and heard what has been said, and I would assume that if anything can be done it will be done.
The files must have been taken away with the object of doing something in connection with this river. Did they do anything while they were away?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No, the file was not taken with the special view of doing anything with regard to this river, but I might have added when I was on my feet a moment ago, that very probably, in fact I think it is altogether likely, that the Pembina river is not mentioned in the treaty between the United States and Canada, notwithstanding that it is an international water. But I would assume that although it is not mentioned in the treaty, a regulation might be agreed to by the two commissioners jointly to improve the .condition of the Pembina river or any other river that crosses the boundary line. It is a small stream, nevertheless there are a great many small streams crossing the boundary, and I think it ought to be the duty of that commission to supervise the fisheries in these small rivers just as well as in the larger waters.

The minister is mistaken if he understood me to say that this government would have anything to do with the obstruction of or the controlling of the dam in North Dakota, because I did not say anything of the kind, and I did not wish to convey that idea at all. The idea I wished to convey is that this government will not follow up and carry out the suggestions that have been made to it in connection with this proposition. There have been 68 letters- between this government and private individuals which are on the file in the department at the present time. Now, the letter I referred to particularly is from the state commissioner for fish and game in North Dakota. It is not addressed to this government, though this government has the orignal in their department. It is addressed to R. N. Lea, game warden, Pembina Crossing, Manitoba, and it says:
Dear Sir,-Your courteous letter of November 5 is under consideration, also copy of letter to T. M. Daly, Esq. I thank you for calling my attention to this matter of obstructing on Pembina river in North Dakota. It is my duty to see that fish sluices are placed upon all dams of the streams and rivers in North Dakota for the free passage of fish over the same. Can you forward the names of owners of the dams that you refer

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
to, giving their names and addresses. I will commence such action as I trust will result in the construction of the needed fishways or sluices. This department is anxious to provide sluiceways for the passage of fish over all obstructions in all waters, especially those rivers and streams passing into Manitoba.
Now, the department has had this letter in their care for four or five years that I know of, because Mr. Greenway, my predecessor, got these letters from R. N. Lea and gave them to the department. But the department has not followed up the suggestions or tried to have the sluice or fishway put into this dam, and I claim it is the department that is to. blame for the fact that we have no fish coming into Manitoba up the river Pembina.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Of course, I am not prepared to admit that it is the department that is to blame at all, and I do not think my hon. friend in his own statement of the case has shown that it is the fault of the department. The facts are, that in the state of North Dakota a dam has been put on the Pembina river on American territory and by Americans, and the game warden in that state has written to somebody saying that if the department will point out where the obstructions are he will undertake to have them removed.
That has been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The first thing that occurs to me is that if the game warden of that state wishes to know where the obstructions are he does not need to write to the city of Ottawa to find out. He ought to know where they are.
He did not write to Ottawa at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He is not a very good game warden if he does not know'. There is some correspondence in the department in regard to this matter. Will my hon. friend (Mr. Sharpe) give me the date of the letter he has just Tead?
On November, 1894.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is a very old complaint.
Certainly it is an old complaint, that is what we are kicking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Probably the grievance does not now exist.
I stated before that I was there last summer wdien I made a special trip to see it myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The Department of Marine and Fisheries has been in communication with the state of North Dakota,

and the two last letters sent by the department have not been replied to, and they were written long after that date of the letter quoted by my hon. friend.
Will, the minister be good enough to have the department look into this matter and try to give us relief in southern Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: All right.

Before we got onto the fisheries, I wanted to ask a question about the marine. A short time ago the steamer ' Lansdowne ' ran on a rock on the coast of Nova Scotia. At the investigation which was held shortly afterwards, the captain of the steamer stated that he had received no sailing directions. Now, what I wanted to ask the minister was, whether it is the case that all the fishery or government steamers receive no sailing directions for the safe navigation of waters through which they are likely to pass. Capt. Lugard, who was chairman of that commission, and one of the other commissioners, expressed surprise that the captain of the ' Lansdowne ' should have been sent to sea without any sailing directions. I bring this to the notice of the minister, and ask if that is the condition of things generally with regard to these government steamers, because if it is, it certainly ought to be remedied.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am told that all the captains of government vessels have sailing directions, and it is the duty of the captain before he sails, to see that he gets them.
Well, this, the captain certainly stated on oath, that he had not received sailing directions, and that he could not get them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I understand it is the fact that that captain had not sailing directions. But, the sailing directions are comprised in a small book which is supplied freely to all captains of vessels. If any captain has not a copy, he ought to procure it. It is no fault of the department if he loses his copy of the directions and does not supply himself with another.

I have here the report of the examination

The formal examination in connection with the stranding of the steamer ' Lansdowne,' on January 24, at Pubnico, commenced yesterday morning before Captain Lugard, with Captain James Hayes and E. C. Elkin as nautical assessors. In the course of his evidence, Captain Burns said he had no sailing directions for the Bay of Fundy. He had asked for them, but hadn't yet received any.	[DOT]
And, later on,-
Murdoch McLean, chief officer of the steamer, testified that there was no proper place on the ' Lansdowne ' to take soundings, which drew the remark from Captain Hayes that it was a strange condition of affairs on board a government steamer.
There is a statement that the captain had applied for directions and could not get them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am advised that the department are prepared to dispute that statement. Every person who applies for the instructions gets them-not only captains, but every person. It is a captain's duty to get them. If he applied for them and did not receive them, the department has no knowledge of that matter. It is the easiest thing in the world for a captain to provide himself with them.
Is there any record of that application in the department? For this captain makes this statement on oath.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The deputy minister tells me that there is no record of the captain applying for these papers.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member for St. John if he is reading from the transcribed record of the hearing or from a newspaper report?
From a newspaper report.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: That might make a difference. They do not always get the statements accurate.
They very often get them the opposite.

I was glad to hear the minister declare in favour of rivers being taken care of and fishways being put in where necessary. I called to the minister's attention the need of a fishway at the mouth of the White Mouth river. I do not wish to detain the House at this stage of the session, but I would like an assurance from the minister that the matter will be investigated, and, if found necessary, that the fishway will be provided.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) handed me two letters which I carried in my pocket for several days. But, this morning I sent them to the officer of the Fisheries Department and asked him to advise me with respect to the request made. Probably I shall be able to give an answer on Monday.
I am to be absent on Monday. I would like to have the assurance of the minister that the matter will be investigated, and, if found necessary, the fishway put in.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It will be investigated, but I do not want to make too many promises about putting in fishways.

I have expressed my own personal opinion that appliances for conserving the fish in our rivers should be provided as far as possible. These fishways do not cost much money.

We have settlements all along that river. The river empties into Lac du Bonnet, which abounds in fish. But, a small fall prevents the fish from getting up. Now, an inexpensive fishway would provide the people all along that river with fish.

I would like to bring to the attention of the minister, a matter of importance to the people living along the Salmon river in Digby county. Several years ago, complaint was made by certain fishermen with regard to a dam on the Salmon river at a mill owned by a Mr. Saulnier. The department required Mr. Saulnier to place a fishway in the dam. He replied that he did not know how to construct one and asked for advice. The local officers stated, as I am informed, that they did not know how to construct one and called on the department for information. The department, as, I am informed, gave information and plans and a fishway was constructed by Mr. Saulnier under the immediate direction of the fishery officers on the grounds, up to the plans which has been furnished by the officers of the department. About a year ago, further complaint was made to the department that the fishway was not giving satisfaction, that it did not allow fish to get up the river. Later some letters were written to me. I visited the place and obtained a statement from Mr. Saulnier, a statement of the facts, the substance of which I have given. Having already put a fishway in that dam under the direction of the officers of the department and according to the plans furnished by the department, he naturally objects to defraying the cost of building a new one. If a new one is found to be necessary, I trust that the department will provide it at its own expense, and out of this appropriation of $10,000 which is being asked for to-day. In fact, I enter a protest now on behalf of Mr. Saulnier against his having to pay any part of the cost of a new fishway.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am advised that instructions have been given already to the inspector of fisheries for that district, to visit that locality and prepare plans for a new fishway.

I know that this matter has been before the department for upwards of a year. But, do I understand the minister to agree with the position Mr. Saulnier takes, that he, having built the fishway according to the plans of the department and under the direction of the

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: officers of the department, should not be required to pay any part of the cost of a new fishway?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The record does not show anything with regard to that position. The hen. member (Mr. Jameson) wants me to admit that Mr. Saulnier is not liable for the fishway. I do not know enough about the facts to be able to make any such statement. I am told that the Act holds him responsible. The department is acting upon it. They sent an officer there to prepare plans and advise as to the best kind of fishway to construct. I suppose it is not a very expensive matter, but I am not going to say whether the party or the department will build it. I assume, from the actions of the department, that the fishway will be put there this summer.

Mr. Saulnier is a poor man, and it will be a serious matter if he has to defray the cost. The department, in all fairness, should defray the cost.
Fisheries-salaries and disbursements of fishery inspectors, overseers and guardians, $220,000.
I would like to know what is paid to the fishery inspector at Winnipegosi3 in Manitoba, for the last year, and what work he has done for the salary that has been paid him.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Colliston is the fishery overseer living at Winnipegosis. His salary is $700.	,
When was Mr. Colliston appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Last year.
What time last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The official of the department, speaking from recollection, says that he was appointed some time in the fall of last year.

I am not asking thesq. questions from any desire to be factious, or to make fun; I am asking because the inspector who was in charge of that district until some time last fall, was a man by the name of Olenny, who was not only inspector for this government, but who was the secretary of the Northwest Fish Company that held, under this government, the monopoly of fishing up in that northwestern part of Manitoba, and which extended up into Saskatchewan. While, I say, he was inspector for this government, he was at the same time secretary for this American fish company, which was robbing the people, my constituents, right and left, under the patronage of this government. I want to know if there was any dissatisfaction with his services, and why he was deposed and Colliston appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend has just stated the reason himself. I am informed that Mr. Clenny -was asked to resign because he occupied a position with a private company, and Mr. Colliston was appointed in his stead.
Who asked for Clenny's appointment?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The appointment was made by the minister some two or three years ago.
Who recommended him?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He was appointed by order in council on the recommendation of the minister.
But who recommended him to the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: 1 have not the slightest idea.
Can you not find out who recommended him?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: If I was the minister who made the appointment, perhaps I could say.

I would like to draw the attention of the minister to the new regulation for Lake Winnipeg. I received a copy of those regulations to-day, and I noticed a very lyise provision to the effect that after 2,400,000 pounds of fi3h have been taken out of Lake Winnipeg the fishing would cease, and that the inspector would have power to order all the nets to he lifted. I commend the department for making this arrangement. Now, how is the officer in charge going to arrive at the amount which has been caught? I understand there was a recommendation made by the commission that all these fishermen would be compelled to make a sworn statement to the fishery officer of the quantity of fish they had taken. I do not notice any protection of that kind in the regulation, and unless some check of that kind is provided. I would like to know how the officer at Selkirk is going to know when there are 2,400,000 pounds of fish taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I understand the companies have entered into agreement that the maximum amount of whitefish to be taken by them this year shall not exceed 2,400,000 pounds. The inspectors will have to be responsible to see this regulation is carried out. The particular method by which he will do so has not yet been evolved by the department, but probably affidavits will be required as to the quantity of fish taken. The inspector will probably report the quantity landed at Selkirk each week, will keep a close check upon it by personal observation, and take
every means in his power to see the regulation carried out.
If what the minister suggests, and that only is done, I fear the regulation will not be enforced. There should be some provision -made in the license that you give-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It will probably be embodied in the license.
There should be a sworn statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It will be a condition in the license that when the stipulated quantity of fish is taken fishing will have to stop. The particular methods by which our inspectors will check up the catch will be decided upon by the department. I suppose we can require the companies to make a sworn statement, and the inspector can report at intervals that they have landed so many fish, and no more.

I urge on the minister the suggestion made by the commissioners, that a sworn statement should be made by the fishermen themselves as to the amount of fish they catch. The mere fact that the companies agree that they will only take
2,400,000	pounds- does not mean that they will not take more if they get the chance. But if there is a condition m the license, and a sworn statement required, and a severe penalty provided for infraction, then, there will be a possibility of the regulation being carried out. If a man makes an incorrect sworn return his license should be cancelled, and he should not be allowed a license in the future. I speak from experience when I urge the adoption of these precautions upon the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think the department will attend to that.

I direct the attention of the minister to the following facts: About fifteen years ago, a dam twenty-two feet high was constructed in the Chambly river between Chambly and Richelieu, by the Chambly Manufacturing Company. There was no fish run provided for in that dam, and the consequence is that the Chambly river which was once full of fish is now almost entirely depleted. Is it the intention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to force the Chambly Manufacturing Company to construct proper fish passes in that dam, so as to permit the fish coming from the St. Lawrence to reach their habitat in Lake Champlain. No action has been taken by the department for the last fifteen years in this direction, and it is high time that we should now ask the department of government concerned to force this wealthy company which is rated at $15,000,000 to spend a few thousand dol-

lars for the benefit of the fishermen who live along the Chambly river. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries should give some promise that this matter will be attended to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I will call the attention of the officers of the department to what my hon. friend (Mr. Gervais) has said, and if the thing is possible I will ask them to attend to it. That is all I can say.

I understand that a fish run may be constructed there at a cost of about $3,000, and there is a law at present under which the company can be compelled to do that work. The people of the county of Chambly, and of the other constituencies along the Chambly river have suffered long enough in this regard, ahd the minister should now give a specific promise that he will ensure the construction of a fish run in this dam.

I wish to have some assurance from the minister that there will be a declaration required under oath with regard to the catch of white fish. The hon. gentleman may think I am unreasonable, but I may tell him that I have a good deal of experience in this matter, and my experience leads me to believe that unless my suggestion is carried out the law will be evaded. If a sworn declaration is required from these fishermen they will have no excuse for making a false return, and if they do so they can be prosecuted for perjury. If you take from them a mere statement they may say they have only taken
2,400,000	pounds, but if it is afterwards found they have taken 5,000,000 pounds you cannot successfully prosecute them because their plea will be that they did not know they had taken so many fish. I hope the minister will assure me that there will be a sworn declaration required from each of these companies as to the quantity of fish they take.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I thought I was very explicit in stating that the department is bound to see that this regulation is carried out.
I know you say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not think I ought to be asked now to give an assurance that we will make every man give a sworn affidavit.
It is the only way that is any good.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It is one way, but
possibly it may not be the best way. I think the fish are landed for Wininpeg at Selkirk, and we can station our inspector there to check every fish landed at the wharf, and charge them up against each Mr. GERVAIS.
company, and when they have readied their limit we will stop them fishing. I will give my hon. friend the assurance that this regulation will be carried out in the very best way that the department can devise.

The statement of the minister is not satisfactory in view of what the hon. gentleman from Selkirk has said. I should think the time of the inspector of the department is more valuable than that he can stay there watching these fishermen take the fish. After all, is not the suggestion of the member for Selkirk the best that can 'be adopted? If a sworn declaration is required, the man cannot afterwards say that he did not know he had taken so many fish, and give other excuses. If a fisherman makes false affidavits, he would know there was no technical way of escaping the consequences of his deception. He knows, and is the only one who does know, and if he stated what was not true, he would be liable to perjury. If the license contained a provision that these affidavits were to be made by the fishermen themselves, they would fear to. run the risk of being imprisoned for per-, jury. If, on the other hand, the affidavit, is made by an officer of the company who must depend on the statements of the fish-, ermen, and who would have no personal knowledge of the facts, so that he could, evade conviction by saying that he was informed or instructed that the statements were true, there would be no protection. If the minister expects the inspectors to go up and inspect every fish, he is placing a very low value on the inspectors' time.
Salaries, building and maintenance of fishbreeding establishments, $322,300.

speechtext:
Provision is made
for two new hatcheries on the great lakes costing about $10,000 each, a salmon trout hatchery on the north shore of Lake Superior, and a whitefish hatchery on the northern end of the Georgian bay. Would the minister give some account of the work of the fish hatchery at Lake Winnipegosis?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I can get that information.	.
I want it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
That hatchery has been in operation two seasons. This year

60,000,000 young whitefish are to be distributed.
He closed the hatchery last season.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The hatchery was closed the season before, as my hon. friend is no doubt aware, because there was no supply of eggs with which to fill it.

I am sorry the minister is so lost to knowledge of the conditions there as to make a statement of that kind. It was not closed for the reason he alleges. Two million eggs were taken ia the fall of 1908.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is very little.

The minister will find in the Public Accounts $1,500 paid on contract to Coffey and Company for 25,000,000 eggs which were not delivered in the fait of 1908. The contract provided that no fish were to be taken at that time except for the purpose of collecting the eggs. Fish were not to be taken for commercial purposes. Coffey and Company employed inexperienced men and wrong methods and collected only 2,000,000 eggs. The eggs were put in the hatchery on October 25,
1908,	and the staff was employed there taking care of their hatching until on in January, when they found that owing to the methods that had been employed by the government employees and contractors the eggs were absolutely unfertile, and they dumped them into the lake in January,
1909.	That cost this government $1,500. This occurred during the time the minister said the hatchery was not in operation. In getting this spawn, 151,200 pounds of whiteflsh, 43,540 pounds of pickerel, and
43.000	pounds of jacks were taken and were all shipped to points in the United States, absolutely against the wording of the contract entered into by that company with the government. In other words, about
75.000	full-grown whitefish, two-thirds of which were females-and I understand that is a very small proportion-were destroyed. The average, I believe, is something like 4,000 eggs to each female, so that if you make the computation you will see that this means that 200,000,000 eggs were destroyed in an attempt to secure 25,000,000 eggs, which attempt proved absolutely abortive, as no eggs were hatched; and the minister has cloaked his department under the excuse that the hatchery was not running. The hatchery was closed during the spring of 1905, and was only opened in 1908; and during the time that the lake was open in 1908, 175 cars of fish were shipped from the shipping point nearest the lake, and every one of those cars was a case of law-breaking on the part of Coffey and Company, who shipped them. They had no permission to do this and in
fact had signed a contract in which they bound themselves not to ship any fish. We have seen that the cost of the hatchery up to last year was $18,754, and not even a sucker has been hatched out during the three years that it has been more or less in operation. I understand that this year there has been some change for the better, and I am glad of it, because I heartily approve of hatcheries being established in those northern lakes. I want to point out another matter which pertains to the fisheries up there; that is, the fact that the hatchery requires a large amount of cord-wood to keep it going-to keep up the steam in the boilers and tjo keep the hatching rooms at a proper temperature, and that the contracts for the cordwood are given to partisan friends of the government. I think it is only right that tenders for supplies for a government institution should be called for, and that all parties, whether Liberals supporting the government, or Liberals antagonistic to the government, or Tories, should have an equal right to tender. This year I know that the men who got the contract were partisan friends of the government, and I hope that the minister, if he is going to act for any length of time in charge of his department, will see that this does not occur again, or I will talk a little more Ifreely on the next occasion than I am doing now.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Public tenders have been called, for cordwood and other supplies, for the Selkirk hatchery, and the same thing is going to obtain hereafter in respect to the other hatcheries.
Why the delay? Whv has not this been done before?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I cannot give the reason why it has not been done before this.
It was just as easy to do it at Winnipegosis as at Selkirk. While we live far back, we have both mail and telegraphic communication.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I may as well confess at once that I cannot possibly enter into a discussion of all the matters brought up by my hon. friend in regard to the Winnipegosis hatchery, the cost of its building, the cost of the eggs and the reason -why 25,000,000 eggs were not obtained and 2,000,000 were obtained. I am afraid that it would take too long to master the letters which have been placed in my hands, and I do not suppose my hon. friend would care for me to read the instructions given to the officer in charge who made the contract for the delivery of these eggs. My hon. friend, I imagine, rather desires to make his own statement and get it on 'Hansard' and in the press.

The department is quite willing to let it go at that.

I must take exception to that. I am asking for information. There have been the worst kind of abuses in the north end of my riding. I tried last year to bring them to the attention of the minister. I pointed out to him how this Northwest Fish Co., an American company, who shipped all their fish to the United States held a monopoly under this government, were protected by this government in every way, robbed the fishermen, failed, and did not pay their just debts to the fishermen, who were compelled to sell to them at a less price than the market would have afforded them had this government and its officials not insisted in upholding this monopoly. Then, in the case of this hatchery, I am drawing to the attention of the government again the abuses that have existed there and that exist to-day, and I want the government to sit up and take notice. I am not making a grand-stand play for the sake of getting on ' Hansard.' I never look at ' Hansard.'
1 only try to bring to the attention of the government abuses that exist in my riding, in the hope that the government will at some time wake up and correct them.
Fisheries-legislation and incidental expenses, $4,000.
What are these expenses for?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: They are for minor cases which the department may have to prosecute for violations of the regulations about which they may know nothing, and they instruct the Department of Justice to prosecute.
Does the Department of Justice instruct local lawyers to do the prosecuting? Where are those lawyers situated and what do they do?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

But where were they, they might be in the moon?

Again I ask where do they live?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

Where. There is a good deal of money going out from the departments in that general way for legal and incidental expenses. It is a very handy way of rewarding political friends Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
for doing party work, and sometimes rather disgraceful party work. We are beginning to find it necessary to know who these gentlemen are.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know where these people reside. They may be in any province of the Dominion, or in any city. The expenses would be paid to the lawyer who wras retained for the time being to prosecute a particular case.
At what rate are the} paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know. The Justice Department certifies the expenses and the department pays it.

Perhaps. I can help out the minister. There was a legal gentleman of the name of Markey, who was mixed up in some of those fish leases. Perhaps the government paid him for accepting these monopolies, and the payment may be included in that charge. Does his name appear among the legal lights who have been paid?
Mr, TEMPLEMAN. The department is not aware that Mr. Markey has been paid any fees whatever. .
Canadian fisheries exhibit, $16,000.
What is that used for. Is it used for exhibits in the Dominion, or for exhibits abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There is in the city here a fishery building, and this item is largely to pay the cost of maintaining that. A small sum goes to a small exhibition in the province of British Columbia where a miniature hatchery is exhibited yearly.

We have a provincial exhibition in the city of Halifax which is conducted by the provincial government and the city. It is more or less an agricultural exhibition, but the fish interests have been trying to arrange a fishery exhibit there. As no funds are provided for that purpose by either the province or the city I think it would be fair and reasonable if the department could see its way to assist that exhibition, because it is in the centre of the Atlantic coast fisheries. We have the exhibition there every year, and a small annual contribution for the fishery exhibit would help materially the fishing interest of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and perhaps New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The request of my hon. friend appeals to me, because I am a little familiar with the good results that have followed from the slight assistance given to the fisheries exhibit at the New Westminster exhibition, and with the success that has attended the fishery exhibit

is the most popular one on the grounds. They show the fish alive and the process of hatching. Without making a distinct promise I may say to my hon. friend that I will request the deputy minister to do what he can along the lines we have followed in New Westminster, as we recognize that the maritime provinces are a great centre of the fishing industry., and ought to have a fishery exhibit at its annual industrial exhibition.

To assist in the establishment, maintenance and inspection of cold storage for bait, and the conservation and development of the deep-sea fisheries, $40,000.

While we approve of the system of cold storage and admit that it has been of great assistance to -the fishermen, I am sorry to say that in a great many cases it has not proved of such assistance as might have been expected. When the cold storage systems were established it was understood that they were for the purpose of enabling the fishermen to put in their bait during the season *when they could collect it, so that they could get it out of cold storage when they could not get fresh bait from the sea. I do not wish to say anything derogatory to the gentlemen who have those cold storage systems in charge, but there are complaints that the fishermen cannot get the storage facilities for their bait that they expected. It is said that they cannot get their bait in storage and that they have to pay the cold storage men very high prices sometimes, and in some cases have to make a contract to give the fish that they catch with the bait back to the cold storage men at their own prices. The department might make some inquiries during the recess into this matter. I (have no doubt that the government established this cold storage system for the purpose of helping the fishermen, and if it is the case that they are not being (helped, I think it would be wrise for the government to ascertain the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue

We will do so.

\
