To pay customs officers for services in connection with issuing of modus vivendi licenses, $700.

Has the department taken into consideration doing away with these licenses? I do not wish to take up time at this stage of the session. But that matter was gone into very fully by Mr. Maclean the former member for Lunenburg. Has the department in view the bringing of this to an end?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The department has not been considering the question of doing away with the modus vivendi in regard to this matter. I am not certain, but, probably, the questions being submitted to the Hague tribunal will have an effect unon the government's policy in this matter.
To pay customs and other officers for services in compiling and forwarding daily reports in connection with the fisheries intelligence bureau for the season of 1910-11, $500.

The minister of Marine and Fisheries is asking parliament to vote $828,000 this year, an advance of $69,000 over the amount asked for last year. I wish to make a few remarks on fisheries generally. I do not believe in criticism for criticism's sake, but I believe that there are many ways in which the condition of the fisheries and those connected with them may be improved. It is in that spirit I offer the suggestions that I propose to offer, very briefly, and I trust the minister will receive them in the same way. If he does so, I think he will find that many of the suggestions I make are practical and can be carried out to the benefit of the fisheries and fishermen and with little trouble to the department.
First, as to the reports of the fisheries intelligence bureau. The minister is asking $500 for this purpose the same as last year. I think a much more generous vote should be taken for this service. The reports are very meagre. They are telegraphed to the daily papers, but they do not in all cases, or even in many cases, reach the fishermen in time to be of much value. If they were telephoned to the fishery stations, many of which have telephones, they would be of great utility. I think also the weather probabilities should be telephoned to the fishery stations. In my own county of Digby the weather forecast is telephoned every day to the signal at Westport down Digby neck. The fishermen have frequently said that if this weather forecast could be taken off the wire at the different fishing stations when it was sent down to the signal station and placed in a bulletin, [DOT]Mr. LANCASTER.
it would be of the utmost assistance to them. And the same on the opposite side of St. Mary's bay, and in almost every part of Nova Scotia. This system would be of the greatest advantage to the fishermen when they are leaving home, it would enable them to know what the weather was likely to be .during the next 24 hours. I think an appropriation should be made for that purpose. I could recite many instances of fishermen who have been blown off the coast of Nova Scotia, and who have suffered great hardships and perils by reason of not knowing when a storm was approaching.
Another suggestion I wish to make is for the establishment of a fishermen's library at the various fishing stations. In many places there now exist fishermen's unions, associations which are formed amongst the fishermen. These have been established in many parts of Nova Scotia through the initiative and assistance of Mr. M. H. Nickerson, M.P.P., who resides at Clark's harbour. These associations are gradually extending their influence and are well patronized. Where they now exist I do not think there would be any difficulty in establishing fishery libraries, and where they do not exist the libraries could be developed by the assistance of the customs house officer, postmaster or other prominent person. Reports of the Department of Fisheries, together with the results of investigations made by the department could be furnished to those libraries, and other information along that line. We are desirous of improving the condition of the fisheries and those engaged in them. At the present time the fishermen are scattered along 5,000 miles of the coast and there is little community of interest among them. We wish to improve their condition, and I think this would be a very effective means of doing so, and it would tend to secure co-operation among the fishermen in a better observance of the laws. Many of the fishermen are educated men, they are great readers, and very intellectual people.
Another subject which of late years has received a good deal of consideration by the people engaged in the fishing industry, is the question of bounty paid to fishermen. This was begun by the government of Sir John A. Macdonald, in 1882, and I understand that an amount of $160,000 has been voted from year to year for that purpose. The amount of the Halifax fishery award was capitalized, and the interest from year to year is applied to this purpose. Now, the bounties which have been paid to the fishermen have varied from year to year, according to the number engaged in the industry. The vessel fishermen receive a much larger bounty than the boat fishermen, and the boat fishermen

consider that now, since they are obliged to have more expensive boats, fitted up generally with gasoline engines, they should receive more equitable treatment, they should receive a larger sum. The fishermens' union have discussed this matter and taken strong ground. I do not mean to say that there should be any reduction in the amount paid, either to vessels or to vessel fishermen, but I think a more generous grant should be made for the purpose of paying these bounties.
The amount received by the government from yeaT to year for licenses under the modus vivendi is about $10,000; something less than $500 of this is paid to officers of the department who issue the license, and the balance of $9,500 might very properly be turned into their fishery bounty fund. The fisheries are developing, and the revenues of the country are increasing, and it seems to me a further amount towards the fishing bounty might be voted. The boat fishermen, as I say, are now using boats much larger and better equipped than in years gone by. A fishing boat now costs five to eight times more than it did ten years ago, and it also costs considerably more to maintain and operate it. This is a further suggestion I would commend to the consideration of the department.
Now, on the subject of the oyster fishery. We had during the sessions of the Fishery Committee last year, -the evidence of Captain Ernest Kemp, the oyster expert of the Department -of Marine and Fisheries, who gave his testimony on the 25th of March, 1909. I see there is a sum of $10,000 in the estimates this year, an increase of $4,000 over the amount voted last year for this purpose and I hope the work will be proceeded with systematically. Sometime ago there was an experiment made in Digby basin, but I have not been able to learn the result. I will quote from the evidence of Capt. Kemp on the occasion to which 1 refer when I asked him with regard to the subject:
Q. You have given us some information with regard to your knowledge of Nova Scotia coast. Have you any knowledge of the conditions in the Bay of Fundy, St.. Mary's Bay or Digby Basin with respect to oyster culture?-A. I have examined the area in Digby Basin. Some years ago I planted oysters as an experiment on Goat Island and I have heard that those oysters have grown well. I have not had an opportunity of ascertaining whether there has been any spat derived from there or not. These oysters were planted in different places and grew well, I am told.
Q. Do you remember the year in which they were planted?-A. They were planted in 1902.
Q. Have you visited' the locality since?- A. I do not think so.
Q. Those oysters were planted in Annapolis Basin?-A. Yes.
Q. Did you at that time examine St. Mary's Bay, or are you familiar with the formation of the bottom there?-A. No.
Q. Are you familiar with the formation of the bottom of the Bay of Fundy ?-A. No, that is the only place that I have no knowledge of.
Q. You found the conditions were favourable within Digby or Annapolis basins for the culture of oysters?-A. The waters on the north of Goat Island, I think it is, were the most suitable. I had difficulty in finding suitable bottom on account of the heavy sediment on the sides of the basin and river.
Q. There is a large volume of fresh water from the Annapolis river flowing into the basin, would that interfere with oyster culture?-A. I did not want to go up too far. I thought if I could plant any on Goat Island that would be a suitable locality. The farther I went up the shore I found more mud bottoms. Suitable bottoms are limited there.
Q. Who has charge of the cultivation of the oysters which you planted in Annapolis Basin ? -A. The ground was in charge of the light-keeper on the opposite side, as far as I know.
Q. On the Grenville side?-A. Yes.
Q. You have had no reports from him?-A. No.
Q. Was the oyster farm leased to any person?-A. No, I do not think so. My time has been so wholly taken up that I have not had the opportunity of going dowrn to see how those oysters were getting on. I wanted to go there last fall but was detained with my boat and did not have the opportunity.
Now, this seems to me to be a most extraordinary way to conduct experiments of this kind. The oyster industry can be made a most profitable one, and I hope the minister will see that Captain Kemp' visits Digby basin and inquires into the condition of this oyster bed that was set out there. There are other places along the Bay of Fundy and St. Mary's bay where I believe oyster culture is not only a possibility, but where there is very strong reason to believe that it would prosper and flourish and become a profitable industry. I trust the minister will take pains to see that Captain Kemp shall adopt a more systematic method of procedure. I do not think it is right at all that he should leave an oyster bed set out nearly seven yeaTs ago and not have any reports from it. If this industry is worth spending $10,000 a year on, it is certainly worth while that the department should keep in touch with it and see what progress is being made from time to time. These suggestions are not offered in the way of hostile criticism, but-merely with the view of placing before the department the ideas I entertain on the subject. I believe that if the minister will take them into consideration he will find they can be worked out profitably and beneficially to the fisheries and to the people who are interested in them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The department appreciates the suggestions made by my hon. friend (Mr. Jameson), and I am quite sure they -will be taken into serious consideration. I am advised that the department has at present under consideration very considerable improvements in connection with the fishery intelligence service. It is hoped that the service will develop into issuing bulletins and even embrace telephonic communication. As to the libraries, my own view is that they do not come within the scope of the Marine Department or even of this government. I cannot, of course, speak with full knowledge as to the bounty question, but I think the bounty money was fixed at five per cent on the Halifax award. Of course, the more fishermen there are, the dess will be paid to each in the division, and the fewer there are, the higher the bounty will be to each. Whether it would he advisable to pay a higher interest than that provided is a question of policy on _ which I would not care to express an opinion. I will call to the attention of the experts of the department the suggestions made by my hon. friend as to oyster culture, and I shall ask for them the very best consideration.
Do I understand that the minister will take the question of weather bulletins into consideration, and endeavour to have them communicated to the fishermen by telephone.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am advised that the meteorological service is being extended very rapidly, and that still further extension will be made.

There is now in the county of Digby a very perfect system of telephonic communication between the fishing stations, so that the experiment would cost very little indeed. I believe that if it were once given a trial, the department would be so impressed with its advantages that they would beyond doubt continue it and extend it.

I endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Digby with regard to the fishing bounties. The Halifax award was $4,500,000, which would produce $225,000 yearly at five per cent, but I understand that we only pay $160,000 a year in bounties. The boat fishermen get a very small amount of this, and I would urge on the minister that their bounty should be augmented. In many sections the fishermen have to come to the fishery officer, 10 or 15 miles in some cases, to file their claim, and then have to travel the same distance again to get $3 or $4 of fishing bounty, so that it is hardly worth the trouble. The Washington treaty, of which the fishing bounty is an outcome, was Mr. JAMESON.
brought about by the admission of the American fishermen within the three-mile limit, so that in reality the compensation granted by the award belongs more strictly to the boat fishermen who fish wdthin that limit. I do not say that a bounty should not be given to the fishing, vessels and the1 men engaged on them, but I do hold that that bounty should come out of the sgen-eral revenues of the country. The deep sea fishery is open to the world, and every* dollar we take out of it is so much brought into the country, whereas the inshore fisheries and the fisheries in our inland lakes may in a sense be said to belong to the country, and they, therefore, stand on a different footing from the other fisheries. Did time permit, I could prove .that all countries in the world interested in fisheries are paying bounties to their fishermen. The people of the little island of St. Pierre Miquelon, whose fish comes into competition with our Nova Scotia catch, have a bounty from the French government of nine francs for every quintal exported from St. Pierre to Canada or to any other part of the world outside of France, and in addition to that a considerable bounty is paid to the men and to the ships. I would urge on the government that they should consider the question of paying the bounty to the deep sea vessels and deep sea fishermen from the general revenues of the country, and permit the interest on the Halifax award to go to the shore fishermen to whom it specially belongs. Now that we require a great many men for our navy, whether it is a tin-pot navy or a runaway navy, or whatever else you like to call it, your recruits must come from amongst the deep sea fishermen, and they deserve encouragement from the national treasury.
To provide for the settlement of the claim of the British Columbia government for a share of revenue from fishery licenses collected by the federal government from 1901 to 1907, both years inclusive, $56,137.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This is a final disposition of a question between the province of British Columbia, and the Dominion which has been pending for some years. After the decision of the Privy Council which placed the ownership of the fish in the province, the provincial govern-' ment made a demand on the Dominion government for a share of the revenue which this government had been collecting from fishing licenses in that province. In 1901, Sir Louis Davies, then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, entered into a modus vivendi with the province whereby the Dominion government continued the administration of the fisheries, and collection of revenue, a balancing of accounts to be made (later. In 190*7, British Columbia

passed its own Fishery Act, and proceeded to administer its fisheries, as far as it had authority to do so, and began the collection of licenses, imposing a license fee of $5 for salmon-fishing license. This terminated the modus vivendi. This amount is the sum arrived at between the province and this government as the share of the province in the revenue collected by this government between 1901 and 1907.
Investigation of ore deposits and economic minerals; examination and delimitation of peat bogs, determination of fuel values, coals and peat of Canada, including salary of a producer gas expert and mechanic; investigation of ore dressing; collection of information regarding mineral and metallurgical industries and operations, $41,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It would save time if the minister would explain all these increases together.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
In the total vote for the Mines branch there is a decrease of $2,000. In this particular item there is a decrease of $7,500. This is for the publication of a monograph on various subjects in connection with the investigation of ore deposits and minerals. The increase can be accounted for by the desire of the department to carry on this work on a larger scale.
Operation of government peat bog, $4,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The department acquired a peat bog in Alfred, near Caledonia Springs, of 300 acres. We are now putting into operation a plant for the experimental manufacture of peat to determine how cheaply it may be manufactured. I invite all members to visit the bog in the next three months, and see the process in operation. We are hopeful of very considerable results from this experiment. This $4,000 will pay the expense of operating this peat bog. There may be another small sum in the supplementary estimates. We expect in this experiment to manufacture 2,000 or 3,000 tons of peat. If we were going to sell it, we might make some money out of it. The experiment is for the purpose of demonstrating the production of power from peat, the object being to show that peat will make gas which will produce electric power as cheaply as water-power. My hon. friend can see the demonstration going on any day in Ottawa at the experimental station, very successfully, and very cheaply.
Is there any quantity of the raw material in Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
There are millions of tons all over Ontario. Another part of the work of the Department is the locating of peat bogs in the settled portions of On-271
tario and Quebec, and especially in the maritime provinces.
Can the gas be used for fuel purposes as well as for power?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I imagine that it can be, but when it is used in a gas-producer engine it goes into the engine as quickly as it is manufactured and is used in that way to produce power. We believe that it will be much more economical for this purpose than coal.

Coming from a prairie province, I am interested somewhat in these experiments with peat. Is it the intention of the government to experiment in making peat brickettes to take the place of coal or wood for heating purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes. The operation of the peat bog is simply to make brickettes to be burned in furnaces or stoves for heating purposes. The purpose of this experiment is, first, to demonstrate how cheaply peat can be produced as a fuel instead of coal; and, secondly, to demonstrate that peat can be put into a gas-producing engine, and the gas used direct to create power.
How far west have these experiments been made? Have they been made in Manitoba or in any of the western provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The department is making the experiment with this particular bog of 300 acres which we bought at Alfred. We put a plant on it, and last week we started to make peat. This is the only place in Canada where we have done any experimenting. We have also put up the experimental testing plant in Ottawa. But the location of peat bogs has been carried on for a number of years by officers of the department, and we now have in the department a record of hundreds of peat bogs in the country. Our investigations have been chiefly in Ontario and Quebec and the maritime provinces, although we know that there are peat bogs in Manitoba and other western provinces. Although the peat bogs in the more populated parts of the country will be the first to be brought into use, we will not neglect the west. For instance, if it is possible to make peat cheaper than you can buy coal in the city of Winnipeg, we will try to demonstrate to the people there that it is their duty to utilize the peat bogs which are not very far from that city.	.
Is it the intention of the department to get the report made by Mr. Mystrom translated?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The translator is very busy getting our reports translated,



but I am not sure whether that is one of them or not.

I have read the report Which Mr. Nystrom has made to Dr. Haanel. I have also read the letter of instructions from Dr. Haanel to Mr.' Nystrom, and I notice that Mr. Mystrom has been instructed to inspect the peat bogs of Denmark, Ireland, Belgium and Germany, but there is not one word said about the French peat bogs. As a matter of fact, the largest area of peat bogs, as many as 4,000,000 acres, and the most complete and perfect instruments for the manufacture of peat are to be found in France. I hope that this report, which is only a partial one, will be translated into French for the benefit of the province of Quebec, where many large peat bogs are to be found. I regret that Dr. Mystrom should not have been instructed to visit France, where there is the largest area of peat and where the comparative value of peat, soft, Anthracite, Cardiff coals for self-producing gas engines have been tested and studied more especially by Mr. Frangois Depeaux, of Rouen.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am not sure about the instructions, but there is no doubt that Mr. Mystrom was the engineer who went to Europe on that occasion some years ago. I know he visited the northern countries of Europe, Denmark, Sweden, Germany and Russia, where the manufacture of peat and the utilization of peat are on a larger scale, even than in France, though there is in France a very large quantity.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Peat is more plentiful in the countries I have named. However, Mr. Mystrom's report T think should be published in French, and that will probably be done if it has not yet been done.
Geological Survey Branch-for explorations and surveys in Canada, including wages of explorers, draftsmen and others, $140,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why that increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The explanation is that more parties are being sent out, and they are being made a little larger and stronger. There will be more men in the field, covering Canada as well as they can, from Nova Scotia to British Columbia, this year than ever before.
Does this cover the exploration of Canada in conjunction with the work of the Conservation Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We have nothing to do with the Conservation Commission.
Does not the Conservation Commission cover the same ground as is covered by this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I do not think so.
For the publication of reports, maps, plans, illustrations, &c., $75,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The increase here is due to the increased number of publications and reports.
For the purchase of hooks, instruments, laboratory apparatus, chemicals, mapping material, stationery, maintenance of offices and museum, transfer and packing of specimens, clothing for three firemen, miscellaneous expenses, $40,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The same reason for the increase here, the increase in departmental work.
To pay for specimens for Victoria Museum, $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This is an increase of $2,000. We have in view the occupation of the new museum probably before the next session of parliament, and we desire to be in a position to acquire all the specimens that may be offered.
Investigation of the manufactures and storage of explosives in Canada, $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
That item is due to the fact that we purpose next session introducing a Bill to regulate the manufacture and importation of explosives of all kinds, based upon the English Act. There is nothing of the kind in this country at present. The many fatal accidents that have occurred in mines, and that have been due to premature explosions, and that kind of thing; have brought the matter to the attention of the department, and meetings have been held in mining communities at Cobalt, in British Columbia, and elsewhere, and have adopted resolutions asking the government to pass an Act regulating the manufacture and importation of explosives of all kinds. We have entered into the collection of information already and have some information prepared, but we thought it wise to let the Bill stand over until next session. In the meantime we are going to continue our investigation. We expect to bring an expert from England, an official of the British government who enforces the explosives Act there, with the view of examining all the manufacturing establishments where explosives are made, and with the view of helping us to frame an Act, and of giving us whatever information may be necessaray. That is the purpose of this $10,000 vote. We will certainly require to pay the expert a decent fee, and travelling expenses.
Militia and defence-chargeable to income -ordnance, arms, lands, rifle ranges, reserves, stores and equipment-transferred from militia capital, $1,300,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
For the
convenience of hon. members I have had

a memorandum printed and circulated, and I hope that every hon. member of the committee has a copy. I have endeavoured to explain the items as fully as possible, and perhaps at this late hour, and at this late period of the session it would be better for me not to make a statement, but simply to endeavour to answer any questions respecting points, which are not dealt with in this memorandum, as we go along. This particular item is one which has been voted for a number of years in capital account. It was changed this year to revenue as it was thought desirable to do so. But, that is the _ only change, a mere matter of book-keeping. The object for which the money is voted is the same as in former years, and the explanation will be found in the memorandum on page 16, namely the purchase of military stores of various kinds, armament, rifles, artillery, reserve clothing, lands, and constructing rifle ranges.
That is to be expended during the coming year?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Will that include any of the Mark II * * Ross rifles?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Is that the rifle you expect to arm the militia with?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: In part. We shall have about 80,000 of the Mark 2 rifle with the Mark 3 sight. About 30,000 are being distributed to the cadet corps throughout the country, which will leave about 50,000, which are being distributed to the troops. It js possible that the sight called the Mark 3 sight-which is not the best; there have been many improvements -may be changed to give us the latest up to date sight. We consider that rifle quite as good as any rifle, except, perhaps, the Mark II * *. It is intended to secure the manufacture of, probably, 5,000 of the Mark II * * at the earliest moment, and, later on, a still larger number. But we do not intend to throw over tihe rifles which have been manufactured; that is not necessary. In point of fact, there is practically no difference between the Mark 2 with the Mark 3 sight,, and the Mark II * *, except the length of barrel.
Is there not a difference in tlhe rifling?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There is practically no difference except in length of barrel, and the weight of barrel^ which makes the rifle about one pound heavier than the Mark 2 with the Mark 3 sight.

Is tihere any difference in the price?
271$

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: None, except that we have had to pay $12 more for the Mark II * *, because we have simply had the other rifle converted-the Mark 2 with the Mark 3 sight converted to the Mark II * *. But the company claim that they should receive more for the Mark II * *. We do not admit that, but there is means under the contract by which any difference of that kind can be settled by one expert appointed on either side, and, if they do not agree, these appointing a third.
What does the department pay apiece for the new rifle?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The price under the contract is $25.
But the new one?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I say that we pay for the conversion about $12, and we had converted some 700, I think.
Making $37 for the new rifle?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes, those that have been converted.
The Mark II** is the rifle we heard of in the early part of the session as having been issued to >a few of the members of the House. Have any more been issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We provided 500 made last year, and 200 more are being converted now, and I nlaced an order with the company for 1,000.

I refer to the discussion with regard to certain members getting rifles for the use of their constituents, the Mark II * * and I want to know whether any more members have got them. I would suggest to the Minister of Militia that all members of this House who are interested in rifle practice should have the privilege of having these rifles sent out for the use of the rifle clubs in their constituencies.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: More have been issued, and I have stated in tihe House that it was a perfectly proper thing to do. I have had a number of applications since, and shall be very glad to receive others.
From every member?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Has the minister decided what new rifle ranges should be established in Manitoba this summer?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Tihere are some places mentioned in the memorandum. I would refer the hon. gentleman to page 17-' under consideration '. That does not mean that these will all be constructed,

nor does it mean that some others may not be. We have not been able to settle on the list yet. As soon as parliament prorogues, I expect to take, that matter up with my officers of the Militia Council.
Are the rates of annual pay to the volunteers who go to camo uniform throughout the Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Would the minister tell us what they are.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The basis of the pay is 50 cents a day. There is a further sum of 50 cents for good conduct and excellence in rifle shooting. It is the same throughout the Dominion, but the pay a man receives depends upon the way he comports himself in camp.
I understand it is regulated rather by marksmanship and that good conduct does not enter into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The man who misbehaves does not get it.

There is a good deal of dissatisfaction at the camps in regard to that, arising out of the inefficient marking. As a rule the green men, the worst men in the company, are sent to the butts to do the marking, and consequently it is apt to be inaccurately done. Pay should depend in large measure upon the length of service. Marksmanship might enter into the matter, but there should be more emphasis placed on the length of service.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Great difficulty was found in the first place in ascertaining correctly the length of time an individual may have served, and there is the temptation to misrepresent. Further than that, you might have a man in camp who had attended six years, say, yet who would be unable to hit the target at fifty yards. Such a man is no good as a soldier, we do not want him. I am advised by the adjutant general and other military advisers, that, after careful note of the experience, the present plan is decidedly the best. If the system of marking is defective, that is a very serious matter. I am glad the hon. member (Mr. S. Sharpe) has called attention to it. What he has said here will be carefully read by the officers in charge, and, in any case, I should consider it my duty to bring the subject to their notice. We must see that absolute fair play is given to all the men in this matter which is so vital to them, and on which the amount of pay they receive depends.

The point referred to by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. S. Sharpe) is very important. But there is another matter which I have officially drawn to the attention of the minister. Sir FREDERICK BORDEN
and which I desire to impress upon him now. Many of the men in camp shoot at a target for the first time. They do not understand sighting the rifle, and unless some one in the regiment is detailed to see that each rifle is properly sighted before the competitor fires, he loses a round or two before he gets his elevation properly. As I pointed out to the minister in a letter some time ago, four or five of tlip best shots among the officers in a camp last year failed to qualify by reason of having rifles handed to them and having to find the sighting. Major King and Captain Farrell, of the 46 Regt. expert shots took the trouble to sight every rifle before the volunteer fired it. It was a very useful expenditure of ammunition, but it took a couple of rounds extra per man, which were provided at the expense of the regiment. The sighting is a very important matter, because none of the sights put on the rifle are absolutely accurate for the range they are sighted for. I am afraid that there is too much truth in what the hon. member for North Ontario has stated. A good many scorers are not experts, and sometimes, possibly, sufficient care is not taken with the register keepers. That will always require oversight on the part of the range officers and musketry instructors. But the rifles should be tested by one of the officers on the range to see that they are accurate. This will mean a couple of rounds extra per man, and it would be worth it to the department to provide these.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I quite agree with that.

I would like to read a resolution I have here from the municipality of Halifax:-
Moved by Councillor C. E. Smith of Sam-bro, seconded by Councillor J. V. Reno of Herring Cove.
Whereas the big gun ball and shell practice by the artillery at the forts at the entrance to Halifax harbour causes the fish to swim into deep water and prevents the mackerel from schooling on the south shore of this county and therefore deprives the fishermen living on said shores of the chances of catching these fish with their seines and nets as hex-etofore, more particularly in the vicinity of said forts.
And whereas the fisheries of our country are of great importance to this province as well as being the chief means of livelihood to hundreds of our fishermen and their families living to the south of Halifax, and every protection should be given to the toilers of the sea in prosecuting their occupation.
And whereas the said big gun practice could be done between the 30th day of November and the 15th day of June in each year, when the fisheries are of less importance to our fishermen as mackerel do not school in such quantities up to that time as they do later in the season.
Therefore resolved that the Dominion gov-

eminent be requested to make suck regulations with regard to the time of the big gun practice as will result in the least injury to the fisheries, and to the fishermen on the south shore of Halifax harbour as aforesaid.
Further resolved that a copy of this resolution be sent to the Minister of Militia of Canada, and also copies be sent to our representatives in parliament, Messrs Borden and Crosby.
I hereby certify the above to be a true and correct copy of the resolution passed by the Municipal Council of the Municipality of Halifax, Nova Scotia, on the 28th day of February, A.D., 1910.
PARKER ARCHIBALD, Municipal Clerk.
I presume that the Minister of Militia has received this resolution.
Is that from the county of Halifax or is it the city?

Yes, the county. For the benefit of those who may not understand the schooling of mackerel on our Atlantic coast, I may say that during the months of July, August and September, the mackerel school in large quantities on the surface. They run into our bays and harbours and school along the coast. But, with this heavy gun practice at the mouth of Halifax harbour, the fishermen claim the fish are disturbed and they have not the opportunity to catch the fish that they otherwise would. I have heard that the department is trying to meet the views of the fishermen. I hope the minister will see to it that their wishes are met as far as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I received a copy of the petition which the hon. member has read, direct from the municipality. My attention was also drawn to the matter by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). The question was at once referred to General Drury, who took it up with the fishermen. And I believe that an entirely satisfactory arrangement has been reached for the future.
I am glad to hear that.

So far as I know, there is no Tide Tange north of Toronto in the section in which my riding is located, that is, there is no rifle range either in the county of Simcoe or in the county of Grey. I do not wish to press upon the minister any unnecessary expenditure, but I think that possibly a couple of thousand dollars would purchase land and rig up a range that would do for the regiment there, and that possibly could be used by both the Grey and Simcoe regiments.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: At what place?

It could be around the shore of Georgian bay, in the vicinity
of Collingwood, or on the sand plains south of Collingwood. I think that a hundred acres of land could be got for, perhaps, $1,500. That is, there is waste land that could be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: A rifle range at Barrie is in the list of those proposed. That would be in that neighbourhood, I think.
I suppose that would do, but I should think it could be put further north than Barrie. If located in the place I have in mind, there would be no danger of people being shot.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I am glad to have my attention called to this. We are extremely anxious to afford all the accommodation possible. It is vital to the militia to afford the means of using the rifle at every possible point, because that is the most important part of the training of the militia. I shall be glad to look into this again with a view to seeing whether Barrie is the best point at which to place a range.
What is the minister doing with regard to cadet rifles?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: With regard to cadets, I stated before my hon. friend came in, that 30,000 of Mark II. rifles are to be issued to the cadets wherever possible. I suppose the ordinary rifle ranges will be used. The cost of constructing special ranges for the use of gallery ammunition is not very great and we will be prepared to afford the necessary expenditure to give the accommodation at every point where it seems to be justified by the numbers who are taking advantage of it.	5
Is the minister buying any sub-target guns now, and how many has he purchased?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I think there are none provided for this year. We have on hand 550. I gave to the House some time ago the points at which these sub-target guns are distributed. So soon as there is a further demand for them, I expect to ask for a vote. But we do not want to buy them until they are actually required. I think in connection with the very general cadet movement throughout the country, it is probable there will be a considerable demand for these guns at schools and colleges. They have proved to be a most useful accessory to the militia force in teaching the use of the rifle. They are looked upon as indispensable: we could not get along without them in the camps. Men who try to shoot with the rifle and fail, are given a course with the sub-target gun, then they return to the targets and make very good shooting. So I think the
. COMMONS
results have fully justified, our course in purchasing this sub-target gun. I may say that in England it is becoming more and more popular, and I think the same is true in the States.

Has the department under consideration the adoption of a new rifle in line with the rifle which the British War Office is supposed to be experimenting with at the present time? I understand they propose purchasing a rifle of about -25 to -28 calibre, and adopting a fire arm of automatic action. Now, a Canadian has the honour of inventing a rifle that has been in use in the British army for a great many years. I think the minister ought to take into consideration the advisability of offering some reward for the best invention along those lines, to stimulate the inventive mind of Canadians to produce a weapon for the British army. I think that in a few years a very modern arm will be made with an automatic rifle of 'a small calibre. The advantage is that the ammunition required is so small that a discharge can he carried over and above what is carried even with the '303 which has a small cartridge, and a soldier can carry about half as many again. Has the minister taken that into consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes. Of course we know that experiments have been carried on in England with a view to procuring possibly an automatic rifle. We are perhaps not experimenting exactly in that direction, but I have employed the services of two or three expert men in that respect, who have been engaged in the matter of perfecting the Ross rifle with great success. The question of offering a premium or a prize is worth considering. But I say in answer to my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Currie) that if a rifle is adopted by the war office which is better than, our rifle and better than theirs, I would consider it my duty to recommend that that rifle should be adopted b,y Canada; and notice given under our contract to the Ross rifle factory, that at the expiry of a certain time provided by the contract, a year I think it is, we want that rifle manufactured. They would have to do it, and it would be our duty to give them such notice.

Experiments are being carried on in England at the present time, and I may say-it is not necessary to keep the secret any longer-that we have been carrying on experiments in Canada with automatic rifles. However, I am a little conservative in this matter, and I have very little use so far for an automatic rifle. I think that the experience of riflemen the world over goes to show that it is impossible to keep up the supply of ammunition for automatic rifles in the firing Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
line. I think it would be much better to have long range machine guns with telescopic sights. In my opinion, at all events, until I see an automatic rifle that will win me over, the best rifle in the hands of the soldier would be one with, say a -280 or [DOT]285 calibre, with a high velocity of 3,000 feet per second, and with telescopic sights. If this were carried out, I am satisfied that the enemy would hesitate a long time before they would advance to any position held by men armed in this way. However, the automatic rifle seems to be the fad at present, and they are experimenting with them in various places, buti I have not yet heard that they have been successful.
What is the difference between a repeating and an automatic rifle?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I cannot say; not very much I should think.

My experience with tire automatic rifle is different from that of the hon. member (Mr. Hughes). I have used a military rifle for many years of course, and for three years I have used a sporting automatic rifle in the bush foT days and weeks and under what are equal to war conditions, and I found it not only reliable but just as simple in action as the Snider. There are always prejudices among military men, especially those who are growing older, about changes in equipment. The Duke of Wellington prevented the adopting of the repeating rifle through having laid it down that the bullet must be sufficiently large to break the leg of a horse, and if we apply that rule to-day we could not have high power rifles. Germany and Japan are adopting the automatic rifle as well as Norway and Sweden, and France and England are experimenting. Automatic rifles having proved successful for sporting purposes which is a good test, I think we should begin to consider the matter. When the -303 rifle was adopted the opinion was generally expressed by officers that it would be useless because the men would not keep it clean, but I know of four or five hundred of these rifles which have been in use for over 12 years, and fully 50 per cent of them are good for active service to-day. I have every confidence that a satisfactory automatic rifle can be obtained.
Militia annual drill, $881,250.
Will this drill the whole force?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.

I would suggest to the minister that he might curtail on certain items and increase the pay of the men. Fifty cents a day when everything is so ex-

pensive is not much inducement to a young man to join the militia.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Quite true.

There should be a minimum per day of 75 cents and the efficiency pay added, so as to attract men of better character and better education. We must make our militia more attractive to the young men if we want to get the better class into it. There has been some criticism, how well-founded it is I do not know, against the Militia Department as to the headquarters staff being too large and being over paid. If the minister can make any curtailment there and add it to the pay of the men it would meet with the approval of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I think that would be false economy, but of course it is impossible to discuss that question fully to-night. I do not think there is a dollar more paid to the staff than ought to be paid, provided the staff does its work properly. The question of increasing the pay of "the militia is well worth considering. In former days my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) brought up that question a great many times and we eventually adopted the 50 cents efficiency pay idea. I think it is our duty to throw no unnecessary obstacles in the way of the men earning the extra 50 cents efficiency pay, but rather we should make it as easy for them to do so as possible.
Mr. HUGHES And as honest and as accurate.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Certainly. I would think that all deserving men should earn the dollar per day without difficulty. We shall watch the matter closely during this season, and when we come together again we may take some action
How many on the headquarters staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: About 28.

I have long advocated increased pay to the volunteers, and I may say that I am requested to do so again. In fact, the inadequacy of the pay of the volunteers has been, I think, my only criticism with regard to the Militia Department. I do not see why the minister should hesitate to give the men something more than they are getting now.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The statute limits us, and we would have to amend it to increase the pay.

Then I think I may say that parliament will amend that statute just as soon as the minister brings down the Bill. I believe the sentiment of the House and of the country is in favour of
giving our militiamen a little more pay than they are getting now. It is unreasonable to expect men to leave employment at $1 or $2 a day to go to camp for 50 cents. If you increase the pay a little, I am sure you will get a better class of men, and I would ask the minister to consider the propriety of doing so.

I am not going to advocate a decrease in the pay of the men, but I am going to advocate an increase in the pay of training officers. The only system of training that has been successful in this or any other country is to train the officers as cadets and let them take their place in the ranks as privates, corporals and sergeants, and holding their certificates, work their way up to the command. Then we could select our officers from the men who in subordinate positions had proven their efficiency. The record shows that the increased pay has not brought out a better class of men; indeed,
I verily believe that we have not as good a class of men in the militia now as we had when we had well trained officers and the men were paid only 50 cents a day. What you want is efficient and energetic officers in the regiments who will inspire enthusiasm in the men. I know one company in my own regiment in which the assessed value of the property held by the young men and their fathers was over $3,000 each, and that was common in the old davs when the pay was only 50 cents, and when the officers were efficient and enthusiastic for the service. The chief inducement to a young man now to go to camp is: Come along and if you make good shooting you will get the increased pay. That is not the way to build up a militia force. A militia force must be a patriotic force. Many regiments, city corps and some rural corps, never touch their pay, they turn it into a fund for other purposes, and I am satisfied that what is wanted is to see that the officers are trained and well trained, and that each company is equipped with officers and non-commissioned officers capable of putting spirit into the men and of leading them on the camp field or in action.

If you compare the militia list of to-day with the militia list of twenty years ago, you will find as many qualified officers now as then and more. However, the young man who takes a commission in a militia regiment is put to a large expense, probably $250 for qualifying and uniforming himself. In Great Britain formerly they granted to each volunteer officer to assist in paying for his uniform twenty to twenty-five guineas. Then to-day the militia uniforms have to pay duty, running $30 or $35. If officers who qualified themselves at a school or military instruction were given an allowance towards pro-

viding their uniforms, in two years there would not be a single unit in the country that would not have well qualified, and efficient officers. The pay given officers white attending the schools is really not sufficient to meet their expenses. The social advantages obtained by taking a commission are not great. The officers all over the country give their services, they do not expect pay for them, in fact they invariably fund their pay, and I think it would be highly desirable to adopt some plan as I have suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The suggestion is a very good one, and I agree with my bon. friend that the allowance to officers attending schools of instruction is ridiculously small. I found it there when I came into office. I was discussing it the other day with one of the staff, and I think a change should be made.
Has the minister inquired into the system of messing, and the general mode of living in barracks?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
We are doing that now.
Mr. HUGHES Proper supervision should be exercised even over officers high in the permanent corps in connection with mess rooms, &e., at the schools. Office^ should be taught also that their chief function is to educate those attending the schools along military lines, and not along social or other lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There is sufficient supervision now. I think, we can scarcely remove the duty on officers' clothing, and I see no reason why uniforms should not be made in Canada, although of course the price would be greater. I agree that the better way out of the difficulty is to give some special allowance for uniforms, and I feel disposed to do that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I wish to call attention to the case of a messenger who was employed in the Auditor General's office. He had been there about ten years, and although technically a temporary officer he was virtually permanent in the same sense as many men in the service, until the passing of the recent Act. He went to South Africa, fought in the war, and his position seemed to have been exactly the same as that of other men who received full pay during their absence, and were reinstated in their positions as soon as they returned. For example, I understand, that his case is exactly the same as that of Cawdron of the Justice Department and Ross of the Dominion Police. He was not reinstated and remained idle for nine months. He lost the continuity of his service, certain statu- | tory increases, and his pay for the nine

months during which he was absent, and his pay from the department white he was in South Africa, Certainly in their case there was no delay after they returned. They were reinstated at once, as I am informed, in the positions which they had left to go to South Africa. I do not see why there should be any discrimination in the case of this man.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I may say that this man was employed by the Auditor General, and he refused to reinstate him. My hon. friend from Victoria and Hal'-burton brought this case to my notice the other day, and I read all the papers relating to it, and I cannot see in what respect the Militia Department could have any responsibility in the matter at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not say that it has, except that the order in council under which some of these men were re-instated in their positions and received their pay was made on a report of the Minister of Militia and Defence. It seems, therefore, proper to bring it to his attention now.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That was as to the service; but we could not change the rule. The Auditor General insisted on the letter of the rule being followed, and as he employed this man in his department, when he raised that difficulty we could do nothing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have been informed that the present Auditor General takes a different view of it. I do not see why one department of the government should take a different view. The government ought to come to some conclusion about these men. There should be one rule for all and no discrimination. I am informed that there has not been the same rule for all, and that there has been discrimination. If that is so, it ought to be rectified.

I might point out to the minister that this matter was up years ago. The Auditor General employed this man, and he declined to recommend him for reinstatement, and I presume that the minister took for granted that that settled the case. I wrote to the minister the other day, calling his attention to the fact that Cawdron and Ross had both received their gratuities, although they served under the same conditons as young Cottee. In the same way the friends of two or three men who died on their way to South Africa have received gratuities while the friends of others who died have been refused them. There should be even-handed justice all round.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister, I hope, will look into this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I really do not see that I have anything to do with

it; but I shall be glad to take it up and see who is the proper officer to deal with it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has the attention of the Minister of Finance been called to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I remember that there was a young man of that name, and my recollection is that he was a temporary employee, and that when he returned his services were not needed. Hpwever, I have only a hazy recollection of the facts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He may have been a temporary employee, as other men, who have been in the service of the government fcr 25 or 30 years, are technically called temporary employees. It is useless to consider these men as in a different position from permanent men in the service, because in honesty and common sense they are not. They are called temporary employees in the statute, but in reality they are permanent employees. This man, I am informed, had been 10 years in the service of the department before he went to Africa. It is idle to talk of that man as a temporary employee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hardly think that is right. There are two classes of temporary employees-the permanent temporary, if one may call them so, and the temporary temporary. There are men who are technically temporary employees, but have been in a department a great many years. Then there are the bona fide temporary employees who are only employed for a short time. I understood that this man belonged to the latter class.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I will read this memorandum in more detail than I have done :
Prior to his South African service he had been in the employ of the government for ten years. He had applied in the usual way for leave of absence to serve his country in the war in South Africa. He served in the 6th Regiment Canadian Mounted Rifles. On his return he reported for duty and was told that his position had been filled, as the work could not wait, and for nine months after his return he had no regular or steady employment.
We know that even private corporations kept positions open for men who went to South Africa to fight in that war, and I think it would be very petty for the government to adopt a different principle.
Militia and defence - engineer services, $.300,000.
Mr..S. SHARPE. There is an increase of $25,000. Will the minister explain the necessity of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The increase is simply returning to the normal vote.
We had to cut down the vote last year owing to the shrinkage of the revenue, and we are putting it back where it was.
Grant to 65th regiment for armoury, $50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This is to assist in the construction of a large armoury, the government paying one-half. That has been done in two or three cases, and we think it is a very advisable thing to do in the city of Montreal.
Grant to 5th regiment for armoury, $15,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is the same thing, the balance of our contribution.

I would like to urge upon the hon. minister the desirability of considering, where the Department of Public Works is erecting a post office or customs building, of placing the headquarters of the militia company, if there should be a company, in the building, and of providing an armoury for the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: In the same building?

Yes, say in tlhe basement of the building. There has. been an appropriation for a post office in the town of Uxbridge, and there is no reason why an armoury should not be constructed in the basement of the building. It would save the officers paying the expense of rental. I would strongly urge the minister to have that done. The Minister of Public Works stated the other night that he had had tlhe matter under consideration, and thought favourably of the idea.
It would be even better to have it in the rear of the building where the boys could have miniature rifle practice, and where the arms could be stored.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Where there is one company, or even two companies the suggestion made by my hon. friend (Mr. Sharpe) would be a very good one. It. is being carried out in one or two cases. I think there is a case in the eastern townships, >and I think there are one or two others. I will be very glad to take it up with the Minister of Public Works, for 1 believe it would be an economical arrangement, and it would help us to get armouries more quickly than in any other way.
There are one or two in New Brunswick.
I think it is very unfair that officers should have to pay rental for an armoury out of their own pocket.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There is a special allowance.
Yes, but it is only a small sum, not sufficient to cover the rent of an armoury. I think it is unfair to the officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Of course the old practice was in the rural district for the captain to provide a room in his own house, or to take some outbuilding, and then the $60, or whatever the allowance is was given to him to pay somebody to keep the arms and the clothing in order. That was the origin of the provision many years ago, and it has worked fairly well. Perhaps the country is outgrowing that system, and we have got to adopt a better and a more expensive one.

A few years ago in Uxbridge we had a building and in one room we kept the stores, and we used it for drill, but the department took all the stores to the regimental town of Whitby, and took away our armoury. _ Now, I think this is a splendid opportunity for the minister. Uxbridge is a suitable town to have a good company headquarters in, and I trust the minister will favour the idea of providing an armoury in conjunction with the post office.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I do.
Gratuities, $6,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I want to reduce that amount by $4,000.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The intension was to pay a gratuity to Colonel White, but it has turned out as a result of the amendment to the Pension Act that he
is entitled to a small pension by counting time he served in the active militia, so that the gratuity will not be necessary.
There was a gratuity to an officer in my corps who caught disease in Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Henderson?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That is to be paid. The gratuity is to be $1,000 and it will be paid.
Maintainance of military properties, $80,000.

I would like to make my annual request for a drill hall in the town' of Minnedosa.	'
' Mr. BLAIN. Is it not in the supplemen-taries?

I have failed to see it in the supplementaries. For a number of years I have been urging the minister to construct in my town a drill hall. We have a number of enthusiastic young men there who have banded themselves together and Sir FREDERICK BORDEN
have a very good company of dragoons. They have carried away first prizes in competitions at the annual drills, but they have not a suitable place for the storing of the government arms. They constructed a frame building at their own expense, but unfortunately that building was burned this winter, and the stores, saddles, bridles and other accoutrements were consumed. I do not know whether there was any insurance on the property or not. I presume a request has been sent in for a new supply. I heard that the town council had been looking for a site which they would be willing to tender to the government in order to secure a drill hall. I think it1 rather petty that the government would ask them to furnish a site. It is.a comparatively small town with 1,700 of a population, and the price of property is comparatively low. Some intimation must have come to them, but if the government will not give a drill hall on other grounds they are willing to give the site. I would strongly urge the minister to give a drill hall to that town. They are very much." disappointed and discouraged that they have not one, especially seeing that it was partially promised some years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Roche) has brought the matter to my notice more than once. If there was any correspondence with the town council in Tegard to a site, it must have been with the Department of Public Works. I have no knowledge of anything of the kind emanating from my department. There is a general vote for the construction of armouries, and it is not necessary that the place should be named in the estimates. *
I was told that six yearsi ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think the misfortune which our militia friends there have met with in the loss of their building fortifies their claim to have something done, and we will see whether we cannot do something this year.

I wish to bring to the attention of the hon. minister the need for an armoury at Digby. There is now, as the minister knows, a battery of artillery, and they are very seriously handicapped for lack of a suitable place to store their accoutrements. I understand there are likely to be some guns placed there, and with the added interest which is being taken in the battery, I would like to see better facilities afforded the men. I trust the minister will provide the necessary grant.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
We will either have to construct a suitable build-, ing or rent one in three or four of thet

towns in Nova Scotia where the heavy artillery has its headquarters. Yarmouth, I think, is one place, Digby, Pictou and Mahone bay are other places. They are all under consideration, and we will have to provide a proper place for the storage of these expensive guns and equipment.
Then the matter is receiving the consideration of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Yes, but I am not saying whether we shall rent a suitable building or build one. That will depend upon the money at our disposal.
Pay, allowances, provisions and supplies of the permanent force, $1,950,000.

In connection with the headquarters staff and the district staff, it has been the custom for many years to issue a sort of syllabus from time to time for the camps of instruction, prepared, I presume, by some clerk in the department, and these are supposed to form the routine for the instruction in camp. I need not say to any one who has had any experience with them, that those sent out are utterly absurd. The department should undoubtedly prescribe the sections and subjects to be taken up in camp and in which the volunteers should be proficient, but it should toe left to the discretion of the officer in command of the camp to prepare his own routine. Where you are out for twelve days camping, and have officers who are supposed to know their business, it is quite out of place to issue such a syllabus.
Salaries and wages of civil employees, $155,000.

I think the minister has adopted a good plan in issuing a memorandum explaining the estimates. Unfortunately it has not been issued soon enough to be of much service to us. I desire to register a protest against allowing the estimates to stand until this_ late day in the session, near Sunday morning, when we are putting through several million dollars without examination and criticism. The members cannot do themselves justice, nor the public justice, under those circumstances. If that memorandum had been issued earlier in the session we would have been better able to study it. This item, and a previous item for paying allowances at headquarters to command and district staffs, seem to be large amounts in connection with our militia affairs, they seem to be out of all proportion to the number cf men we have on the permanent staff. It seems to me the staff is overcrowded. I cannot understand why we should require so much expense at the headquarters staff and so many civil employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The explanation with regard to civil employees is to be found here. The small increase is due to the fact that certain things that were done by the Public WoTks are taken over by the Militia Department. As regards the staff, it is altogether too late to discuss that question. But I agree entirely with my hon. friend that it would be much more desirable that these estimates should be discussed earlier in the session. I expected that would be done, and this memorandum was prepared in the month of December. It was not issued, because I thought it would be better to issue it only two or three days before taking up my estimates in the House, and it was issued the day before yesterday. I hope next session we will be able to take the matter up earlier, and I think I will be able to prove to my hon. friend, who is himself ai militia man, the absolute necessity of having a large and efficient headquarters staff. I think I can demonstrate to him that our staff is less expensive, even taking into consideration the relative strength of our militia, than is the staff of Switzerland, whose militia is, of course, ahead of the world. There is no other force in the world that, for cheapness and efficiency, caq be compared with the militia of Switzerland. In a memorandum that I laid before parliament two years ago, I demonstrated that fact beyond doubt; and I had the advantage of laying before the House a carefully prepared memorandum made by General Lake, which entirely supported the view I have presented. I hope at some other time to have an opportunity of discussing this matter more fully.
How does the minister explain the large increase of $75,000 in salaries and wages to civil employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
$17,000 is taken over from the Public Works, and $39,706 which was' paid out of clothing vote, is put into this vote. So the only 'difference 'consists in certain new appointments, and increasing the rate of wages, $7,800.
Topographical survey, $30,000.
Speaking of the general staff, how many members of that general staff are supposed to be in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Five I think. We change them from time to time.
Are they elected on account of any general fitness?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
They must all have passed the staff college, that is their only recommendation. As I explained to the House a few days ago in connection with the Royal Military College, we have

brought out an officer to take charge of the Royal Military College, and two persons who are specially qualified to be members of the general staff. General Lake and General Otter are members of that staff.
Monuments to battlefields - amount required towards the erection of a monument to commemorate the battle of Stoney Creek- revote, $5,000.

I desire to draw the minister's attention to a matter which I had the honour of speaking to him about a few days ago. In the county I represent, in the township of Nelson, on Lake Ontario, there is a small graveyard in which are buried some of those who took part, I am informed, in the battle of Stoney Creek, Queenston Heights, Lundy's Lane, and also at Detroit. The graveyard has been practically abandoned for over forty years, and the descendants of those old warriors who were, buried there seem to have all passed away or left that section of the country, and there is no one to look after this old cemetery. It is the desire of the people living in that neighbouring that it should be cared for in some way, and I think it is fitting, when the minister is asking a sum in connection with the battlefield of Stoney Creek, that something should be done to commemorate the memory of those who fought for their country and who lie buried in this old graveyard. I hope the minister will take the matter into consideration. The old graveyard is 80 yards long and 30 yards broad and it would not cost much to build a wall round it to protect it from desecration. I hope the minister will meet the wishes of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I shall be very glad to look into the matter.

I call the attention of the minister to the conditions with reference to Fort Malden on the Detroit river. From that point issued the expedition under General Brock that captured Detroit, and so it is an epoch making land mark in our country. I understand Fort Malden is now owned by private parties and is being laid out for town lots so that in a few years that famous spot will disappear from the ken of the public. Fort Malden is just as worthy of preservation as Fort George or any other of the historic places along the frontier. Mr. Clarke of Essex and I have received communications from parties interested in having the land at Fort Malden taken over by the government. I hope the minister will see what can be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I shall be very glad to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence

speechtext: Where is the monument'to be erected at Stoney Creek?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Where the battle was fought, I think.
What is the cost to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think it is to cost $10,000, and we are contributing one-half.
Is the government contributing to the Laura Secord memorial?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a contribution to the association.
Is the government grant on condition that the memorial should be in the form of a monument?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is in the hands of the association, but I believe the monument is being erected.
I have had correspondence at the beginning of the session with a lady who is in charge of that, and she understood then that no provision was made for a contribution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have given direction that the amount should be paid before the close of the present fiscal year, and I think the matter has been arranged satisfactorily.
These people are not in my county, but I have promised them to do what I could in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will find it is satisfactory.
The prevailing opinion now is that it would be better to erect a memorial hall rather than a monument. Is the government insisting that it should take the form of a monument?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My recollection is that the proposal made was for the erection of a monument and that we granted aid to that. I do not think we have imposed any condition that it should be a monument.
If those interested change their idea and decide on erecting a memorial hall rather than a monument, I hope the government will not insist that their original request -be adhered to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the monument, if not constructed is under contract.
I do not think it is, because it is only this session I was asked to advocate this with the Minister of Militia.
Is it the intention of the government to give a grant to the memorial tower at Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think there is a vote in the estimates for that.
Some resolutions reported.

Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.

speechtext: What business will be taken up on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MESSAGE FROM THE GOVERNOR GENERAL-SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES.
speechtext: Private Bills, and when we reach government orders all the resolutions that stand on the order paper will be taken up in their turn.
